lessons.plain: Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure Active Directory) is Microsoft's cloud directory: one list of who people are and how they sign in to Azure and Microsoft 365. Creating a user adds a person's sign-in account to that list. Creating a group bundles users so you can give access once instead of person by person. Think of a building's front desk. Each employee gets a badge (a user). Badges are placed on lists like 'Finance floor' (a group), and a door checks the list rather than every individual. Adding someone to the list opens the right doors.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company has 40 people in Finance who all need the same access, and staff join or leave Finance every month. Would you rather add each person to the access by hand, or have them land in a shared list automatically based on their job details? What could go wrong with the automatic way?
lessons.teach:
A user in Microsoft Entra ID is an identity that can sign in. A cloud-only user is created directly in Entra ID. A synchronized user is copied from an on-premises Active Directory by a sync tool (Entra Connect) and is mostly edited at the source, not in the cloud. Every user has a user principal name (UPN), the sign-in name in email format, such as ana@contoso.com. The part after @ must be either the tenant's default onmicrosoft.com domain or a custom domain you have verified. The tenant is your organization's own copy of Entra ID. You can create users one at a time in the portal or upload many at once from a CSV (comma-separated values) file, which is bulk create.

A group collects users, and sometimes devices. There are two group types. A security group is used to grant access to resources and apps. A Microsoft 365 group adds collaboration features like a shared mailbox and calendar. Each group also has a membership type. Assigned means an admin adds members by hand. Dynamic user or dynamic device means a rule, written against attributes such as department, adds and removes members automatically. Dynamic groups need an Entra ID P1 or P2 licence, a paid feature tier.

Worked example. You create a security group, Finance-Staff, as dynamic user with the rule user.department -eq "Finance". You create Ana with department set to Finance. Entra ID evaluates the rule, sees a match, and adds Ana. Any access granted to the group now reaches her. Later her department changes to Sales. The rule no longer matches, so she is removed and loses that access without anyone acting.

Common mistake: trying to add a person by hand to a dynamic group. It cannot be done, because the rule alone controls membership. Fix the attribute instead. A typo in the rule, such as "Finanse", leaves the group empty and silently denies access to everyone relying on it.

questions.prompt: Northwind Clinic has a security group called Ward-Nurses with the membership type dynamic user and the rule user.jobTitle -eq "Nurse". The group grants access to a shift-scheduling app. Step 1: The admin creates a new user, Omar, with jobTitle set to Nurse. Entra ID evaluates the rule, finds a match, and adds Omar, so he can open the app. Step 2: The admin creates another user, Lena, with jobTitle set to "Staff Nurse". The rule does not match, so Lena is not a member and cannot open the app. Step 3: MISSING. Step 4: Entra ID re-evaluates the same, unchanged rule against Lena, finds a match, adds her to Ward-Nurses, and she can now open the app. What did the admin do in Step 3?
choices: Changed Lena's jobTitle attribute from "Staff Nurse" to "Nurse"
Converted Ward-Nurses from a security group into a Microsoft 365 group
Opened Ward-Nurses and added Lena as a member by hand
Deleted Lena and re-created her through bulk create from a CSV file
questions.why: In a dynamic group only the rule controls membership, so with the rule unchanged the fix is to correct the user's attribute so it matches the rule.

questions.prompt: Tailspin's tenant has the default domain tailspintoys.onmicrosoft.com and one verified custom domain, tailspin.com. The company also owns tailspin.org, but it has not been verified in Entra ID. An admin is creating a cloud-only user named Raj. Which user principal name (UPN) can the admin assign?
choices: raj@tailspin.com
raj@gmail.com
raj
raj@tailspin.org
questions.why: The part of a UPN after the @ must be the tenant's default onmicrosoft.com domain or a verified custom domain, and tailspin.com is the only choice that meets this rule.

questions.prompt: A project team at Adatum needs a shared mailbox and a shared calendar. The team lead wants an admin to choose the five members personally rather than have them chosen by a rule. Which group type and membership type fit this need?
choices: Security group with dynamic user membership
Microsoft 365 group with dynamic device membership
Microsoft 365 group with assigned membership
Security group with assigned membership
questions.why: A Microsoft 365 group adds collaboration features such as a shared mailbox and calendar, and assigned membership means an admin adds the members by hand.

questions.prompt: At Wingtip, an admin creates a dynamic user security group with the rule user.department -eq "Engeneering". The rule is meant to match the department value "Engineering". The group is then used to grant access to a build server. What happens?
choices: Entra ID blocks the group from being saved until the typo is fixed
The group stays empty, and every engineer relying on it is silently denied access to the build server
Entra ID corrects the spelling and adds all Engineering users automatically
The admin can still add the engineers by hand to fill the group
questions.why: The misspelled value matches no one's department, so the rule adds no members, and anyone who depends on the group loses access without any warning.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would set up users and a group for a team whose staff change often, and name one tradeoff of using dynamic membership instead of assigned membership.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd create each person as a cloud user in Entra ID, with a UPN on our verified domain, or bulk-create them from a CSV if there are many. Then I'd make a security group, because we want it to control access, not to share a mailbox. Since people join and leave often, I'd use dynamic user membership with a rule like department equals Finance. Entra ID adds and removes members as their attributes change, so access follows the HR data. The tradeoff is that the group is only as accurate as the attributes. A wrong department value or a typo in the rule can quietly add the wrong people or leave the group empty. I also can't add an exception by hand, and dynamic groups need a P1 or P2 licence. Assigned groups give exact control but need manual upkeep.
rubricPoints: Users are sign-in identities created in Entra ID, either cloud-only or synchronized from on-premises.
A UPN must use a verified domain or the default onmicrosoft.com domain.
Security groups grant access, while Microsoft 365 groups add collaboration features.
Assigned membership is manual, while dynamic membership follows attribute-based rules.
Dynamic groups depend on accurate attributes, allow no manual adds, and need a P1 or P2 licence.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine works in an identity directory, so the skill is best built by reasoning through exam-style scenarios that ask you to choose a user source, group type and membership type.

lessons.plain: Every person and every group in Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft's cloud directory of identities, carries a set of descriptive details called properties. For a user these include a name, sign-in name, job title, department, manager, and whether sign-in is allowed. For a group they include its type, its owners, and how members get in. Think of a staff ID card plus the HR file behind it. Keeping those details accurate matters because other systems read them to decide who belongs where and who can do what. Managing properties means editing them safely, one at a time or in bulk.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a group automatically includes everyone whose department is listed as Sales. If HR changes one person's department to Marketing, what do you think happens to that person's access to the files shared with the Sales group?
lessons.teach:
A user property is a named field on a user object in Microsoft Entra ID, the directory that stores accounts. Common ones are display name (what people see), user principal name or UPN (the sign-in name, shaped like an email address), job title, department, manager, usage location (the country the user mainly works in), and account enabled, the switch that blocks or allows sign-in. Blocking sign-in stops new logins without deleting the account or its data.

A group property describes a group, which is a named collection of identities. Group type is either security (used to grant access to resources) or Microsoft 365 (adds a shared mailbox, calendar and files). Membership type is assigned, where an administrator adds members by hand, or dynamic, where a rule, a condition written against user properties, adds and removes members automatically. Owners are people allowed to manage the group without being full administrators. Dynamic membership needs a premium Entra ID licence tier (P1 or above).

Why this matters: properties are data that other controls consume. A dynamic rule reads them continuously, so editing a property can change group membership, and group membership often decides access.

Worked example. A dynamic security group has the rule user.department equals "Sales". Step one: Priya's department is Sales, so the rule matches and she is a member. Step two: the Sales group is given read access to a storage account. Step three: HR updates Priya's department to Marketing. Step four: the directory re-evaluates the rule, it no longer matches, and Priya is removed. Step five: she loses access to that storage account, with no one touching the group directly.

Common mistake: trying to add a person manually to a dynamic group. You cannot; you must fix the property the rule reads, or use an assigned group instead. A related slip is a typo like "sales " with a trailing space, which silently drops users. For many changes at once, the portal offers bulk operations driven by an uploaded file, which reduces hand-editing errors.

questions.prompt: A regional hospital has a dynamic security group in Microsoft Entra ID with the rule user.department equals "Radiology". Step 1: Marco works in Pharmacy, so the rule does not match and he is not a member. Step 2: The Radiology group is given access to a file share holding scan images. Step 3: Marco transfers, and HR changes his department property to Radiology. Step 4: (missing). Step 5: Marco can now open the scan-image file share, even though nobody edited the group directly. Which statement correctly fills Step 4?
choices: Marco's account is blocked and then re-enabled, which forces his group memberships to refresh.
An administrator adds Marco to the Radiology group by hand so the new department takes effect.
A group owner approves Marco's request to join, and only then does the rule start to apply to him.
The directory re-evaluates the rule, finds that Marco's department now matches, and adds him automatically.
questions.why: A dynamic rule reads user properties continuously, so once Marco's department matches "Radiology" the directory adds him without anyone touching the group.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's contractor finishes a project tomorrow. The manager wants to stop the contractor from signing in to anything right away, but must keep the account and its files in case they are needed for an audit. Which user property change does this?
choices: Delete the user account from Microsoft Entra ID.
Clear the usage location so the account has no country.
Change the user principal name to a new sign-in name.
Turn off the account enabled setting to block sign-in.
questions.why: Account enabled is the switch that allows or blocks sign-in, and blocking stops new logins without deleting the account or its data.

questions.prompt: An accounting firm creates a dynamic security group for its 40 finance staff, whose department property is Finance. A week later the group still shows zero members, and access to a finance database fails for everyone. The rule is user.department equals "Finance ". What is the most likely cause?
choices: Security groups cannot be granted access to databases, only Microsoft 365 groups can.
The staff need a manager property set before any dynamic rule can include them.
The rule value has a trailing space, so it does not match "Finance" and silently excludes everyone.
Dynamic groups only fill up after an administrator adds the first member by hand.
questions.why: A rule is matched exactly against the property, so a typo like a trailing space silently drops every user whose department is spelled correctly.

questions.prompt: A design studio's project team wants one group that gives them a shared mailbox, a shared calendar and shared files. Their team lead, who is not an administrator, must be able to manage the group. What should be created?
choices: A Microsoft 365 group with the team lead added as an ordinary member.
A security group with the team lead set as an owner.
A Microsoft 365 group with the team lead set as an owner.
A dynamic security group whose rule matches the team lead's job title.
questions.why: Microsoft 365 groups add the shared mailbox, calendar and files, and owners can manage a group without being full administrators.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how editing a user's properties in Entra ID can change what that user can access, and name one limit or tradeoff of using dynamic groups instead of assigned groups.
lessons.modelAnswer: Users in Entra ID have properties such as department, job title, manager, usage location, and whether sign-in is enabled. Groups have properties too: a type (security for granting access, or Microsoft 365 for collaboration), owners, and a membership type. With assigned membership an admin adds people by hand. With dynamic membership a rule reads user properties, for example department equals Sales, and keeps the member list up to date automatically. Because access is often granted to groups, changing a single property like department can add or remove someone from a group and therefore grant or remove access, without anyone editing the group. The tradeoff is that dynamic groups save manual work but depend entirely on clean directory data: a typo or a late HR update silently changes access, you cannot hand-add exceptions, and the feature needs a premium licence tier.
rubricPoints: Names several user properties such as department, UPN, manager and account enabled.
Distinguishes security from Microsoft 365 groups and assigned from dynamic membership.
Explains that dynamic rules read user properties, so property edits change membership and access.
States a limit: no manual members in dynamic groups, reliance on accurate data, or premium licence requirement.
Mentions blocking sign-in stops logins without deleting the account.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing the right property or membership type in a scenario, so reasoning through situations like a department change cutting off access teaches it best.

lessons.plain: A license in Microsoft Entra ID (Microsoft's cloud directory of users and groups) is a paid permission slip that switches on a cloud product, such as email or advanced security features, for one specific user. Your organization buys a pool of these slips, and an administrator hands them out. Think of a gym that bought 50 memberships: each member needs a card before the doors open for them, and when the cards run out, nobody new gets in. Managing licenses means handing out cards, choosing which parts of a product each person may use, and taking cards back when people leave.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company bought 50 licenses for an office product and has 200 staff who join and leave often. Would you rather assign each license to people one at a time, or attach the license to a group so members get it automatically? What could go wrong with each approach?
lessons.teach:
A license plan (also called a product or SKU, a stock-keeping unit) is a product your organization bought, such as Microsoft 365 E3, with a fixed number of seats. Each plan bundles several service plans, which are the individual features inside it, like a mailbox service or a chat service. You can switch individual service plans off for a user while still giving them the rest of the product.

There are two ways to assign licenses. Direct assignment gives a license to one user. Group-based licensing attaches a license to a security group, so every member receives it automatically and loses it when removed from the group. Group-based licensing needs a paid Entra ID tier, such as Entra ID P1, or a product that includes it. It works because membership changes, which you already manage, drive licensing for you.

Before any license can be applied, the user must have a usage location, which is the country where they will use the service. Some services are not available in every country, so Entra refuses the license without it.

Worked example: Contoso owns 50 E3 seats. The admin assigns E3 to the group Sales-Licensed, leaving the chat service plan switched off. Ana is added to the group. Her license shows an error because her usage location is blank. The admin sets her usage location to France and asks Entra to reprocess the group. Ana now has E3 without the chat service, and 49 seats remain.

A common mistake is assuming group licensing always succeeds. It can fail when seats run out, when the usage location is missing, or when two plans conflict, and these failures appear only as errors on the group's license page, so admins must check it.

In a running system, removing a license (or removing someone from a licensed group) cuts off their access to that service, and after a grace period the service's data, such as a mailbox, can be deleted.

questions.prompt: Tailspin Toys owns 12 seats of a license plan (a purchased product with a fixed number of seats). The admin attaches it to the security group Design-Licensed, so the plan is assigned through group-based licensing. Twelve designers are already members and all 12 seats are in use. Every designer has a usage location (the country where they use the service) set. Step 1: Raj, a new designer, is added to Design-Licensed. Step 2: The admin opens the group's license page and sees an error next to Raj because no seats are left. Step 3: ??? Step 4: The admin asks Entra to reprocess the group, and Raj receives the license. What is the missing Step 3?
choices: Make a seat available, either by buying more seats or by removing a license from someone who no longer needs it
Give Raj the same license by direct assignment, which does not count against the 12 purchased seats
Set Raj's usage location again, because a seat error always means the country field is wrong
Switch off one service plan inside the product for Raj so that his assignment uses fewer seats
questions.why: The error is caused by running out of seats, so a seat must be freed or bought before reprocessing can succeed; turning off service plans or switching to direct assignment still uses a whole seat.

questions.prompt: Woodgrove Bank wants its tellers to have every feature of a productivity product except its video-meeting feature. In Entra ID terms, what is that video-meeting feature, and what can the admin do with it?
choices: It is a separate license plan, so the admin must buy a cheaper product that leaves it out
It is a service plan, one of the individual features inside the product, and it can be switched off for those users
It is a security group, so the admin removes the tellers from that group to disable the feature
It is a usage location setting, so the admin hides it by changing the tellers' country
questions.why: A license plan bundles several service plans, and individual service plans can be turned off for a user while the rest of the product stays assigned.

questions.prompt: Northwind Health wants new nurses to get their software license automatically when HR adds them to the Nurses security group, and to lose it when they leave the group. Their tenant currently has only the free Entra ID tier. What must be true before they can use this approach?
choices: Every nurse must first be given the license by direct assignment, one person at a time
The Nurses group must have a usage location set on the group itself instead of on each user
Each nurse must have every service plan in the product switched on
They need a paid Entra ID tier such as Entra ID P1, or a product that includes it
questions.why: Group-based licensing, where group membership drives license assignment, requires a paid Entra ID tier like P1 or a product that includes it.

questions.prompt: At Litware, Mei is removed from the security group Finance-Licensed, which grants her a product that includes a mailbox service. She has no other assignment of that license. What happens to her mailbox?
choices: Her mailbox is moved immediately to another member of Finance-Licensed to free the seat
She keeps access until her usage location is cleared, because the country controls the license
She loses access to the mailbox, and after a grace period its data can be deleted
Nothing changes; licenses assigned through a group stay with the user permanently once applied
questions.why: Leaving a licensed group removes the license, which cuts off access to the service, and after a grace period the service's data, such as a mailbox, can be deleted.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would license a 200-person department in Entra ID, why you picked that method, and name one limit or way it can fail.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would use group-based licensing: put the department in a security group and assign the license plan, say Microsoft 365 E3, to that group. Anyone added gets the license automatically, and anyone removed loses it, so joiners and leavers are handled through membership instead of 200 manual assignments. I can also switch off service plans inside the product, like the chat service, for the whole group at once. The tradeoffs: group-based licensing requires a paid tier such as Entra ID P1, and assignments can quietly fail. If we run out of seats, if a user has no usage location set, or if two plans conflict, that user shows an error on the group instead of getting the license. So I would check the group's license errors regularly, fix the cause, and reprocess. Removing someone also cuts their service access, and their data can be lost after a grace period.
rubricPoints: Defines a license plan as a purchased product with a limited number of seats that enables services for a user.
Distinguishes direct assignment from group-based licensing driven by group membership.
Mentions that service plans inside a product can be disabled individually.
States that a usage location must be set before a license applies.
Names a failure or limit such as running out of seats, conflicts, missing usage location, or the paid tier requirement.
Notes that removing a license cuts access and may lead to data loss after a grace period.

suggested.rationale: No existing mission or planned engine covers directory licensing, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios like a failed group license caused by a missing usage location or exhausted seats builds the most useful skill.

lessons.plain: A guest user is someone from outside your organization who gets a sign-in to your Microsoft Entra ID directory (Microsoft's cloud identity service, formerly Azure AD) so they can work with your resources. Think of a visitor badge at an office. The contractor keeps their own ID card from their own company, and your front desk prints a badge that lets them into certain rooms. In Entra ID, the outsider keeps their own account and password from home. Your directory only holds a pointer to them, marked as a guest, and you decide what that badge opens and when it stops working.
lessons.guessPrompt: A partner company's consultant needs to read files in one of your Azure storage accounts for two months. Would you create a brand-new account with a password you hand them, or let them sign in with the account they already have? What could go wrong with each choice?
lessons.teach:
An external (guest) user is an account in your Entra ID tenant that stands for a person whose real identity lives somewhere else. A tenant is your organization's own instance of Entra ID. The other place could be another company's Entra ID, a Microsoft account, Google, or a one-time email passcode. This arrangement is called B2B collaboration (business-to-business). The account carries a property called UserType set to Guest rather than Member. Guests get more limited default rights to browse the directory.

Why it works: the guest authenticates at their home provider, so you never store or reset their password. When they leave their own company, their home account is disabled and their access to you stops with it.

Worked example. First, an administrator, or anyone holding the Guest Inviter role, opens Users and chooses Invite external user, entering ana@partner.com. Second, Entra ID creates a guest object and sends an invitation email. Third, Ana clicks the link and redeems it. Redeeming means she signs in with her partner account and accepts consent, and the guest object changes from pending to accepted. Fourth, the administrator assigns Ana the Storage Blob Data Reader role on the storage account, or adds her to a group that holds that role. Only now can she read files.

You control guests through External collaboration settings. These decide who may invite: admins only, members, or even guests. They also set how much guests can see in the directory, and they hold an allow or deny list of email domains you can invite from. Where it is licensed, an access review is a scheduled check where owners confirm each guest still needs access. Use it to remove stale guests.

Common mistake: assuming the invitation itself grants access. A guest with no role or group membership can sign in but can reach nothing. The opposite risk is worse in a running system: guests who are never reviewed or deleted keep working access long after the project ends.

questions.prompt: Tailspin Toys has set its External collaboration settings to allow invitations only from an allow list of two domains: fabrikam.com and northwind.com. A team member now needs a freelance designer, mia@studio.io, to help with a project. Step 1: The team member, who is allowed to invite guests, tries to invite mia@studio.io, and Entra ID blocks the invitation. Step 2: (missing). Step 3: The team member sends the invitation again, and this time it goes through. Step 4: Mia redeems it by signing in with her studio.io account. Step 5: An administrator adds her to a group that holds the role she needs on the project's resources. What is Step 2?
choices: An administrator creates a password for Mia in the Tailspin Toys tenant
An administrator changes Mia's UserType from Guest to Member before inviting her
An administrator adds studio.io to the domain allow list in External collaboration settings
An administrator gives the team member the Guest Inviter role so the invitation is allowed
questions.why: The invitation was blocked because studio.io is not on the domain allow list, so adding that domain to the list in External collaboration settings is the fix; the inviter already had permission to invite.

questions.prompt: Woodgrove Bank invites an outside consultant who uses a Google account. Which statement correctly describes the account that appears in Woodgrove's Entra ID tenant (Woodgrove's own instance of Entra ID)?
choices: It is a guest object with UserType set to Guest, and the consultant signs in at Google, so Woodgrove never stores or resets that password
It is a Member account with a new password that Woodgrove's administrators must reset when it expires
It is a copy of the consultant's Google account, including the password, kept in sync by Woodgrove
It is a Member account that is converted to Guest only after the consultant leaves the project
questions.why: In B2B collaboration (business-to-business), the guest object has UserType Guest and the person authenticates at their home provider, so the inviting organization never holds their password.

questions.prompt: At Litware Inc., a supplier contact, raj@supplier.net, redeemed his invitation three days ago and his guest object shows as accepted. He can sign in to Litware's tenant but cannot open any of the files in the storage account he was meant to work with. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Guests can never be given access to storage accounts
He has not been given a role or added to a group that holds a role on that storage account
His invitation is still pending, so his sign-in only partly works
Litware must reset his password before any access works
questions.why: Inviting and redeeming only create and activate the guest object; a guest with no role assignment or group membership can sign in but can reach nothing.

questions.prompt: Proseware ran a joint project with 40 outside partners as guests. The project ended eight months ago, but most of those guest accounts still have working access to project resources. Proseware is licensed for it. Which control is designed to find and remove guests who no longer need access, on a regular schedule?
choices: Adding the partners' domains to the deny list in External collaboration settings
Changing every guest's UserType from Guest to Member
Removing the Guest Inviter role from the people who sent the invitations
An access review, where owners confirm on a schedule whether each guest still needs access
questions.why: An access review is a scheduled check in which owners confirm each guest still needs access, so stale guests can be removed; the other options do not take away existing guests' access.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would give an outside consultant access to one resource group using a guest account, and name one risk or limit you would manage.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd invite the consultant as a B2B guest in our Entra ID tenant. That creates a user with UserType Guest, but they keep signing in with their own company account, so we never hold their password. They get an email and must redeem the invitation before the account is active. The invite alone gives them nothing, so I'd add them to a group that has, say, the Reader role on that one resource group. That keeps their scope narrow. Our external collaboration settings control who is allowed to invite and which domains are allowed, and they limit what guests can see in the directory. The main risk is stale access. When the contract ends, the guest still exists until someone removes them. So I'd put an end date on the work and use an access review or a manual cleanup to delete the guest.
rubricPoints: A guest is a directory object with UserType Guest whose identity and password live with an external provider.
The guest must redeem an invitation before access works.
Inviting grants no resource access; a role or group assignment at a scope is still needed.
External collaboration settings control who can invite, which domains are allowed, and what guests can see.
Stale guests are a risk and should be removed or reviewed, for example with access reviews.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing the right guest-related control in a scenario, such as invite settings, domain restrictions, role assignment or access reviews, so reasoning through situations adds the most and no mission or planned engine covers directory guests.

lessons.plain: Self-service password reset, usually shortened to SSPR, lets people who have forgotten their password, or whose account is locked, set a new password themselves instead of calling the help desk. Before they are allowed to, they must prove who they are with something set up earlier, such as a code sent to their phone or a prompt in an authenticator app. Think of a hotel guest locked out of their room who can show ID at a kiosk and get a new key card without waiting at the front desk. In Microsoft Entra ID, the cloud directory that stores Azure user accounts, an administrator decides who may use SSPR and which proofs count.
lessons.guessPrompt: If anyone could reset a forgotten password just by typing their username, what would stop an attacker from taking over the account, and what would you ask the user to prove first?
lessons.teach:
SSPR is a Microsoft Entra ID feature that lets a user replace a forgotten or locked password after passing identity checks. An administrator configures it under the directory's Password reset settings. It works because the user registers proof methods in advance, while they are signed in and trusted. Later, when they are locked out, those registered methods stand in for the password.

There are five settings to know. Scope is who may use SSPR: None, Selected (one chosen group), or All. Number of methods required is how many separate proofs a reset needs, one or two. Authentication methods are the allowed proofs, such as a mobile app notification, an app code, email, a text or call to a mobile phone, an office phone, or security questions. Registration settings can force users to register methods at their next sign-in and ask them to reconfirm those methods every set number of days. Notifications can email users when their password is reset and alert administrators when another administrator resets theirs.

Administrator accounts follow a stricter built-in policy whatever scope you choose. Admins can always use SSPR, must pass two methods, and cannot use security questions.

Worked example: you want to pilot SSPR for the Sales team only. First, set Scope to Selected and pick the Sales group. Second, set methods required to 2. Third, allow the mobile app and mobile phone methods. Fourth, require registration at sign-in. A Sales user now signs in, registers their phone and app, and can later reset alone. A Finance user sees no reset option because they are outside the scope.

A common mistake involves hybrid users, meaning accounts synchronized from on-premises Active Directory by Microsoft Entra Connect. Their password really lives on-premises. Unless you enable password writeback, which sends the new cloud password back to on-premises AD and needs a Premium licence, their reset does not reach the on-premises directory where their real password lives. In a running organization, help-desk tickets keep arriving even though SSPR looks enabled.

questions.prompt: A college runs Microsoft Entra Connect, which synchronizes (copies) its student accounts from on-premises Active Directory into Microsoft Entra ID, so each student's real password lives on-premises. The college holds the needed Premium licence. The IT lead configures self-service password reset (SSPR), the feature that lets users reset their own forgotten password after identity checks. Step 1: set Scope to All. Step 2: set the number of methods required to 1. Step 3: allow email and text to a mobile phone. Step 4: require users to register methods at their next sign-in. Step 5: ______. Result: a student who resets in the cloud can then sign in to a campus lab PC with the new password. Which step completes the setup?
choices: Set the number of methods required to 2 so the reset is stronger
Enable password writeback so the new cloud password is sent back to on-premises Active Directory
Turn on the notification that alerts administrators when another administrator resets their password
Add security questions as an allowed method so students have a fallback proof
questions.why: Synchronized (hybrid) accounts keep their real password on-premises, so only password writeback carries the cloud reset back to that directory.

questions.prompt: A design studio configures SSPR with Scope set to None, the number of methods required set to 1, and security questions as the only allowed method. A Global Administrator, an administrator account with full rights, forgets their password. What happens?
choices: They can use SSPR by answering the security questions, since one method is required
They can use SSPR with any single method because administrators skip the method rules
They can use SSPR but must pass two methods, and security questions do not count
They cannot use SSPR because Scope is None, so another administrator must reset it
questions.why: Administrators follow a stricter built-in policy whatever the scope: they can always use SSPR, must pass two methods and cannot use security questions.

questions.prompt: At an engineering firm, SSPR Scope is set to Selected, with the group Contractors chosen. Priya is in the Marketing group only, and she has registered her mobile phone. She forgets her password. What does she experience?
choices: She is forced to register a second method, then can reset
She sees no reset option, because she is outside the group in scope
She can reset using her phone, because having a registered method is enough
She can reset, but only after an administrator approves the request
questions.why: Scope Selected limits SSPR to members of the one chosen group, so a non-member gets no reset option regardless of registered methods.

questions.prompt: A charity enables SSPR for all staff, but locked-out users keep discovering they have no proof methods on file. SSPR depends on users registering proof methods in advance, while they are signed in and trusted. Which setting most directly fixes this?
choices: Raising the number of methods required from 1 to 2
A registration setting that requires users to register methods at their next sign-in
Changing Scope from All to Selected so fewer users are included
A notification that emails users when their password is reset
questions.why: Forcing registration at next sign-in makes users store their proof methods while trusted, so the methods exist when they are later locked out.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would roll out SSPR to one department, what each key setting controls, and name one limit or tradeoff they should know about.
lessons.modelAnswer: SSPR lets users reset their own Entra ID password after proving who they are with methods they registered earlier. For a single department, I'd set the scope to Selected and choose that department's group. Scope only accepts one group, so the group has to contain exactly the right people. I'd require two methods, allow strong ones like the authenticator app and mobile phone, and force registration at next sign-in so nobody is stuck later. I'd also turn on notifications so users get an email if their password changes. One tradeoff is that requiring two methods is safer but adds friction and means more registration work. Another limit is that admins always get a stricter policy regardless of my scope, with two methods and no security questions. Also, for users synced from on-premises AD, resets only take effect on-premises if password writeback is enabled, and that needs a Premium licence.
rubricPoints: Defines SSPR as users resetting their own password after proving identity with pre-registered methods.
Names scope options None, Selected (one group), or All.
Mentions the number of required methods and which authentication methods are allowed.
Mentions registration enforcement or notifications.
Notes that admins always get a stricter two-method policy without security questions.
Names a tradeoff or limit, such as the friction of more methods or needing password writeback for hybrid users.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or engine exercises Entra ID settings, so reasoning through exam-style rollout scenarios about scope, method count, admin policy and writeback builds the needed judgement best.

lessons.plain: A built-in Azure role is a ready-made bundle of permissions that Microsoft provides, so you do not have to list every allowed action yourself. You hand a role to a person, group, or app, and they can do exactly what the bundle allows on the resources you choose. Think of an office building's key cards: instead of programming each door for each employee, the front desk has standard cards, such as visitor, cleaner, and manager, and picks the one that fits the job. Azure has a few general roles that work on everything and many narrower roles for specific services, like virtual machines or storage.
lessons.guessPrompt: A teammate needs to start, stop, and resize virtual machines, but must not be able to give anyone else access. Would you pick a role that lets them do everything, a role that only lets them look, or something in between, and why?
lessons.teach:
A built-in role is a role definition, meaning a named list of permissions, that Microsoft writes and maintains in Azure role-based access control (Azure RBAC, the system that decides who can manage Azure resources). Each definition has four lists. Actions are allowed management operations, such as creating a virtual machine. NotActions are operations carved back out of Actions. DataActions are allowed operations on the data inside a resource, such as reading a file in a storage container. NotDataActions carve those back out. A wildcard (*) means "everything here."

Four general roles appear everywhere. Owner allows all management actions, including granting access to others. Contributor allows all management actions but excludes writing or deleting role assignments, so it cannot grant access. Reader can view resources but change nothing. User Access Administrator can manage who has access but not build or change other resources. Beyond these sit service-specific roles, such as Virtual Machine Contributor or Storage Blob Data Reader, which follow least privilege: grant only what the job needs.

Worked example. A support engineer must restart and resize VMs. Step 1: Owner fits, but it also lets them grant access, which is too much. Step 2: Contributor drops access-granting but still lets them edit networks, databases, everything. Step 3: Virtual Machine Contributor covers managing VMs without managing the virtual network itself or role assignments. Pick that one.

A common mistake is assuming Owner or Contributor automatically lets someone read blob or queue data when sign-in uses Entra ID. Those roles grant management Actions but no DataActions, so the user can see the storage account yet gets denied opening its contents until they also hold a data role like Storage Blob Data Reader. In a running system this shows up as a confusing "authorization failed" error for an apparently powerful admin. Note also that Azure RBAC roles are separate from Microsoft Entra roles (like Global Administrator), which govern the directory, not Azure resources.

questions.prompt: A logistics company stores shipment PDFs as blobs in a storage account. Priya, a data analyst, signs in with Entra ID and only needs to open and read those files. She must not change any settings or resources. Her manager works through the choice of role. Step 1: Owner would allow every management action and access granting, but it carries no DataActions, so it is far too broad and still would not let her open the files. Step 2: Contributor also carries only management Actions and no DataActions, so it is still too broad and still would not open the files. Step 3: ______. Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Global Administrator gives full control of the directory, so it covers the storage data too.
Reader lets her view the storage account without changing anything, so it is enough to open the PDFs.
Virtual Machine Contributor is a service-specific role, so it follows least privilege and fits here.
Storage Blob Data Reader grants the read DataActions on blob contents and nothing more, so pick that one.
questions.why: Opening blob contents with Entra ID sign-in needs a DataAction, and Storage Blob Data Reader grants only blob read access, which is least privilege for this job.

questions.prompt: In an Azure RBAC role definition, what does the NotActions list do?
choices: It removes specific management operations from the ones allowed by Actions.
It lists management operations the role holder may grant to other people.
It denies the role to any user who is not already an Owner.
It lists operations on the data inside a resource that are blocked.
questions.why: NotActions carves management operations back out of the Actions list; blocked data operations belong in NotDataActions instead.

questions.prompt: At a regional hospital, a security officer must decide who gets access to resources in a subscription. The officer must not create, change or delete any virtual machines, databases or networks. Which built-in role fits best?
choices: Contributor
Reader
User Access Administrator
Owner
questions.why: User Access Administrator can manage who has access but cannot build or change other resources, which matches the job exactly.

questions.prompt: Tomas holds the Contributor role on a resource group at a retail company. He can create and edit web apps and databases there. When he tries to give a new colleague access to the resource group, the request fails. What is the most likely reason?
choices: Contributor carries no DataActions, so it cannot read the resource group's contents.
Granting access needs an Entra role such as Global Administrator, not an Azure RBAC role.
Contributor excludes writing or deleting role assignments, so it cannot grant access to others.
Contributor is a service-specific role and only works on virtual machines.
questions.why: Contributor allows all management actions except writing or deleting role assignments, so it can build resources but cannot grant access.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between Owner, Contributor, Reader, and a service-specific built-in role for a new team member, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on built-in roles.
lessons.modelAnswer: Built-in roles are Microsoft-maintained permission bundles. Each lists allowed management Actions and data DataActions, with NotActions and NotDataActions removing exceptions. Owner can do everything including granting access; Contributor can manage everything except access; Reader only views; User Access Administrator only manages access. I start from the job: if someone just restarts VMs, Virtual Machine Contributor fits better than Contributor, because least privilege limits damage from mistakes or a stolen account. I also remember management and data are separate: Contributor on a storage account does not include DataActions, so reading blobs with an Entra sign-in needs a data role such as Storage Blob Data Reader. The tradeoff is that built-in roles are fixed bundles; sometimes none matches exactly, so you either grant slightly more than needed or create a custom role, which you then have to maintain yourself.
rubricPoints: Defines a built-in role as a Microsoft-maintained bundle of permissions assigned to a user, group, or app.
Distinguishes Owner, Contributor, Reader, and User Access Administrator, especially that Contributor cannot grant access.
Applies least privilege by preferring a service-specific role when it fits the job.
Notes that management Actions and DataActions are separate, so admin roles may not read data.
Names a limit, such as built-in roles being fixed bundles that may not match a job exactly.

suggested.rationale: An authorization policy evaluator would let the learner test which built-in role's actions allow or deny a given operation, which is the core judgment this objective needs.

lessons.plain: Assigning a role at a scope means deciding who can do what, and where. In Azure, the who is a person, group or app, the what is a role (a named bundle of allowed actions), and the where is the scope: a level in a nesting of containers, from very broad down to one single resource. Think of an office building: a key to the whole building opens every floor and room, a floor key opens only that floor's rooms, and a room key opens one room. Access given at a higher level flows down to everything inside it, never upward.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you give a colleague permission to manage everything in one container of cloud resources, do you think they automatically get permission over the resources inside that container? Do they get permission over the larger container that holds it?
lessons.teach:
A role assignment in Azure role-based access control (Azure RBAC, the system that decides who may act on Azure resources) joins three things. The security principal is the identity receiving access: a user, a group, or a service principal or managed identity, which are identities used by apps. The role definition is a named list of allowed actions, such as Reader (view only) or Virtual Machine Contributor (manage virtual machines). The scope is where the assignment applies.

Scopes form four nested levels. A management group is a container that holds subscriptions. A subscription is a billing and access boundary that holds resource groups. A resource group is a logical folder of related resources. A resource is one item, such as a single virtual machine or storage account. An assignment at any level is inherited by every level beneath it. Assignments are additive: a principal's effective access is the sum of all roles that reach them, directly or through groups.

Worked example: Priya must restart web servers in the resource group rg-web, but nothing else. Step 1, pick the principal: Priya, or better, a group she belongs to. Step 2, pick the role: Virtual Machine Contributor. Step 3, pick the narrowest scope that covers the job: rg-web. Result: every virtual machine inside rg-web inherits the assignment, so Priya can restart them. The resource group rg-db sits beside rg-web, not under it, so she has no access there, and the subscription above is untouched.

Common mistake: assigning at the subscription "to be safe", then trying to restrict one resource group with a weaker role lower down. A lower assignment cannot take away an inherited one, because roles only add access. In a running system this leaves people able to change or delete production resources they were never meant to touch. Start at the lowest scope that does the job, and assign to groups so access is easy to review and remove.

questions.prompt: Northwind Health has a management group called mg-clinical. It holds three subscriptions: sub-clinical-dev, sub-clinical-test and sub-clinical-prod. An audit team, already placed in the Entra ID group Clinical-Auditors, must be able to view everything in all three subscriptions but change nothing. Nothing outside mg-clinical should be visible to them. Step 1 (principal): the group Clinical-Auditors, so membership can be reviewed and removed later. Step 2 (role): Reader, because the team only needs to view. Step 3 (scope): ??? Result: the audit team can view every resource group and resource in the three clinical subscriptions, and nothing outside mg-clinical. Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Assign at one resource group inside sub-clinical-dev. Resource groups pass access up to the subscriptions above them.
Assign at the subscription level and then add a weaker role on each resource group to block changes.
Assign at sub-clinical-prod only. Inheritance also flows sideways to the sibling subscriptions dev and test.
Assign at the management group mg-clinical. All three subscriptions sit beneath it and inherit the Reader assignment.
questions.why: An assignment is inherited by every level beneath it, so a single Reader assignment at mg-clinical reaches all three subscriptions it holds and nothing outside it.

questions.prompt: In Azure role-based access control (Azure RBAC), which three things does a role assignment join together?
choices: A user, a password, and a virtual network
A billing account, a resource group, and a policy
A security principal, a role definition, and a scope
A subscription, a management group, and a resource
questions.why: A role assignment links who gets access (the security principal), what actions are allowed (the role definition), and where it applies (the scope).

questions.prompt: At Fabrikam, the group Ops-Team holds Virtual Machine Contributor at the subscription sub-fab-main. Someone then also gives Ops-Team the Reader role on the resource group rg-payroll, which is inside that subscription. What can Ops-Team members do to a virtual machine in rg-payroll?
choices: Manage it, because roles are additive and the lower Reader assignment cannot remove the inherited Virtual Machine Contributor access
Only view it, because the assignment closest to the resource always replaces the ones inherited from above
Nothing at all, because two different roles on the same principal cancel each other out
Manage it only after the Reader assignment is moved up to the subscription level
questions.why: Effective access is the sum of all roles that reach a principal, so the inherited Virtual Machine Contributor still applies and Reader only adds view access.

questions.prompt: A managed identity used by a nightly archiving app must manage exactly one storage account, sa-archive07. That account is in the resource group rg-storage, which also holds 11 other storage accounts. Following the lowest-scope practice, where should the role be assigned?
choices: On the storage account sa-archive07 itself, the narrowest scope that covers the job
At the management group, so a single assignment covers every future account
At the subscription, so the app keeps working if the account is moved
At rg-storage, because resource groups are the lowest scope Azure RBAC supports
questions.why: A single resource is a valid scope, and assigning there gives the app what it needs without reaching the other 11 accounts through inheritance.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how choosing the scope of an Azure role assignment changes what someone can reach, and name one limit or tradeoff of assigning broadly versus narrowly.
lessons.modelAnswer: A role assignment has three parts: who gets access (a user, group or app identity), which role they get (a set of allowed actions), and the scope where it applies. Scopes nest: management group, then subscription, then resource group, then a single resource. Whatever you assign at one level flows down to everything inside it, but never up or sideways. So Virtual Machine Contributor on one resource group lets someone manage only the VMs in that group, while the same role on the subscription covers every resource group in it. The limit is that access only adds up: you cannot assign broadly and then subtract access at a lower level with a weaker role. The tradeoff is that broad assignments are fewer and easier to manage, but they risk over-privilege; narrow ones follow least privilege but mean more assignments to track, which is why assigning to groups helps.
rubricPoints: A role assignment combines a security principal, a role definition and a scope.
Names the four scope levels in order: management group, subscription, resource group, resource.
Access assigned at a scope is inherited by everything below it, not above or beside it.
Assignments are additive, so a lower-scope assignment cannot remove inherited access.
Recommends the narrowest scope that does the job (least privilege), ideally assigning to groups.

suggested.rationale: An authorization policy evaluator would let the learner place assignments at different scopes and watch inheritance decide who can act on which resource.

lessons.plain: Interpreting access assignments means reading who has been given which permissions, and where, and then working out what a person can actually do. In Azure, access is handed out as role assignments. Each one names a person or group, a role (a bundle of allowed actions), and a place where it applies. Think of building keys. A master key works on every floor below it, and a floor key works only on that floor. Holding two keys never takes a door away from you. The skill is combining all of someone's keys to answer one question: can they do this, here?
lessons.guessPrompt: Maya is in a team group that can only view everything in a subscription. She has also been personally given full edit rights on one resource group inside it. Can she delete a virtual machine in that resource group? What about a virtual machine in a different resource group?
lessons.teach:
A role assignment in Azure role-based access control (RBAC, the system that decides who may manage Azure resources) has three parts. The security principal is who gets access: a user, a group, a service principal (an identity used by an app), or a managed identity (an identity Azure creates and manages for a resource). The role definition is a named list of allowed operations. Built-in examples are Reader (view only), Contributor (create, change and delete resources, but not grant access to others) and Owner (everything, including granting access). The scope is where the assignment applies: a management group, a subscription, a resource group, or a single resource.

Three rules let you interpret what someone can do. First, inheritance: an assignment applies at its scope and at every scope beneath it. Second, assignments are additive. A person's effective permissions are the union of every assignment they hold directly or through groups. Third, a deny assignment (a block that Azure attaches in specific cases) removes actions even when a role allows them.

Worked example. Maya belongs to the group Ops. Ops holds Reader on the subscription. Maya personally holds Contributor on resource group RG-web. Can she delete a VM in RG-web? Contributor at RG-web covers that resource, so yes. Can she delete a VM in RG-db? Only the inherited Reader reaches RG-db, so no. Can she give a colleague access to RG-web? No. Contributor's definition excludes authorization writes, so she would need Owner or User Access Administrator.

A common mistake is to think the narrower or weaker assignment wins. Reader at the subscription does not cancel Contributor on the resource group, because roles only add permissions. Another mistake is to treat a role's NotActions list as a deny. NotActions only trims what that one role grants, and another role can still allow the same action.

In the portal, the Access control (IAM) page of any resource shows its role assignments, including inherited ones, and its Check access tool lists a principal's effective roles. Misreading these causes either over-privileged accounts or blocked operators during an incident.

questions.prompt:
Harbor Logistics uses one management group called Corp, with subscription Sub-Ops beneath it. Inside Sub-Ops, resource group RG-data holds two storage accounts, stlogs01 and stbackup02. Priya is a member of the group Analysts, and Analysts holds Reader on the Corp management group. Priya also personally holds Contributor on the single resource stlogs01.

Step 1: Can Priya view the virtual machines in Sub-Ops? Reader at Corp is inherited by every scope beneath it, including Sub-Ops, so yes.
Step 2: Can Priya change the settings of stlogs01? Her Contributor assignment is scoped to that exact resource, and Contributor allows changes, so yes.
Step 3: Can Priya change the settings of stbackup02? ______

Which answer correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Yes. Her permissions are added together, so Contributor now applies everywhere Reader applies.
No. Reader at the management group is broader, so it overrides her Contributor role at every scope.
No. Only the inherited Reader reaches stbackup02, because her Contributor assignment applies to stlogs01 alone.
Yes. Contributor on stlogs01 also reaches the parent resource group RG-data, so it covers stbackup02.
questions.why: An assignment applies at its own scope and the scopes beneath it, never to a parent or a sibling, so only the inherited Reader reaches stbackup02.

questions.prompt: At Northwind Clinic, an administrator turns on a managed identity for a virtual machine. A managed identity is an identity that Azure creates and manages for a resource. The administrator then gives that identity the Reader role on one storage account. In this role assignment, which of the three parts is the managed identity?
choices: A deny assignment, because Azure created and attached it automatically
The scope, because it is attached to one specific resource
The role definition, because it determines which operations the virtual machine may perform
The security principal, because it is who receives the access
questions.why: The security principal is who gets access, and it can be a user, a group, a service principal or a managed identity.

questions.prompt: At Fabrikam, Tomas belongs to a group that holds Contributor on the subscription Sub-Finance. Tomas personally holds Owner on the resource group RG-reports, which sits inside Sub-Finance. Which action can Tomas perform?
choices: Nothing beyond Contributor, because the broader subscription assignment takes precedence
Grant a colleague Reader on a virtual machine in RG-payroll, another resource group in Sub-Finance
Grant a colleague Reader on a virtual machine inside RG-reports
Create new role assignments at the Sub-Finance subscription scope
questions.why: Owner at RG-reports includes granting access and is inherited by resources inside RG-reports, while everywhere else he has only Contributor, which cannot grant access.

questions.prompt: At Tailspin Games, a custom role called VM Operator lists virtual machine delete under NotActions. Lena holds VM Operator on resource group RG-game. She also holds Contributor on RG-game through a group. She deletes a VM in RG-game, and the delete succeeds. Why?
choices: NotActions only trims what VM Operator grants, and her Contributor role still allows the delete
The group assignment is the narrower one, so it cancels her personal assignment
NotActions only blocks actions when the role is assigned at subscription scope
Azure ignores custom roles whenever a built-in role is assigned at the same scope
questions.why: NotActions is not a deny: it only removes actions from that one role, and her permissions are the union of all her roles, so Contributor still allows the delete.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would work out whether a given user can perform a specific action on a specific Azure resource. Name one limit or catch in the reasoning.
lessons.modelAnswer: Every role assignment has three parts: a principal, a role, and a scope. To check what a user can do on a resource, I collect every assignment that reaches that resource. That includes assignments made directly to the user and to any group they belong to. It also includes assignments at the resource itself and at each scope above it: resource group, subscription, and management group, because access inherits downward. The user's effective permission is the union of all those roles, since RBAC only adds rights. So a Reader assignment never cancels a Contributor assignment. The catch is deny assignments. They override allows, so a role that seems to grant an action can still be blocked. Also, a role's NotActions only trims that one role and is not a deny. Finally, Contributor can change resources but cannot grant access to others, so manage and delegate are different questions. The IAM page's Check access view helps confirm all of this.
rubricPoints: A role assignment combines a security principal, a role definition, and a scope.
Assignments inherit from higher scopes down to everything beneath them.
Effective permissions are the additive union of direct and group assignments.
Deny assignments override allows, while NotActions only trims a single role.
Contributor can manage resources but cannot grant access, unlike Owner or User Access Administrator.
The IAM page and its Check access view show assignments, including inherited ones.

suggested.rationale: An authorization policy evaluator would have learners combine assignments across scopes and groups, and see allow and deny outcomes for themselves, which is exactly the skill this objective tests.

lessons.plain: Azure Policy is a rulebook that Azure checks automatically whenever someone creates or changes a resource. Permissions decide who may act; a policy decides what the result is allowed to look like. Examples are allowing resources only in approved regions, requiring a cost-centre tag, or allowing only certain virtual machine sizes. Think of a building code. Having the keys to a site does not let you ignore the fire rules, and an inspector also walks past older buildings to note which ones fall short. Azure Policy can block rule-breaking changes, quietly record them, or correct them, and it reports how compliant your environment is.
lessons.guessPrompt: A user holds the Owner role on a subscription. A rule on that subscription says resources may only be created in West Europe. The user tries to create a virtual machine in Japan East. Do you think it gets created? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Azure Policy is the Azure service that evaluates resource properties against rules and either enforces or reports on them. It has several named parts. A policy definition is one rule: a condition, such as "location is not in the allowed list", plus an effect. An initiative, also called a policy set, groups several definitions so they can be assigned together. An assignment applies a definition or initiative at a scope: a management group, subscription, resource group or single resource. Child scopes inherit the assignment. Exclusions carve out child scopes, and parameters let one definition be reused with different values.

The effect says what happens on a match. Deny blocks the create or update request. Audit allows it but marks it non-compliant. Append and Modify add or change properties such as tags. AuditIfNotExists and DeployIfNotExists check for, or deploy, a related resource, for example a monitoring extension. Disabled switches the rule off.

Why does this work even against powerful users? Role-based access control (RBAC) answers the question "may this person perform this action?" Policy is checked separately and answers "is the resulting resource allowed?" An action has to pass both checks.

Worked example. You assign the built-in "Allowed locations" definition to a subscription. Its parameter is set to West Europe and its effect is Deny. An Owner then requests a virtual machine in Japan East. First, RBAC passes, because Owner may create virtual machines. Second, Policy evaluates the location, matches the rule, and applies Deny. Third, the request fails with a policy error. A storage account already sitting in Japan East is not deleted. It simply shows as non-compliant in the compliance view.

A common mistake is assuming that assigning a policy fixes existing resources. Deny and Audit only affect new or updated resources, and report on the rest. To correct existing resources with Modify or DeployIfNotExists, you run a remediation task. That task uses a managed identity, which is an Azure-managed service account, and the identity needs suitable role permissions. Compliance results also refresh on a periodic cycle rather than instantly, so a freshly made assignment can show stale data for a while.

questions.prompt: Northwind Freight requires every resource in its 'rg-warehouse' resource group to carry a tag named costCenter with the value CC-4410. The steps so far: Step 1, the administrator assigns a tag definition at the rg-warehouse scope. Its parameter is set to CC-4410 and its effect is Modify. Step 2, a new managed disk created after the assignment automatically receives the tag. Step 3, the 37 disks that existed before the assignment still lack the tag and show as non-compliant. Step 4 is missing. Step 5, after that step finishes and the next compliance cycle runs, the 37 older disks show as compliant. What is Step 4?
choices: Change the effect from Modify to Deny so the existing untagged disks are blocked until they are corrected
Give the administrator the Owner role on rg-warehouse so the RBAC check applies the tag to the older disks
Run a remediation task that uses a managed identity with role permissions to change tags on those disks
Remove the assignment and recreate it at the management group scope so inheritance re-tags the older disks
questions.why: Assigning a policy does not change resources that already exist. A remediation task, running as a managed identity with suitable permissions, is what applies a Modify effect to those older disks.

questions.prompt: A security team at Fabrikam Health has eight separate policy definitions about storage encryption and network rules. They want to apply all eight to three subscriptions in one step, so they do not have to manage eight separate assignments per subscription. Which Azure Policy part should they create?
choices: An exclusion on each subscription that names the eight definitions
An effect of AuditIfNotExists that checks for the other seven definitions
A parameter on one of the definitions that lists the other seven rules
An initiative (policy set) that groups the eight definitions, which they then assign
questions.why: An initiative, also called a policy set, groups several definitions so that they can be assigned together as one unit.

questions.prompt: At Tailspin Air, a policy definition that blocks a certain expensive virtual machine size is assigned at a management group with the Deny effect. One of the subscriptions under that management group has a user, Priya, who holds the Owner role on that subscription. Priya requests a virtual machine of the blocked size in that subscription. What happens?
choices: The request succeeds, because the Owner role overrides any policy assigned above the subscription
The request succeeds and is only marked non-compliant, because Deny applies to existing resources only
The request fails, because the subscription inherits the assignment and Policy is checked separately from RBAC
The request succeeds, but the virtual machine is immediately deleted by the policy
questions.why: Child scopes inherit assignments, and an action must pass both the RBAC check and the Policy check. A Deny match blocks the request even for an Owner.

questions.prompt: Ten minutes ago, an administrator at Litware Labs assigned a policy with the Audit effect. It flags resources that lack an 'owner' tag. She knows that about 60 existing resources in the subscription have no such tag. The compliance view still shows no non-compliant resources. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Compliance results refresh on a periodic cycle, so the view is showing stale data for a newly made assignment
The subscription must be listed as an exclusion before the assignment can evaluate it
Audit only ever evaluates new resources, so existing resources will never appear as non-compliant
Audit needs a remediation task with a managed identity before it can report anything
questions.why: Audit does report on existing resources, but compliance data refreshes periodically rather than instantly, so a fresh assignment can show out-of-date results for a while.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Azure Policy differs from RBAC, and how a policy assignment treats resources that already exist. Include one limit or tradeoff of using the Deny effect.
lessons.modelAnswer: RBAC controls who can do something. Azure Policy controls what the resource is allowed to look like, whoever creates it. Both must pass, so even an Owner gets blocked by a Deny policy. You write or pick a definition (a condition plus an effect) or an initiative that bundles several. Then you assign it at a scope such as a management group, subscription or resource group, and child scopes inherit it unless you exclude them. Parameters let one definition serve different needs. Existing resources are not changed or deleted by an assignment. They are evaluated and marked compliant or non-compliant, and fixing them takes a remediation task. That only works with Modify or DeployIfNotExists and needs a managed identity with the right role. The tradeoff with Deny is that it is strong but blunt: it can break deployments or automation unexpectedly. Many teams start with Audit to see the impact, then switch to Deny.
rubricPoints: States that RBAC governs who can act while Policy governs allowed resource properties, and both must pass.
Names definition, initiative and assignment, and notes that assignments are made at a scope and inherited.
Explains that existing resources are reported as non-compliant rather than changed or deleted.
Mentions that remediation tasks with a managed identity fix existing resources for Modify or DeployIfNotExists.
Gives a tradeoff of Deny, such as breaking deployments, and suggests starting with Audit.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing the right effect, scope and remediation for a scenario, so reasoning through situations like a blocked Owner or a non-compliant legacy resource builds the skill best, and no current mission or planned engine models Azure Policy evaluation directly.

lessons.plain: A resource lock is a safety catch you put on something in your Azure cloud account so it cannot be deleted or changed by accident. Think of the clear plastic cover over an emergency switch: anyone allowed to press the switch must first lift the cover on purpose. A lock works the same way. Even a person with full permissions is stopped until they deliberately remove the lock. You can put a lock on a single resource, on a resource group (a folder that holds related resources), or on a whole subscription (the billing and management container), and everything underneath inherits it.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your teammate has the Owner role, which allows everything, on a resource group. Someone has placed a 'do not delete' lock on that group. If your teammate tries to delete a virtual machine inside it, what do you think happens, and why?
lessons.teach:
A resource lock is a setting on an Azure scope that blocks certain management actions regardless of who asks. There are two kinds. CanNotDelete, labelled Delete in the portal, lets people read and change a resource but not remove it. ReadOnly lets people read but blocks both changes and deletion. A scope is the level where the lock sits: a subscription, a resource group, or a single resource. Locks are inherited, so a lock on a resource group protects every resource inside it, including ones added later. If two locks apply, the more restrictive one wins.

Locks work because Azure checks them separately from role-based access control (RBAC), the system that grants permissions through roles such as Owner or Contributor. RBAC answers whether you are allowed. A lock answers whether the action is allowed at all right now. Both must pass. Only someone with permission to manage locks, such as the Owner or User Access Administrator role, can create or remove one.

Worked example. RG-Prod has a CanNotDelete lock. Priya, an Owner, tries to delete VM-Web01. Step one: RBAC says Owner may delete. Step two: Azure finds the inherited lock and refuses the deletion. Step three: Priya removes the lock, deletes the VM, then puts the lock back. Contributors could not do step three, because they cannot manage locks.

A common mistake is assuming ReadOnly is harmless. Locks act on the management plane, meaning operations that configure Azure resources, not the data inside them. Many routine operations count as changes, though. ReadOnly on a storage account blocks listing its access keys, so apps or tools relying on that fail. ReadOnly on a resource group can block starting or restarting virtual machines. In a running system, a well-meant ReadOnly lock can quietly break deployments, scaling, and admin tasks. CanNotDelete is usually the safer default for protecting production.

questions.prompt: Northwind Freight has a ReadOnly lock on its subscription, Sub-Logistics. Inside it, the storage account stfreight01 also has its own CanNotDelete lock. Marco has the Contributor role and tries to change stfreight01's redundancy setting. Step 1: Azure checks role-based access control (RBAC, the system that grants permissions through roles). Contributor may change storage settings, so this check passes. Step 2: Azure gathers every lock that applies to stfreight01. These are its own CanNotDelete lock and the ReadOnly lock inherited from the subscription. Step 3: ??? Step 4: Marco cannot fix this himself, because a Contributor cannot manage locks. Someone with the Owner or User Access Administrator role would have to change the lock. Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: The lock set closest to the resource is CanNotDelete, so it takes over and the change goes through.
RBAC already approved the request in Step 1, so Azure skips the lock check and the change goes through.
The more restrictive lock, ReadOnly, applies, so Azure refuses the change even though RBAC allowed it.
ReadOnly only protects the data stored inside the account, so a configuration change is still allowed.
questions.why: When more than one lock applies, the more restrictive one wins. Locks are checked separately from RBAC and both checks must pass, so the inherited ReadOnly lock blocks the configuration change.

questions.prompt: Tailspin Games keeps its game servers in a resource group called RG-Live. New virtual machines are added to RG-Live every month. Staff must still be able to restart and resize the servers, but nobody should be able to delete one by accident. Which setup fits best?
choices: A CanNotDelete lock on each virtual machine that exists in RG-Live today
A CanNotDelete lock on RG-Live
Removing the Contributor role from everyone who works in RG-Live
A ReadOnly lock on RG-Live
questions.why: A CanNotDelete lock on the resource group is inherited by every resource in it, including ones added later. It still allows changes such as restarts and resizing. ReadOnly could block restarting virtual machines, locks on today's VMs would not cover new ones, and removing a role is an RBAC change rather than a lock.

questions.prompt: At Fabrikam Health, Lena has the Contributor role on a resource group that carries a CanNotDelete lock. She needs to remove an unused disk from that group, so she asks a colleague to take the lock off temporarily. Which of these roles would let the colleague remove the lock?
choices: Contributor on the whole subscription
Any role that is allowed to delete disks
Reader on the resource group
User Access Administrator
questions.why: Only someone with permission to manage locks can create or remove them, and User Access Administrator (like Owner) has that permission. Contributor and Reader do not, and being allowed to delete a resource does not include managing locks.

questions.prompt: An administrator at Adatum Retail puts a ReadOnly lock on the storage account stadatumlogs to keep it safe. Soon afterwards, a reporting tool that retrieves the account's access keys starts failing. What is the most likely reason?
choices: Listing the access keys counts as a change-type operation, and ReadOnly blocks it.
ReadOnly locks block every read of the data stored inside the account.
The tool's RBAC role was removed automatically when the lock was added.
The lock only takes effect on access keys created after the lock was applied.
