questions.why: Locks act on the management plane, where many routine operations count as changes. On a storage account, ReadOnly blocks listing the access keys, so any tool that relies on those keys breaks.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what an Azure resource lock does, how it differs from a role assignment, and name one tradeoff or limit of using a ReadOnly lock.
lessons.modelAnswer: A resource lock is a guard on a subscription, resource group, or resource that blocks deletion, or deletion plus changes, no matter what role you hold. CanNotDelete still lets you edit but not remove. ReadOnly blocks edits and removal. Locks are inherited downward, and the stricter lock wins. They differ from role assignments because RBAC decides whether you are permitted, while the lock is a second check that even an Owner must clear. The Owner has to remove the lock on purpose first, and only roles that can manage locks, like Owner or User Access Administrator, can do that. The tradeoff with ReadOnly is that many ordinary operations count as changes. It can block listing storage keys or restarting VMs and break automation. So I would use CanNotDelete for production protection and save ReadOnly for things that truly should never change.
rubricPoints: Names the two lock types, CanNotDelete and ReadOnly, and what each blocks.
States that locks apply at subscription, resource group, or resource scope and are inherited.
Explains that locks apply even to Owners, separately from RBAC permissions.
Notes that only roles able to manage locks, such as Owner or User Access Administrator, can remove them.
Gives a ReadOnly side effect, such as blocking key listing or VM restarts, that can break operations.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine models Azure locks directly, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios about which lock applies and what it blocks is the most useful practice.

lessons.plain: A tag is a short label you attach to an Azure resource, made of a name and a value, such as Environment = Production or CostCenter = Finance. Tags do not change how the resource works. They are notes that help people and tools sort, search, and report. Think of colored stickers on boxes in a shared warehouse: the sticker doesn't change what's inside, but it lets anyone find all the boxes that belong to one team. Admins use tags to answer questions like which department pays for this virtual machine, or which resources belong to the test environment.
lessons.guessPrompt: You put the tag Department = Finance on a resource group. A colleague then creates a new virtual machine inside that group. Do you think the virtual machine automatically carries the Department = Finance tag? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A tag is a name-value pair of metadata (descriptive data about something, not the thing itself) stored on an Azure resource, a resource group (a container that holds related resources), or a subscription (the billing and management boundary that holds resource groups). Each of these can hold up to 50 tags. Tag names are not case-sensitive, but tag values are, so Prod and prod count as different values. Some resource types do not support tags at all. Tags are stored as readable text, so never put passwords or other secrets in them.

Tags work because Azure's search and cost tools can filter and group by them. Cost Management, Azure's spending report tool, can group charges by tag name, turning a long bill into totals per team or project. You can add, change, or remove tags in the portal, with the command line, or with templates. When updating by script, you choose whether to merge new tags with existing ones or replace the whole set.

Worked example: you tag resource group rg-payroll with CostCenter = Finance. Step one, a developer creates a storage account in rg-payroll. Step two, you open Cost Management and group by CostCenter. Step three, the storage account shows up as untagged, because resources do not inherit tags from their resource group. Step four, you either tag the storage account directly or set up an Azure Policy rule (a governance rule that checks or changes resources) that copies the tag from the group onto resources.

The common mistake is assuming tags flow down automatically from subscriptions or resource groups. A related mistake is running a replace-style update when you meant to merge, which silently wipes the existing tags. In a running system, neither mistake breaks the workload, but cost reports go wrong, automation that targets tagged resources skips some of them, and spending can't be traced to an owner. To let someone manage tags without giving them other access to the resources, Azure provides the built-in Tag Contributor role.

questions.prompt: A retail company's subscription, sub-retail, carries the tag Department = Marketing. Here is what happens next, with one step missing. Step 1: an engineer creates a virtual machine (a cloud-hosted computer) called vm-web01 inside resource group rg-campaigns. Neither vm-web01 nor rg-campaigns has any tags. Step 2: the finance lead opens Cost Management (Azure's spending report tool) and groups costs by the Department tag. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the admin assigns an Azure Policy rule (a governance rule that checks or changes resources) that copies the Department tag onto new resources. What is Step 3?
choices: vm-web01's charges appear under Marketing, because only the resource group is skipped and its resources still pick up the subscription's tag.
vm-web01's charges appear as untagged, because resources do not inherit tags from the subscription or resource group above them.
Cost Management rejects the grouping with an error, because a subscription tag cannot be used to group charges.
vm-web01's charges appear under Marketing, because every resource in a subscription automatically receives that subscription's tags.
questions.why: Tags never flow down automatically, so the untagged VM appears as untagged until it is tagged directly or a policy copies the tag onto it.

questions.prompt: At a logistics firm, half the team tags their resources Stage = Test and the other half uses Stage = test. When costs are grouped by the Stage tag, what does the report show?
choices: One combined Test group, because Azure ignores capitalisation in both tag names and tag values.
No groups at all, because a value that appears in two forms makes the tag invalid.
Two separate groups, Test and test, because tag values are case-sensitive.
One combined group, but only if the tag name Stage is spelled with the same capitalisation everywhere.
questions.why: Tag names are not case-sensitive, but tag values are, so Test and test are counted as two different values.

questions.prompt: A hospital hires a contractor to clean up and standardise tags on hundreds of resources. The contractor must not be able to change any settings on those resources or gain any other access to them. Which control fits best?
choices: The Contributor role on each resource group, so the contractor can edit the resources.
The Owner role on the subscription, so the contractor can reach every resource.
The built-in Tag Contributor role.
An Azure Policy rule that copies tags from resource groups, run under the contractor's name.
questions.why: Tag Contributor lets someone manage tags without giving them other access to the resources, unlike Owner or Contributor.

questions.prompt: A database server at an insurance company has three tags: Owner = Priya, App = Claims, and Tier = Data. An admin runs a script that sets Backup = Nightly, using a replace-style update instead of a merge. What tags does the server have afterward?
choices: Only the original three tags, because a replace update cannot add a tag name that did not exist before.
None. A replace update clears every tag first and then fails to add the new one.
Only Backup = Nightly. The other three tags are silently removed.
All four tags, because a new tag name is always added alongside the existing ones.
questions.why: A replace-style update swaps out the whole tag set for the new one, so the existing tags are wiped unless you merge instead.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Azure tags are, what they are good for, and one limit or trap they should watch out for when relying on tags for cost reporting.
lessons.modelAnswer: Tags are name-value labels, like Environment = Dev or CostCenter = Finance, that we attach to resources, resource groups, or subscriptions. They don't change how anything runs. They're metadata that lets us search, organize, and especially group costs in Cost Management so each team sees its own spending. The big trap is that tags don't inherit. If I tag a resource group, the resources inside it don't get that tag unless we tag them directly or use an Azure Policy rule to copy it down. Otherwise our cost report shows a pile of untagged spending. Also watch updates: a replace operation overwrites all existing tags, while merge adds to them. A few more limits: values are case-sensitive, each item holds at most 50 tags, some resource types can't be tagged, and tags are plain text, so no secrets. The Tag Contributor role lets someone manage tags without other access.
rubricPoints: Defines a tag as a name-value metadata label on a resource, resource group, or subscription.
States that tags organize and filter resources and let costs be grouped by tag.
Notes that tags are not inherited from resource groups or subscriptions by default.
Mentions Azure Policy or direct tagging as the way to get tags onto child resources.
Names at least one other limit, such as the 50-tag cap, case-sensitive values, untaggable types, replace wiping tags, or no secrets.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine practices tagging directly, and the main exam skill is reasoning through scenarios such as the no-inheritance trap and choosing between direct tags, Azure Policy, or the Tag Contributor role.

lessons.plain: A resource group is a named folder in Azure that holds related cloud resources, such as a virtual machine, its disk and its network card. Every resource lives in exactly one group. The group lets you treat everything inside it as one unit: you can grant people access to the whole folder, view its costs together, or delete the whole lot in one action. Think of a moving box labelled "Kitchen". Everything for the kitchen goes in it, and when you are done with the kitchen, you throw the whole box away. Grouping things that share a life together keeps that safe.
lessons.guessPrompt: You put a test website's server, disk and network address into one resource group, then delete that group. What do you think happens to the server, disk and address inside it?
lessons.teach:
A resource group is a logical container in an Azure subscription. A subscription is the billing and access boundary that holds your resource groups. A resource is any single thing you create, such as a virtual machine (a rented server), a storage account or a virtual network. The rules are simple. Every resource belongs to exactly one resource group. Groups cannot be nested inside each other. A group's name must be unique within its subscription, and you cannot rename it later. A group is created in a region (an Azure datacentre location), but that region only says where the group's own metadata, its description of what it contains, is stored. Resources inside the group can sit in other regions.

This works because the group gives you a scope, meaning a level where settings apply to everything below. Access roles, policies and locks set on a group reach every resource in it. Costs can also be filtered by group.

Worked example. You create rg-web-test in East US. You add a virtual machine in West Europe, plus its disk, network card and public IP address. That is allowed, because the group's region does not limit where resources go. Later the project ends and you delete rg-web-test. Azure deletes all four resources, then removes the group. You can also move resources between groups or between subscriptions. While a move runs, both the source and target groups are blocked from changes. The moved resource gets a new resource ID, its full address in Azure, so any scripts that refer to the old ID must be updated. Not every resource type can be moved.

Common mistake: putting things with different lifecycles in one group, for example a shared production database next to throwaway test servers. Someone deletes the test group to clean up and the database goes with it. In a running system that means an outage and possible data loss. The rule of thumb is to group resources that are created, managed and deleted together.

questions.prompt: Northwind Clinic keeps a storage account named stclinicscans in the resource group rg-clinic-dev. The team wants it in rg-clinic-prod, in the same subscription. A nightly backup script refers to the storage account by its resource ID, which is its full address in Azure. Step 1: confirm that this resource type is one Azure allows to be moved. Step 2: start the move, knowing that neither rg-clinic-dev nor rg-clinic-prod will accept changes while it runs. Step 3: (missing). Step 4: run the nightly backup script once by hand to confirm it still finds the storage account. What is Step 3?
choices: Update the backup script to use the storage account's new resource ID
Nest rg-clinic-dev inside rg-clinic-prod so the old ID keeps working
Rename rg-clinic-dev to rg-clinic-prod so the script's old path still matches
Change the region of rg-clinic-prod to match the storage account's region
questions.why: A moved resource gets a new resource ID, so any script that used the old ID must be updated to the new one.

questions.prompt: An engineer at a logistics firm creates the resource group rg-tracking in the Central India region. She then wants to place a virtual machine (a rented server) in Japan East inside that group. What does the group's Central India region actually control?
choices: It sets where the group's own metadata, its record of what it contains, is stored
It forces every resource in the group to be created in Central India
It limits the group to resources in Central India and its paired region only
It sets which region the group's costs are billed to
questions.why: A resource group's region only sets where its metadata is stored. Resources inside it can sit in any region, so the Japan East virtual machine is allowed.

questions.prompt: A payroll application uses 12 resources, all held in the resource group rg-payroll. The administrator wants one lock (a setting that guards against accidental deletion) to protect all 12 resources, including any added to the group later. Where is the most direct place to apply it?
choices: On the resource group rg-payroll, because settings on a group reach every resource in it
On each of the 12 resources separately, because locks cannot be set on groups
On a new resource group nested inside rg-payroll that holds only the lock
On the region where rg-payroll was created, because the region controls its resources
questions.why: A resource group is a scope, so a lock set on it applies to every resource inside it, including resources added later.

questions.prompt: A training company put a shared production storage account in the resource group rg-training-labs, alongside 30 short-lived lab virtual machines. At the end of a course, a trainer deletes rg-training-labs to clean up. What happens, and what grouping would have prevented the problem?
choices: The storage account is moved automatically to another group in the subscription before deletion
Every resource in the group is deleted, storage account included; it should have sat in its own group because it has a different lifecycle
Azure refuses to delete the group because it holds resources of different types
Only the virtual machines are deleted, because Azure always skips storage accounts when it deletes a group
questions.why: Deleting a group deletes everything in it, so resources with different lifecycles belong in separate groups. Group together only what is created, managed and deleted together.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a resource group is and how you would decide which resources go into the same one. Include one limit or risk they should know about.
lessons.modelAnswer: A resource group is a container in a subscription that holds related Azure resources. Every resource belongs to exactly one group, and groups can't be nested. The group is a scope, so access, policies and locks set on it apply to everything inside, and you can view costs per group. I decide membership by lifecycle: resources that are deployed, managed and retired together share a group. The big risk is deletion. Deleting a group deletes every resource in it, so a shared database should never sit in a throwaway test group. Also, the group's region only stores its metadata, so the resources can live in other regions. Groups can't be renamed. Resources can be moved between groups or subscriptions, but during a move both groups are blocked for changes, the resource ID changes, and some resource types can't be moved.
rubricPoints: Defines a resource group as a logical container where each resource belongs to exactly one group.
States that deleting a group deletes all resources inside it.
Recommends grouping by shared lifecycle.
Notes that the group's region holds only metadata and resources can be in other regions.
Mentions that settings applied at the group scope reach resources inside.
Names a limit such as no nesting, no renaming, or move restrictions and ID changes.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine exercises resource groups, and the exam tests this through short scenarios about deletion, region, moves and grouping choices, so reasoning through situations adds the most.

lessons.plain: An Azure subscription is the account container that everything you build in Azure lives inside. It does three jobs at once: it is where the bill is collected, it is a boundary for who may manage what, and it carries limits on how much you can create. Think of it like a utility account for a building: the meter, the bill and the list of people allowed to change things all hang off that one account. Each subscription trusts exactly one directory of identities (Microsoft Entra ID), so the people who can sign in to manage it all come from that directory. Managing subscriptions means naming them, controlling who owns them, moving them, raising their limits, and closing them safely.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you moved a whole Azure subscription so that it now trusts a different company's identity directory, what do you think would happen to the permissions that people had on it before the move?
lessons.teach:
An Azure subscription is a logical container that ties resources to one billing arrangement and one management boundary. A tenant is a single instance of Microsoft Entra ID, the identity directory holding users, groups and apps. Every subscription trusts exactly one tenant, but one tenant can own many subscriptions. A role assignment, which grants an identity a role such as Owner or Reader at some scope, can be made at subscription scope so it flows down to every resource group and resource inside.

Day-to-day subscription tasks include renaming it, assigning owners, transferring billing ownership to another person or account, registering resource providers (switching on the services the subscription may use), checking quotas (per-region limits such as how many virtual CPUs you may run) and requesting increases, moving resources from one subscription to another in the same tenant, and cancelling a subscription you no longer need.

Why this works: because billing, access and limits all attach at the subscription, splitting workloads into separate subscriptions gives you separate bills, separate permission boundaries and separate quotas.

Worked example: a company acquires a startup and wants the startup's subscription to trust the parent company's tenant. Step 1, an administrator who can sign in to both tenants changes the subscription's directory. Step 2, Azure re-points the subscription to the new tenant. Step 3, every role assignment on the subscription is removed, because the old users no longer exist in the new directory. Step 4, custom roles and managed identities (identities Azure creates for resources) tied to the old tenant stop working and must be recreated. Step 5, the team reassigns roles to users in the new tenant.

Common mistake: assuming a directory change is like moving a folder and permissions come along. They do not. In a running system, applications that used managed identities can suddenly fail to reach storage or key vaults, and administrators can find themselves locked out until access is rebuilt. Plan the reassignment before you switch.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm, Harbourline, plans to run a batch job on 48 virtual CPUs in its West Europe region. The services the job needs are already switched on for the subscription. Step 1: the administrator tries to deploy the virtual machines, and the deployment fails with a message that the regional virtual CPU limit has been reached. Step 2: she checks the subscription's quota for West Europe and sees a limit of 20 virtual CPUs, all of which are free. Step 3: ??? Step 4: once the higher limit is approved, she redeploys and the 48 virtual CPUs start successfully. Which action belongs in Step 3?
choices: Change the subscription's directory to a tenant that has a higher virtual CPU limit
Give the administrator the Owner role at subscription scope so the limit no longer applies
Register the compute resource provider again so the subscription can use more virtual CPUs
Submit a quota increase request for West Europe virtual CPUs on the subscription
questions.why: Quotas are per-region limits attached to the subscription, so the fix is to request an increase to that quota, not to change permissions, providers or the tenant.

questions.prompt: Brightwell Clinics has one Microsoft Entra ID tenant and three Azure subscriptions: Radiology, Pharmacy and Billing. Which statement about this setup is true?
choices: Each subscription must have its own tenant, so Brightwell needs three tenants
A subscription can trust several tenants at once, so Radiology could also trust a partner's tenant
The tenant is the billing container, so all three subscriptions share one bill automatically
All three subscriptions can trust the same single tenant, but each subscription trusts only one tenant
questions.why: Every subscription trusts exactly one tenant, while one tenant can own many subscriptions.

questions.prompt: At Corvane Engineering, an external auditor needs to view every resource group and resource in the Production subscription, and nothing in any other subscription. What is the simplest way to grant this?
choices: Change the Production subscription's directory to the auditor's own tenant
Assign the auditor the Reader role at the Production subscription scope
Register a resource provider for auditing in the Production subscription
Assign the auditor the Owner role on each resource in Production one by one
questions.why: A role assignment made at subscription scope flows down to every resource group and resource inside it, and Reader allows viewing without changes.

questions.prompt: Tallow Foods changed its Analytics subscription's directory to a new tenant. The next morning, an app that used a managed identity can no longer read secrets from its key vault, and several administrators have lost access. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The directory change removed role assignments and broke managed identities tied to the old tenant, so they must be recreated and roles reassigned
The subscription's virtual CPU quota was reset to zero during the directory change
The key vault was automatically moved to a different subscription in the old tenant
Billing ownership was transferred, which cancels all access until the new bill is paid
questions.why: Changing a subscription's directory removes its role assignments and stops managed identities and custom roles from the old tenant working, so access must be rebuilt in the new tenant.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what an Azure subscription is and why you might split work across several of them, then describe one thing that breaks or gets lost when a subscription is moved to a different tenant.
lessons.modelAnswer: A subscription is the container that our Azure resources sit in, and it bundles three things: billing, an access boundary, and quotas. Whatever is inside one subscription shows up on one bill, people given a role at subscription scope get that access on everything underneath, and limits like how many virtual CPUs we can run per region apply per subscription, though we can request increases. That is why splitting dev and production into separate subscriptions is useful: separate costs, separate permissions, separate limits. The tradeoff is more to administer. Each subscription trusts exactly one Entra tenant. If we change that tenant, all existing role assignments are wiped, custom roles go, and managed identities stop working, so apps can fail to reach their secrets or storage. We would need to plan the reassignments in the new tenant before switching.
rubricPoints: A subscription is a billing boundary, an access/management boundary and a quota boundary.
Each subscription trusts exactly one Microsoft Entra tenant, while a tenant can hold many subscriptions.
Role assignments at subscription scope are inherited by everything inside it.
Changing a subscription's tenant removes role assignments and breaks custom roles and managed identities.
Splitting workloads across subscriptions gives separate bills, permissions and limits at the cost of more administration.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine performs subscription administration, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios like a tenant change or quota request is the best way to make the consequences stick.

lessons.plain: Cloud bills grow quietly: a forgotten test server or an oversized machine keeps charging every hour. Azure gives you three cost tools. A budget is a spending target you set for a period, such as a month. A cost alert is a warning sent when spending crosses a level you chose. Azure Advisor is a built-in adviser that scans what you run and suggests ways to pay less. Think of a household budget with a bank text: 'you have spent 80% of this month's grocery money.' The text warns you. It does not lock your card, so someone still has to act on it.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you set a monthly budget of 500 on a subscription and spending reaches 600, what do you think Azure does to the running virtual machines by default: stop them, delete them, or nothing?
lessons.teach:
A budget in Azure Cost Management (the billing and cost analysis service) is a spending limit you define for a scope, meaning the level it watches: a management group, a subscription, a resource group, or a billing account. You also choose a reset period, usually monthly. Inside the budget you add alert conditions. Each condition is a percentage of the budget plus a type. Actual means money already spent. Forecasted means the spend Azure predicts by the end of the period. When a condition is met, Azure emails the listed recipients. It can also trigger an action group, which is a reusable list of notifications and automated actions, such as running a script.

A worked example. You set a 1,000 monthly budget on resource group rg-test. You add three conditions: 50% actual, 90% actual, and 100% forecasted. On day 10, spend is 400, so nothing fires. On day 12, spend is 420, but the forecast predicts 1,050 by month end, so the 100% forecasted alert fires early and gives you time to act. On day 14, actual spend hits 500 and the 50% alert fires. If nobody acts, the 90% alert fires later.

Azure Advisor is a free service that reviews your resources. Its cost category points out underused virtual machines that could be resized or shut down, idle resources such as unattached disks or unused public IP addresses, and steady workloads that would be cheaper with reservations. A reservation is a one- or three-year commitment in exchange for a lower price. Advisor only recommends. A person still applies each change.

The common mistake is believing a budget caps spending. It does not stop or delete anything by itself. Cost data can also lag by several hours, so alerts arrive somewhat late. In a running system, a budget with no owner reading the email, and no action group automation, lets a runaway resource keep billing until someone notices.

questions.prompt: Contoso Marketing sets a monthly budget of 2,000 on its subscription, sub-marketing. It adds three alert conditions: 25% actual (fires at 500 spent), 80% actual (fires at 1,600 spent), and 110% forecasted (fires when the predicted month-end spend reaches 2,200). Day 5: actual spend is 300 and the forecast is 1,800. No condition is met, so nothing fires. Day 8: actual spend is 450 and the forecast jumps to 2,400 after a new ad-rendering job starts. [MISSING STEP] Day 11: actual spend reaches 520, so the 25% actual alert fires. What happens on day 8?
choices: Nothing fires, because actual spend is still below every actual threshold and only actual spend counts.
The 110% forecasted alert fires and emails the recipients, and the ad-rendering job keeps running and billing.
The 25% actual alert and the 110% forecasted alert both fire, because the forecast pulls the actual alert forward.
Azure stops the ad-rendering job, because the forecast is now above the 2,000 budget.
questions.why: A forecast of 2,400 is above the 2,200 forecasted threshold, so that alert fires. Actual spend of 450 is still under 500, and a budget only notifies people and never stops resources by itself.

questions.prompt: Fabrikam's data team has a 5,000 monthly budget on resource group rg-analytics. The team lead wants a warning while there is still time to act, before the money is actually spent, if the month looks likely to end over budget. Which alert condition fits best?
choices: A 100% forecasted condition, because it fires on predicted month-end spend.
No budget condition is needed; Azure Advisor will send the warning.
A 100% condition set to the billing account scope instead of the resource group.
A 100% actual condition, because actual spend is the only reliable number.
questions.why: A forecasted condition compares Azure's predicted end-of-period spend to the threshold, so it can fire before the money has actually been spent.

questions.prompt: At Northwind, Azure Advisor's cost category finds a virtual machine averaging 3% CPU all month and a managed disk that is not attached to any machine. What happens next?
choices: Advisor buys a three-year reservation for the VM to lower its price.
Advisor raises the subscription budget so the idle resources stop triggering alerts.
Advisor lists recommendations, such as resizing or shutting down the VM and removing the idle disk, and a person must decide whether to apply each one.
Advisor automatically resizes the VM and deletes the disk at the end of the billing period.
questions.why: Advisor only recommends. It flags underused VMs and idle resources, but a person still has to apply each change.

questions.prompt: Tailspin's subscription has a 3,000 monthly budget whose alerts email only an engineer who has left the company. A test cluster is left running over a long weekend. The team wants something to happen automatically next time a threshold is crossed. Which change achieves that?
choices: Change the budget reset period from monthly to daily.
Lower the alert percentages to 10% and 20% so the email is sent sooner.
Attach an action group to the budget alert that runs a script to shut down the test resources.
Turn on Azure Advisor so it applies its cost recommendations automatically.
questions.why: A budget alone only notifies people. An action group can trigger automated actions such as running a script. Lower thresholds still just email nobody, and Advisor never applies changes itself.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would keep a new project's Azure spending under control using budgets, alerts, and Azure Advisor. Include one thing these tools will not do for you.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would put a monthly budget on the project's resource group or subscription, since budgets apply to a scope. I'd add alert conditions at a few percentages, for example 50% and 90% of actual spend, plus 100% of forecasted spend. Actual covers money already spent. Forecasted warns me early if we're on track to overspend. The alerts would go to the team by email. I would also attach an action group so the alert can run automation, such as a script that shuts down test machines. Every so often I'd check the cost recommendations in Azure Advisor for oversized or idle virtual machines, unattached disks, and candidates for reservations, then apply the sensible ones myself. The limit is that a budget is not a hard cap. It only warns, and cost data lags by hours, so someone or some automation still has to act.
rubricPoints: A budget is a spending target set on a scope, such as a subscription or resource group, for a period.
Alert conditions are thresholds based on actual or forecasted spend.
Alerts notify people and can trigger an action group for automation.
Azure Advisor gives cost recommendations like right-sizing, removing idle resources, and reservations.
Budgets do not stop resources by themselves, and cost data lags, so action is still needed.

suggested.rationale: Setting budgets and thresholds against a simulated bill in fictional credits lets the learner watch actual and forecasted alerts fire, and shows that nothing stops unless they act.

lessons.plain: A management group is a folder that holds Azure subscriptions, which are the billing and access containers for your cloud resources. Folders can sit inside other folders, forming a tree. Whatever rule or permission you attach to a folder flows down to every subscription inside it. Think of a company handbook: a rule written at head office applies to every branch beneath it, so no one has to repeat it in each branch. Management groups let an administrator govern dozens of subscriptions by setting rules once, high in the tree, instead of over and over.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company has 40 subscriptions and wants every one of them to allow resources only in European regions. Would you rather set that rule 40 times or once? Where in a tree of folders would you put it so it covers all 40?
lessons.teach:
A management group is a container in Azure that holds subscriptions and other management groups, so you can apply governance to many subscriptions at once. A subscription is the unit that groups resources for billing and access. Governance here means two things you attach to a scope: Azure Policy assignments, which are rules that allow, deny, or audit resource settings, and role assignments through Azure role-based access control (RBAC), which grant people permissions.

The tree starts at the tenant root group, a top-level management group created automatically for your Microsoft Entra ID directory (the identity service). Under it you can nest management groups up to six levels deep, not counting the root or the subscriptions. Each management group has exactly one parent, and each subscription sits in exactly one management group. Resource groups and individual resources never go directly into a management group; they live inside subscriptions.

This works through inheritance: anything assigned at a higher scope applies to everything below it. Worked example: under the root you create Corp, and under Corp you create Production, which holds subscription Prod-A. You assign a policy at Production that allows only West Europe, and the Reader role (view-only access) at Corp to an auditor. Someone tries to create a virtual machine in East US inside Prod-A. Azure checks Prod-A, then Production, finds the location policy, and denies the request. The auditor opens Prod-A; Azure walks up to Corp, finds Reader, and allows viewing.

A common mistake is expecting a lower level to cancel a restriction set higher up. A child cannot loosen an inherited deny policy, and permissions granted above cannot be removed by assignments below. Plan the tree carefully, because moving a subscription to a different management group changes which policies and roles it inherits, which can suddenly block deployments or remove access in a running environment.

questions.prompt: Contoso Health builds this tree: tenant root group, then Clinical, then Labs beneath Clinical. Subscription Lab-07 sits in Labs. At Clinical, an admin assigns a policy that allows virtual machines only in the Australia East region. Nothing is assigned at Labs or on Lab-07 itself. A technician tries to create a virtual machine in Southeast Asia inside Lab-07. Step 1: Azure checks Lab-07 and finds no location rule. Step 2: Azure checks Labs and finds no location rule. Step 3: ??? Step 4: The technician sees the request rejected. What is Step 3?
choices: Azure checks Clinical, finds the inherited Australia East location policy, and denies the request
Azure asks the tenant root group to override Clinical, because the root always has the final say on location
Azure checks the resource group inside Lab-07 for a matching management group assignment before deciding
Azure stops at Labs because Lab-07's direct parent has no rule, so the request is allowed
questions.why: Assignments at a higher scope apply to everything below it, so Azure keeps walking up past Labs and applies the Clinical policy that only allows Australia East.

questions.prompt: An administrator at Northwind Traders wants to place items directly inside a management group called Finance. Which items can be placed directly in a management group?
choices: Subscriptions and other management groups
Only Azure Policy definitions, with no subscriptions or groups
Resource groups and individual resources such as storage accounts
Microsoft Entra ID user accounts and the groups they belong to
questions.why: A management group holds subscriptions and other management groups. Resource groups and resources always live inside subscriptions, never directly in a management group.

questions.prompt: Tailspin Toys has a design document that proposes seven levels of nested management groups below the tenant root group, with subscriptions placed under the deepest level. Is this design valid?
choices: Yes, because the depth limit counts only levels that contain subscriptions
No, because management groups cannot be nested inside other management groups at all
No, because management groups can be nested at most six levels deep, not counting the root or the subscriptions
Yes, because the tenant root group counts as one of the seven levels, which brings it under the limit
questions.why: The tree allows up to six levels of management groups beneath the tenant root group. The root and the subscriptions are not counted, so seven nested levels exceeds the limit.

questions.prompt: At Woodgrove Bank, subscription Dev-12 sits in a management group called Sandbox, which has no location policy. The team regularly deploys to Canada Central. An admin moves Dev-12 into a management group called Regulated, which has a policy that allows only UK South. The next Canada Central deployment in Dev-12 fails. A developer then assigns a policy directly on Dev-12 that allows Canada Central. What happens?
choices: The deployment succeeds, because the assignment on Dev-12 is closer to the resource and replaces the Regulated policy
The Regulated policy is removed from every subscription in that management group
The deployment is still denied, because a lower scope cannot loosen a deny policy inherited from a higher scope
The deployment succeeds, but only for resources created after Dev-12 was moved
questions.why: Moving Dev-12 made it inherit Regulated's UK South-only rule, and a child scope cannot cancel a restriction set higher up, so Canada Central stays blocked.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what management groups are and why you would use them instead of configuring each subscription separately. Include at least one limit or tradeoff of the hierarchy.
lessons.modelAnswer: Management groups are containers above subscriptions. They can hold subscriptions or other management groups, forming a tree that starts at the tenant root group. When we assign an Azure Policy or an RBAC role to a management group, every subscription below inherits it. So a rule like 'only European regions' or giving the security team Reader access is set once instead of in each subscription, which keeps things consistent as we add subscriptions. Limits: the tree goes only six levels deep below the root, each subscription can be in only one management group, and resource groups cannot be placed in management groups. The tradeoff is that inheritance cuts both ways: a lower level cannot loosen a restriction set above it, and moving a subscription to another group instantly changes what it inherits, which could break deployments or access if we don't plan it.
rubricPoints: Defines a management group as a container for subscriptions and other management groups, under the tenant root group.
Explains that policy and role assignments made at a management group are inherited by everything below.
Gives the benefit of setting governance once across many subscriptions.
Names a structural limit such as six levels of depth, one parent per group, or one management group per subscription.
Notes that lower levels cannot override inherited restrictions or that moving a subscription changes what it inherits.

suggested.rationale: Mastery means reasoning through exam-style hierarchy scenarios to decide where an assignment belongs and what a subscription inherits, and no current mission or planned engine models management group trees directly.

lessons.plain: A storage firewall is a guest list at the door of your storage account. Even someone holding a valid key or token is turned away unless their request comes from a place on the list. You can allow specific public internet addresses, such as your office's address, and specific subnets, which are slices of an Azure virtual network (your private network inside Azure). Everything else is refused. It answers the question 'where is this request coming from?' Proving who the caller is and what they may do is a separate check, and both must pass.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your storage account's firewall allows only one subnet in Azure. A colleague at home has the account's full access key and tries to list the blobs. What do you think happens, and why?
lessons.teach:
Azure Storage firewalls and virtual network rules are network-level filters on a storage account. They decide which source locations may reach the account at all. They run before, and in addition to, authorization (keys, SAS tokens, or role-based access).

The public network access setting has three choices. 'Enabled from all networks' accepts traffic from anywhere. 'Enabled from selected virtual networks and IP addresses' changes the default action to deny, then allows only listed sources. 'Disabled' blocks all public traffic, leaving only private endpoints. A private endpoint is a private IP address for the account placed inside your virtual network.

There are two main kinds of allow rules. An IP network rule lists public IP addresses or ranges written in CIDR form, such as 203.0.113.0/24. Private ranges like 10.x.x.x are not accepted here. A virtual network rule allows a named subnet. It requires a service endpoint for Microsoft.Storage on that subnet. A service endpoint makes the subnet's traffic reach Azure Storage over the Azure backbone carrying the subnet's identity. There is also an exception for trusted Microsoft services, such as Azure Backup, so they can still get through.

Worked example: a VM in subnet app-sn must read blobs, and so must the office at 198.51.100.7.
Step 1: enable the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on app-sn.
Step 2: set public access to selected networks, so the default becomes deny.
Step 3: add a virtual network rule for app-sn.
Step 4: add an IP rule for 198.51.100.7.
Now a laptop at a café is refused, even if it holds the key.

A common mistake is to switch to selected networks without adding your own client IP. Then the portal's data view and Storage Explorer fail with authorization-looking errors. Another is entering a VM's private IP as an IP rule. That never matches, because traffic from inside Azure is identified by its subnet, not by its private address.

In a running system, a forgotten rule shows up as sudden 403 errors for an application or a backup job, even though its credentials are correct.

questions.prompt: Harbor Logistics has a storage account named hlarchive. Public network access is set to 'Enabled from selected virtual networks and IP addresses'. A VM in subnet data-sn (private IP 10.4.2.15) now gets 403 errors when reading blobs. The admin traces the problem. Step 1: confirm the VM's storage credentials are valid. They are, so this is not an authorization problem. Step 2: confirm the firewall's default action is deny, so only listed sources get through. Step 3: find that the only allow rule is an IP network rule for 10.4.2.15. Step 4: ??? Afterwards the VM reads blobs normally. Which action completes Step 4?
choices: Regenerate the account key and give the new key to the VM.
Replace the IP rule with one for the whole private range 10.4.2.0/24.
Turn on the exception for trusted Microsoft services.
Enable the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on data-sn, then add a virtual network rule for data-sn.
questions.why: Traffic from inside Azure is identified by its subnet, not its private IP, so the subnet needs a Microsoft.Storage service endpoint and a virtual network rule; private addresses are never accepted as IP rules.

questions.prompt: On a storage account, what does choosing the public network access setting 'Enabled from selected virtual networks and IP addresses' do?
choices: It replaces access keys and SAS tokens with network-based checks.
It accepts traffic from anywhere but records which networks connect.
It blocks all public traffic, so the account can be reached only through private endpoints.
It sets the default action to deny and then allows only the sources you list.
questions.why: This setting flips the default to deny and admits only the listed subnets and public IP addresses. Authorization with keys, SAS tokens or roles still applies on top of it.

questions.prompt: Northwind Clinics has a branch office whose public addresses are 192.0.2.32/28. The office must be able to reach a storage account that only allows selected networks. What should the admin add?
choices: A private endpoint with the address 192.0.2.32.
The exception for trusted Microsoft services.
An IP network rule for 192.0.2.32/28.
A virtual network rule naming the branch office's range.
questions.why: IP network rules take public IP addresses or ranges in CIDR form. Virtual network rules name Azure subnets, not office address ranges.

questions.prompt: An admin with the Owner role switches a storage account to 'Enabled from selected virtual networks and IP addresses'. The admin adds a virtual network rule for the application subnet and nothing else. The app keeps working, but the admin's own browser now gets errors that look like permission failures in the portal's data view. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The admin's public client IP address was not added as an IP network rule.
The admin's laptop needs a Microsoft.Storage service endpoint enabled on it.
The Owner role was removed when the firewall setting changed.
The storage account's access keys were rotated automatically.
questions.why: Once the default action is deny, the admin's own public IP is refused until it is listed. The resulting errors look like authorization failures even though the admin's permissions are fine.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a storage firewall with virtual network rules decides whether a request gets in, and name one limit or tradeoff they should watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: The firewall checks where a request comes from before anything else matters. Once we choose 'selected networks', the default action becomes deny. Only listed sources get through: public IPs or CIDR ranges via IP rules, and subnets via virtual network rules. A subnet rule only works if that subnet has the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint turned on. Private IPs don't belong in IP rules, because Azure identifies that traffic by its subnet. Passing the firewall isn't enough on its own. The caller still needs a valid key, SAS token, or role. Holding a key from an unlisted network still gets a 403. The tradeoff is that it's easy to lock ourselves out: if we forget our own client IP, the portal and tools can't read data. Service endpoints also still use the account's public address. If we need a truly private address, we'd use a private endpoint and disable public access.
rubricPoints: Selecting 'selected networks' flips the default action to deny and allows only listed sources.
IP rules take public IPs or CIDR ranges, not private addresses.
Virtual network rules need the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on the subnet.
The firewall is separate from authorization, so a valid key from a blocked network still fails.
Names a limit such as admin lockout, or the difference from private endpoints and fully disabled public access.

suggested.rationale: Tracing whether a request from a given subnet or IP reaches a storage account, with and without a service endpoint, makes the allow/deny logic concrete in a way reading alone does not.

lessons.plain: A shared access signature, or SAS, is a special web link that lets someone reach specific data in an Azure storage account without being given the account's master password. The link carries its own rules: what the holder may touch, what they may do (read, write, delete), and when the permission ends. Think of a hotel key card: it opens only your room, only until checkout, and the front desk never hands you the master key. Anyone holding the card can use it, though, so you keep it short-lived and narrow. That makes SAS a practical way to share files with partners, apps, or customers safely.
lessons.guessPrompt: A partner needs to download one report file from your cloud storage tomorrow, and nothing else. If you could hand them a link with rules baked into it, which rules would you put on that link to limit the damage if they lost it?
lessons.teach:
A shared access signature (SAS) is a token, a string of query parameters added to a storage URL, that grants limited, delegated access to Azure Storage. The token includes a cryptographic signature, a code computed from a secret. Storage recomputes the signature when a request arrives; if anyone edited the permissions or dates, the codes no longer match and the request is refused.

There are three kinds. A user delegation SAS is signed with a key obtained through Microsoft Entra ID (Azure's identity service), applies to Blob Storage, and is the most recommended because no account key is involved. A service SAS is signed with a storage account access key and covers one service, such as Blob, Files, Queue, or Table. An account SAS is also key-signed but can span several services and account-level operations.

Key settings are: signed permissions (read, write, delete, list, and so on), start and expiry time, allowed IP addresses, allowed protocol (HTTPS only is wise), and the resource scope, such as a single blob or a whole container.

Worked example: a partner needs read access to report.pdf for 24 hours. Step one, choose the scope: the single blob, not the container. Step two, pick Read permission only. Step three, set the expiry 24 hours ahead and allow HTTPS only. Step four, generate it in the portal, Storage Explorer, or the CLI, preferably as a user delegation SAS. Step five, send the resulting URL. When the partner downloads, Storage checks the signature, time, and permission, then serves the file. After 24 hours, the same link returns an authorization error.

A common mistake is issuing a broad, long-lived, key-signed SAS. A SAS is a bearer token: whoever holds it can use it. An ad hoc key-signed SAS cannot be cancelled individually; the main fix is rotating the account key that signed it, which also breaks every app using that key. A leaked token therefore stays usable until it expires or you take that disruptive step, so keep scope narrow and expiry short.

questions.prompt: A regional clinic hires a contractor whose script must upload one batch of appointment CSV files into a container named intake tonight. The upload window is 6 hours, and the contractor should not be able to see, download, or remove anything already in the container. The administrator has already decided several things. The scope is the intake container, because the files do not exist yet and so cannot be targeted one by one. The expiry is 6 hours from now, and the protocol is HTTPS only. The token will be generated as a user delegation SAS so that no account key is involved, and the resulting URL will go to the contractor. One decision is still missing: the signed permissions. Which permission choice completes this SAS correctly?
choices: Grant Read and List so the script can confirm its files landed
Grant Read, Write, Delete, and List so the script never hits a permission error
Grant Write only, with no Read, List, or Delete
Leave permissions unset, because the container scope already limits what the token can touch
questions.why: The contractor only needs to add files, so Write alone meets the need, while Read, List, and Delete would expose or endanger existing data and break the narrow-scope rule.

questions.prompt: A security team wants every SAS token for their blob data to be signed without using any storage account access key. They prefer credentials that come through Microsoft Entra ID, Azure's identity service. Which kind of SAS meets this requirement?
choices: Account SAS
An account SAS restricted to HTTPS only
User delegation SAS
Service SAS
questions.why: A user delegation SAS is signed with a key obtained through Microsoft Entra ID and applies to Blob Storage, so no account key is involved, while service and account SAS are both signed with an account key.

questions.prompt: An inventory app at a hardware wholesaler needs a single token that lets it put messages in a queue and also read blobs, both in the same storage account. Which kind of SAS can cover both services with one token?
choices: A service SAS for the Blob service
An account SAS
A user delegation SAS scoped to the container
A service SAS for the Queue service
questions.why: A service SAS covers only one service and a user delegation SAS applies to Blob Storage, but an account SAS can span several services in the account.

questions.prompt: A logistics company created an ad hoc, key-signed service SAS with read, write, and delete permissions on a whole container, valid for 9 months. It was pasted into a public chat today. Five other internal apps use the same storage account key. What is the main way to stop the leaked token from working right away, and what is the side effect?
choices: Edit the expiry date inside the leaked URL, since Storage will accept the shorter date
Rotate the account key that signed it, which also breaks the five apps until they get the new key
Change the container's name, because the token's signature only covers the account
Revoke that single token in the portal, leaving the five apps unaffected
questions.why: An ad hoc key-signed SAS cannot be cancelled individually, so the main fix is rotating the signing key, which disrupts every app using that key. Editing the URL would only make the signature check fail for the edited copy, while the original leaked token stays valid.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a SAS token is, the difference between a user delegation SAS and a key-signed SAS, and the main risk or limitation you have to plan for when handing one out.
lessons.modelAnswer: A SAS is a signed set of URL parameters that gives someone limited access to storage without giving them the account key. The signature locks in the permissions, the resource scope, the start and expiry time, and optionally allowed IPs and HTTPS only, so nobody can widen the access by editing the link. A user delegation SAS is signed with a key from Entra ID and works for blobs; it is preferred because no account key is exposed. Service and account SAS tokens are signed with an account access key; account SAS can cover several services. The big limitation is that a SAS is a bearer token: anyone who gets it can use it until it expires. A key-signed ad hoc SAS cannot be revoked individually, so revoking means rotating the key, which breaks other users of that key. So I keep permissions minimal, scope tight, and expiry short.
rubricPoints: A SAS is a signed token that grants limited, delegated access without sharing the account key.
The token encodes permissions, scope, start and expiry, and optional IP and protocol limits.
User delegation SAS is signed via Entra ID credentials; service and account SAS are signed with an account key.
A SAS is a bearer token, so anyone holding it can use it until expiry.
Revoking a key-signed ad hoc SAS requires rotating the signing key, which disrupts other users of that key.
Best practice is least privilege, narrow scope, short expiry, and HTTPS only.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing the right SAS type, scope, and revocation approach for a scenario, which is best practised by reasoning through situations rather than through an existing mission.

lessons.plain: A stored access policy is a named set of rules you save on a single storage container, file share, queue, or table. The rules can say what a temporary access link may do and when it stops working. Instead of baking those rules into each link, you point the link at the policy. Think of it like a guest list kept at the door instead of on the ticket: tickets only say which list to check, so crossing a name off the list cancels every ticket that points to it, without changing the locks on the building.
lessons.guessPrompt: You emailed a partner a time-limited link that lets them read files in one storage container, and now you need to cancel only that link before it expires. What could you keep on the storage side so you can switch it off without breaking every other link and app that uses the same account?
lessons.teach:
A stored access policy is a named rule set saved on one Azure Storage resource: a blob container, a file share, a queue, or a table. Each resource can hold up to five. A policy has an identifier (its name) and can set a start time, an expiry time, and permissions such as read, write, or list.

A shared access signature (SAS) is a signed token added to a URL that grants limited access to storage. A service SAS is a SAS signed with the storage account key that covers one service, such as Blob or Files. When you create a service SAS, you can reference a policy by its identifier. The SAS then takes its time window and permissions from the policy. Storage checks the policy each time the token is used, so editing or deleting the policy changes what every linked SAS can do.

Why this matters: an ad-hoc SAS has its rules signed inside the token. The only way to cancel it early is to rotate the account key that signed it. Rotating the key also breaks every other SAS, app, and script that uses that key.

Worked example. First, on the container named invoices, you create a policy called partner-read with read and list permissions and an expiry at month end. Second, you issue a service SAS that names partner-read and leaves out times and permissions. Third, the partner uses it normally. Fourth, the link leaks, so you delete partner-read. Within about 30 seconds the SAS is refused. Other tokens and the account keys keep working.

You can also revoke a SAS by setting the policy's expiry to a past time or by changing the policy's identifier.

Common mistakes: setting the same field, such as expiry, in both the SAS and the policy. Each field must come from only one place, or the request fails. Another mistake is recreating a deleted policy with the same name, which brings old tokens back to life. Also, policies work only with service SAS. An account SAS or a user delegation SAS cannot reference one.

questions.prompt: A weather-research group keeps sensor readings in an Azure Storage table named telemetry. Field devices need to add rows for the next 14 days, and the team wants to be able to cut them off early without touching the account keys. Step 1: on the telemetry table, they create a stored access policy called sensor-write with write permission and an expiry 14 days from now. Step 2: they issue a token for the devices. Step 3: the devices use the token to add rows until the policy expires or is changed. Which choice correctly describes Step 2?
choices: Issue a service SAS that names sensor-write and also sets the same 14-day expiry inside the token, so the time limit is enforced in two places.
Issue a user delegation SAS that names sensor-write, so the token is tied to a signed-in identity instead of the account key.
Issue a service SAS signed with the account key that names sensor-write and leaves out the start time, expiry, and permissions, so it takes them from the policy.
Issue an account SAS covering the Table service that names sensor-write as its policy, so it can later reach other services as well.
questions.why: Only a service SAS can reference a stored access policy, and each field must come from only one place, so the token names the policy and leaves the time window and permissions to it.

questions.prompt: A clinic gave a lab partner an ad-hoc service SAS for its file share named results. The token's expiry and permissions are signed inside it, and no stored access policy was used. The link has leaked. What is the only way to cancel this token before its expiry, and what side effect does it have?
choices: Set the token's expiry to a past time in the portal, which cancels only this token.
Delete the file share's stored access policy, which cancels only this token and leaves everything else working.
Rotate the account key that signed it, which also breaks every other SAS, app, and script that uses that key.
Create a stored access policy on the share with a past expiry, which overrides the expiry signed in the token.
questions.why: An ad-hoc SAS carries its rules inside the signed token, so the only early cancellation is rotating the signing key, and that breaks everything else that uses that key.

questions.prompt: An online shop issued several service SAS tokens that reference a stored access policy named courier-list on its container named labels. Last week, after a token leaked, an admin deleted courier-list. Today another admin creates a new policy on the same container and also names it courier-list. What happens to the old tokens?
choices: They fail with an error, because two policies with the same name cannot exist on one container.
They start working again, because they reference the policy by its name and that name now exists again.
They stay refused, because a deleted policy permanently cancels every token that ever referenced it.
They start working with the account's default permissions, because the new policy is ignored.
questions.why: Storage looks up the policy by its identifier each time a token is used, so recreating a policy with the same name brings the old tokens back to life.

questions.prompt: A media company wants one SAS token that grants access to both Blob and Queue storage in its account. It also wants to revoke the token later by editing a stored access policy. Why won't this plan work as described?
choices: A stored access policy can only set an expiry time, not permissions, so it cannot control what the token is allowed to do.
Each storage account can hold only one stored access policy, so it cannot cover two services.
A policy must be referenced by a user delegation SAS when more than one service is involved.
Stored access policies work only with a service SAS, and a token that spans more than one service is an account SAS, which cannot reference a policy.
questions.why: A service SAS covers one service and is the only kind of SAS that can reference a stored access policy, and an account SAS cannot reference one.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a stored access policy is, how it relates to a SAS token, and why you would use one instead of an ad-hoc SAS. Include at least one limit or tradeoff.
lessons.modelAnswer:
A stored access policy is a named rule set saved on one container, file share, queue, or table. It holds a start time, an expiry time, and permissions. When we create a service SAS, we can reference the policy by name, and the token gets its rules from the policy. Storage checks the policy every time the token is used.

The big win is revocation. We delete the policy, move its expiry into the past, or rename it, and every SAS tied to it stops working within about 30 seconds. Nothing else breaks. With an ad-hoc SAS, early cancellation means rotating the account key, which breaks everything signed with that key.

Limits: only five policies per resource, and they work only with service SAS, not account SAS or user delegation SAS. Each field can be set in the policy or the SAS, not both. Recreating a deleted policy with the same name reactivates old tokens.
rubricPoints: Defines a stored access policy as a named start, expiry, and permission set saved on a container, share, queue, or table.
Explains that a service SAS references the policy by its identifier and is checked against it on every use.
States that deleting, expiring, or renaming the policy revokes linked SAS tokens without rotating account keys.
Contrasts with an ad-hoc SAS, which can only be cancelled early by rotating the signing key.
Names a limit: five policies per resource, service SAS only, a field cannot be set in both places, or reusing a name revives old tokens.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing a stored access policy over key rotation or an ad-hoc SAS in revocation scenarios, so reasoning through situations like that builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: A storage account access key is like a master key to an entire building. Azure gives every storage account two of these long secret strings. Anyone holding one can read, change or delete anything in that account: blobs, files, queues and tables. Two keys exist so you can change the locks without locking everyone out. Programs use one key while you replace the other, then switch over. Because these keys are so powerful, managing them means keeping them secret, replacing them on a schedule, and, where possible, turning them off in favour of sign-in with a real identity.
lessons.guessPrompt: Azure gives every storage account two access keys instead of one, and both grant the same full access. Why might it be useful to have two identical-power keys?
lessons.teach:
A storage account access key is a 512-bit secret that Azure creates for each storage account. Every account has exactly two, called key1 and key2. Either one grants full control of all data in the account. This is called shared key authorization, because the same secret is shared by everyone who uses it. A connection string is a ready-made text value that bundles the account name with one of these keys, so programs can connect.

Two keys exist so you can rotate, which means replacing a key with a new random value, without downtime. Regenerating a key immediately invalidates the old value.

Here is a worked rotation. First, an app currently uses key1. Second, you update the app's configuration to use key2 and confirm it still works. Third, you regenerate key1. Nothing breaks, because no one uses it now. Fourth, at the next rotation, you move the app back to the new key1 and regenerate key2. At every moment, at least one valid key is in use.

To make this safer, store keys in Azure Key Vault, a managed secrets store. Apps then read the key at runtime instead of keeping it in code. You can also set a key expiration policy, which flags keys older than a chosen number of days so you remember to rotate. The strongest option is to disable shared key access on the account entirely. Clients must then authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID identities, Azure's sign-in and identity service, and access is controlled by role assignments.

A common mistake is regenerating the key an app is still using. The app fails at once. Also, any shared access signature tokens that were signed with that key stop working too. In a running system this appears as sudden authorization errors across every client holding the old key. The same thing happens if you disable shared key access before every client has moved to identity-based sign-in.

questions.prompt: A logistics company stores shipping documents in a storage account named shipdocs01. Both its invoicing service and its reporting tool currently connect with key2. The team wants to rotate key2 without any downtime. Step 1: They update the invoicing service and the reporting tool to use key1 instead. Step 2: They confirm both services still read and write documents successfully using key1. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: They note that at the next rotation the services will move back to the new key2, and key1 will then be regenerated. Which action belongs in Step 3?
choices: Regenerate key2, because no service uses it any more
Disable shared key access on the account
Regenerate key1, because it is now the key being used
Regenerate both key1 and key2 at the same time
questions.why: Once every client has moved to key1, key2 is unused, so regenerating it invalidates the old value without breaking anything.

questions.prompt: Each Azure storage account has exactly two access keys, key1 and key2. What is the main reason two keys exist?
choices: So key1 gives read access and key2 gives write access
So one key can be replaced with a new value while clients keep working on the other
So one key can be stored in Key Vault and the other kept in application code
So one key is used for blobs and the other for files
questions.why: Having two keys, each granting full access, lets you move clients to one key and regenerate the other, so a valid key is always in use.

questions.prompt: A museum's IT team keeps forgetting to rotate the access keys on its archive storage account. They want Azure to flag any key that is older than 45 days, as a reminder. Which feature fits this requirement?
choices: Store the keys in Azure Key Vault
Disable shared key access on the account
Create a new connection string every 45 days
Set a key expiration policy of 45 days
questions.why: A key expiration policy flags keys older than a chosen number of days so you remember to rotate them; it does not rotate or block anything by itself.

questions.prompt: A retail company's storage account has key1 and key2. Its point-of-sale app uses key1, and several partners download price lists using shared access signature (SAS) tokens that were signed with key1. An administrator regenerates key1 before changing anything else. What happens?
choices: Nothing fails until the old key's expiration policy date is reached
Only the app fails; SAS tokens are separate and keep working
The app and the partners' SAS tokens both start failing with authorization errors
Only the partners lose access; the app keeps working
questions.why: Regenerating a key invalidates its old value at once, so the app using key1 and any SAS tokens signed with key1 all stop working.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would rotate a storage account's access keys without an outage. Name one risk or limitation of relying on access keys at all.
lessons.modelAnswer: Every storage account has two access keys, key1 and key2, and each gives full control of all data in the account. Because there are two, we can rotate without downtime. First, we point every app at key2 and check it works. Then we regenerate key1, which is now unused. Next time, we move apps back to the new key1 and regenerate key2. Regeneration kills the old value instantly, so if we regenerate a key something still uses, that client fails right away. Any SAS tokens signed with that key also stop working. The keys should live in Key Vault rather than in code, and an expiration policy can remind us to rotate. The big limitation is that a key is all-or-nothing and not tied to a person, so a leak exposes everything. Where we can, we should disable shared key access and use Entra ID identities with roles.
rubricPoints: Each account has two keys and either one grants full access to all data in the account.
Rotation means switching clients to the other key, then regenerating the unused one.
Regenerating a key immediately breaks clients and SAS tokens that rely on it.
Keys should be stored in Key Vault and rotated on a schedule, with an expiration policy as a reminder.
Keys are all-or-nothing and not tied to an identity, so disabling shared key access in favour of Entra ID is safer.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing the right rotation order and knowing when to disable keys, which is best practised by reasoning through outage-style scenarios rather than any current mission.

lessons.plain: Azure Files is a managed network file share in the cloud that computers reach the same way they reach a shared drive on an office server. Identity-based access means people open the share as themselves, using their normal work sign-in, instead of everyone using one shared master password for the whole storage account. Think of an office building: rather than handing out copies of the master key, each employee badges in, and the building checks what rooms that badge may open. You can then grant, limit, or remove access per person or group, and every action is tied to a real person.
lessons.guessPrompt: If fifty employees need a shared drive in Azure, and some should only read files while others may edit them, why might giving everyone the storage account's single master key be a bad idea?
lessons.teach:
Identity-based access for Azure Files lets users mount a file share over SMB (Server Message Block, the Windows file-sharing protocol) with their own identity, verified by Kerberos, a ticket-based sign-in protocol. You enable one identity source per storage account: on-premises Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS, a company's own directory of users and computers), Microsoft Entra Domain Services (a managed domain service hosted by Microsoft), or Microsoft Entra Kerberos (lets Microsoft Entra ID, Azure's cloud identity service, issue Kerberos tickets for hybrid users who exist in both on-premises AD and the cloud).

Access is then checked in two layers. Share-level permissions are Azure role-based access control (RBAC) roles, meaning named permission sets assigned to users or groups: Storage File Data SMB Share Reader (read), Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor (read, write, delete), and Storage File Data SMB Share Elevated Contributor (also change file permissions). You can also set a default share-level permission that applies to every authenticated identity. Directory and file-level permissions are Windows ACLs (access control lists, the per-folder permissions in Windows Explorer). A user needs both layers to allow an action; the stricter one wins.

Worked example: Maria in group Finance mounts the share. First, her domain-joined PC gets a Kerberos ticket from the identity source. Second, Azure checks share level: Finance holds SMB Share Contributor, so she passes. Third, she opens the Payroll folder, whose ACL grants Finance read only. Result: she can read Payroll but cannot save edits there.

A common mistake is assigning the general Reader or Contributor role on the storage account. Those manage the resource itself, not file data, so users are still denied. Another is mounting with the storage account key, which bypasses both layers with full access. In a running system, either error means users get locked out or, worse, everyone silently has unrestricted access with no per-person audit trail.

questions.prompt: At a law firm, Devon (group Paralegals) mounts an Azure Files share over SMB. Step 1: his domain-joined laptop gets a Kerberos ticket from the configured identity source. Step 2: Azure checks share-level permissions. Paralegals holds the Storage File Data SMB Share Reader role. Step 3: [missing]. Result: Devon can open files in the Cases folder but cannot save changes to them. Which statement correctly fills Step 3?
choices: The Cases ACL grants Paralegals modify, so the ACL raises Devon to full read-write access.
Azure skips the ACL check because a share-level role exists, so only the Reader role is used.
The Cases ACL grants Paralegals read only, and a Windows ACL always overrides any share-level role.
The Cases ACL grants Paralegals modify, but share-level Reader is stricter, so writes are denied.
questions.why: Both layers must allow an action and the stricter one wins, so a read-only share-level role blocks writes even when the folder ACL would permit them.

questions.prompt: A hospital's IT team needs a group of records administrators to read, write, and delete files on an Azure Files share, and also to change the Windows file and folder permissions on that share. Which share-level role should the group receive?
choices: Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor
Contributor on the storage account
Storage File Data SMB Share Reader
Storage File Data SMB Share Elevated Contributor
questions.why: Only the Elevated Contributor role adds the ability to change file permissions on top of read, write, and delete.

questions.prompt: A retail company's users exist both in on-premises Active Directory and in Microsoft Entra ID. The company wants Microsoft Entra ID itself to issue the Kerberos tickets used when these users mount an Azure Files share. Which identity source should be enabled on the storage account?
choices: Storage account key authentication
Microsoft Entra Kerberos
Microsoft Entra Domain Services
On-premises AD DS
questions.why: Microsoft Entra Kerberos lets Microsoft Entra ID issue Kerberos tickets for hybrid users who exist in both on-premises AD and the cloud.

questions.prompt: At a logistics firm, a technician maps a shared drive for all warehouse staff by mounting the Azure Files share with the storage account key instead of their own identities. What is the effect?
choices: Share-level roles and folder ACLs are bypassed, so everyone has full access with no per-person audit trail.
Each user is still checked against share-level roles, but the folder ACLs are ignored.
Users are denied because the account key only grants rights to manage the storage resource.
Each user still gets a personal Kerberos ticket, so both permission layers still apply.
questions.why: Mounting with the storage account key bypasses both permission layers and grants full access, so actions cannot be traced to individual people.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a user gets permission to edit a file in an Azure file share using identity-based access, and name one limit or tradeoff of this approach.
