lessons.modelAnswer: With identity-based access, people mount the Azure file share using their own domain identity instead of the storage account key. First we enable one identity source on the storage account: on-premises AD DS, Microsoft Entra Domain Services, or Microsoft Entra Kerberos for hybrid users. The user's machine gets a Kerberos ticket, then two checks happen. At share level, an RBAC role such as Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor must allow writing. At folder and file level, Windows ACLs must also allow it. Both must say yes, so the stricter layer wins. Note that general storage account roles like Contributor do not grant file data access. A tradeoff is extra setup: you need a supported directory, often domain-joined clients and network reach on SMB, and only one identity source per account. Also, anyone mounting with the account key bypasses all of this, so keys must be guarded.
rubricPoints: Users authenticate with their own identity via Kerberos instead of the shared account key.
Names the supported identity sources and that only one is enabled per storage account.
Share-level access uses the Storage File Data SMB Share RBAC roles or a default share-level permission.
Directory and file-level access uses Windows ACLs, and both layers must allow the action.
Notes that general management roles do not grant file data access or that the account key bypasses identity checks.
States a limit such as setup complexity or the single identity source.

suggested.rationale: Evaluating whether a user passes both the share-level role check and the file ACL check is exactly the layered decision an authorization policy evaluator would let the learner practise.

lessons.plain: A storage account is the container Azure gives you for keeping data in the cloud. It is like renting a unit in a storage warehouse. You pick the building's location (the region), whether you want standard shelving or a fast climate-controlled unit (the performance level), and what kinds of things the unit is built to hold. Everything you store, whether files, large unstructured objects, simple message queues or table data, lives inside one account. The account gives that data a unique web address, and most settings apply to everything inside it. Some of those choices are hard to change once the unit is rented.
lessons.guessPrompt: If every storage account gets its own public web address, what do you think that means for the account's name, and could two companies use the same name?
lessons.teach:
A storage account is a named Azure resource that holds your data services: Blob Storage (object storage for unstructured data), Azure Files (managed network file shares), Queue Storage (a simple managed message queue) and Table Storage (a basic key-value store). When you create one, you make several decisions.

The name must be unique across all of Azure, 3 to 24 characters long, and use only lowercase letters and numbers. It needs to be unique because it becomes part of each service's address, called an endpoint, for example https://contosodata.blob.core.windows.net. The region is the Azure datacenter location where the data lives. Performance is either Standard, which runs on lower-cost hard-disk-backed storage, or Premium, which runs on solid-state drives for low, consistent latency. The account kind decides which services you get. General-purpose v2 (GPv2) is the everyday default. It supports all four services on Standard performance. Premium accounts are specialised. Block blob premium is for blobs. File shares premium (FileStorage) is for Azure Files only. Page blob premium is for page blobs, the kind used for virtual disks. You also pick a redundancy option, which sets how many copies of the data are kept and where. For a GPv2 account you also set a default access tier (Hot or Cool) for blobs. Those last two choices are covered in their own lessons.

Worked example: a team needs high-speed SMB file shares (SMB is the Windows file-sharing protocol) for a database workload. Step 1: it is file data, so the service is Azure Files. Step 2: it needs low latency, so the performance is Premium. Step 3: Premium plus files means the FileStorage account kind. Step 4: pick the region nearest the servers that use it.

Common mistake: assuming you can switch an account from Standard to Premium later. You cannot change the performance tier in place. You must create a new account and copy the data across. In a running system, that means a migration and a new endpoint for applications to point at.

questions.prompt: A medical imaging company, Litware Health, stores millions of scan images as unstructured objects. Radiologists need fast, consistent read times. Step 1: the data is unstructured objects, so the service is Blob Storage. Step 2: the team needs low, consistent latency, so the performance is Premium. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: choose the region nearest the radiologists' viewing servers. What is Step 3?
choices: Premium plus ordinary blobs means the block blob premium account kind
Premium plus blobs means the page blob premium account kind
Premium plus files means the FileStorage account kind
Blobs mean the general-purpose v2 (GPv2) account kind on Premium
questions.why: Ordinary objects such as images are block blobs, and the premium account kind for them is block blob premium, while page blob premium is for virtual disks and GPv2 offers all four services only on Standard.

questions.prompt: An administrator at Northwind Traders is naming a new storage account. Which proposed name is valid?
choices: nw
northwindbackupstorageaccount2025
northwindbackup01
Northwind-Backup
questions.why: A storage account name must be 3 to 24 characters and use only lowercase letters and numbers, and only northwindbackup01 meets every rule; the others have uppercase letters and hyphens, are too short, or are too long.

questions.prompt: A small logistics firm is building an app that keeps uploaded delivery photos in blobs, passes jobs between components through a message queue, and stores simple key-value records. Cost matters more than speed. Which account kind and performance fit best?
choices: General-purpose v2 (GPv2) on Standard performance
Page blob premium on Premium performance
FileStorage on Premium performance
Block blob premium on Premium performance
questions.why: GPv2 is the everyday default that supports Blob, Queue, Table and Files storage on lower-cost Standard performance, while each premium kind serves only one specialised service.

questions.prompt: Tailspin Toys has a GPv2 Standard storage account in production. The team now decides it needs Premium performance. What must happen?
choices: Set the default blob access tier to Hot, which gives Premium performance
Edit the account's performance setting from Standard to Premium
Create a new Premium account, copy the data, and point apps to its new endpoint
Change the account's redundancy option, which raises its performance tier
questions.why: The performance tier cannot be changed in place, so the data must be migrated to a new account, and because the new account has a different name, applications need its new endpoint.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between a general-purpose v2 account and a Premium account when creating storage, and name one choice that is hard to undo afterwards.
lessons.modelAnswer: A storage account is the Azure resource that holds blobs, file shares, queues and tables. Its name must be globally unique, 3 to 24 lowercase letters and numbers, because the name becomes part of each service's web address. For most workloads I'd create a general-purpose v2 account on Standard performance. It is cheaper, supports all four services, and lets me set a default Hot or Cool tier for blobs. I'd only pick Premium when the workload needs low, consistent latency on solid-state storage. Then I'd choose the matching kind: block blob for blobs, FileStorage for file shares, or page blob for virtual disks. The tradeoff is that Premium costs more and each Premium kind supports only one data type. The performance tier can't be changed in place. Moving from Standard to Premium means building a new account, copying the data, and repointing applications at the new endpoint.
rubricPoints: Defines a storage account as the resource that holds blob, file, queue and table data.
States the naming rules and that the name must be globally unique because it forms the endpoint address.
Contrasts Standard GPv2, which supports all services, with Premium kinds that each support a single service on solid-state storage.
Matches a requirement to the right performance and account kind.
Notes that performance cannot be changed in place, so changing it means migrating to a new account.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine creates storage accounts, and the exam skill is reasoning from a requirement to the right performance and account kind, which scenario questions practise best.

lessons.plain: Storage redundancy is how many copies of your data Azure keeps, and how far apart those copies sit, so a hardware failure or disaster does not lose it. Think of important papers. You can photocopy them three times and keep every copy in one drawer. You can spread the copies across three buildings in your town. Or you can also mail a set to a relative in another city. Each step costs a little more and survives a bigger disaster. Azure Storage gives you the same choice for each storage account, which is the container that holds your blobs, files, queues and tables.
lessons.guessPrompt: If your company keeps three copies of its data, but all three sit in the same building, which kinds of disaster would still destroy all of them?
lessons.teach:
Redundancy is set per storage account and controls where Azure keeps copies of your data. A region is a geographic area holding Azure datacenters. An availability zone is a physically separate datacenter group inside a region, with its own power and cooling. A paired secondary region is a second region, usually hundreds of kilometres away, that Azure chooses for you.

Locally redundant storage (LRS) keeps three copies inside one datacenter. It is the cheapest option and it survives a failed disk or server, but not the loss of the building. Zone-redundant storage (ZRS) writes three copies across three availability zones in one region. It survives a whole zone going down, and your data never leaves that region. Geo-redundant storage (GRS) keeps LRS copies in the primary region, then copies the data asynchronously to the secondary region. Asynchronously means the copy happens shortly after your write is confirmed, so the newest changes can be lost if the primary region fails. Geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS) combines ZRS in the primary region with a geo copy. The RA- versions (RA-GRS and RA-GZRS) add read access: you can read from the secondary region through a separate secondary endpoint at any time, even before any failover.

Here is a worked example. The requirement is that a blob service must survive a datacenter fire, keep the data in one country's region for legal reasons, and cost as little as possible. LRS fails the first test, because a fire destroys all three copies. GRS and GZRS break the residency rule, because they copy data to another region. That leaves ZRS as the answer.

A common mistake is assuming GRS lets you read from the secondary region during an outage. It does not. Plain GRS secondary data is only reachable after a failover, which is the act of promoting the secondary region to become the new primary. Only the RA- options give you a readable copy without one. In a running system, an app on plain GRS goes dark during a regional outage until someone triggers a failover. Even after the failover, any writes not yet copied across are lost.

questions.prompt:
A logistics company stores shipment photos in one storage account. Requirement 1: the photos must stay available if one availability zone (a separate datacenter group inside the region) in the primary region fails. Requirement 2: during a full outage of the primary region, customers must still be able to view photos without waiting for anyone to trigger a failover (promoting the secondary region to primary). The choice is worked through below with one step missing.

Step 1: LRS is ruled out because all three copies sit in one datacenter, so a zone loss takes them all.
Step 2: ZRS is ruled out because, although it survives a zone loss, every copy stays in one region, so a regional outage cuts off access.
Step 3: Plain GRS and plain GZRS are ruled out because their secondary copy can only be read after a failover.
Step 4: ???

Which statement correctly completes step 4?
choices: Choose RA-GZRS, because it spreads copies across zones in the primary region and allows reads from the secondary at any time.
Choose ZRS and plan a manual failover, because ZRS already protects against zone loss.
Choose GZRS anyway, because the photos become readable once the secondary region is promoted.
Choose RA-GRS, because adding read access to the secondary region satisfies both requirements on its own.
questions.why: Only RA-GZRS combines zone-spread copies in the primary region (requirement 1) with a secondary copy that can be read without a failover (requirement 2), whereas RA-GRS keeps only LRS copies in the primary region.

questions.prompt: An online bookshop's storage account uses geo-redundant storage (GRS). A customer's order record is written and the write is confirmed. Two seconds later the whole primary region fails before anything else happens. What is true about that order record?
choices: It is guaranteed to be safe in the secondary region, because the write was confirmed before the failure.
It may be lost, because GRS copies data to the secondary region shortly after the write is confirmed, not before.
It is safe because GRS stores three copies across availability zones in the primary region.
It is readable right away from the secondary endpoint, because GRS gives read access to the secondary.
questions.why: GRS copies to the secondary region asynchronously, meaning after the write is confirmed, so the newest changes can be lost if the primary region fails.

questions.prompt: A software team keeps temporary build logs in a storage account. The logs can be regenerated at any time, the only protection needed is against a single failed disk or server, and the team wants the lowest possible cost. Which redundancy option fits best?
choices: GRS, because it keeps a backup copy in another region in case the logs are needed.
ZRS, because it is the cheapest option that keeps copies in one region.
LRS, because it keeps three copies in one datacenter, survives a disk or server failure and is the cheapest.
RA-GRS, because it lets the team read the logs from a second region.
questions.why: LRS is the cheapest option and survives a failed disk or server, which is all this requirement asks for; the other options add protection and cost the team does not need.

questions.prompt: A ticketing website keeps its event data in a storage account set to plain GRS (no RA- prefix). The primary region suffers a full outage. What happens to the website's ability to read that data?
choices: Reads keep working because GRS spreads three copies across availability zones in the primary region.
Reads fail permanently, because GRS secondary data can never be reached by the account owner.
Reads fail until someone triggers a failover that promotes the secondary region, and any writes not yet copied across are lost.
Reads switch automatically to the secondary endpoint, so the site keeps working with no action needed.
questions.why: Plain GRS secondary data can only be reached after a failover, so the site goes dark until one is triggered, and writes not yet copied asynchronously are lost.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how LRS, ZRS, GRS/GZRS and their RA- versions differ, and name one tradeoff or limit you would warn them about when picking one.
lessons.modelAnswer: Each option says where the copies of our data live. LRS keeps three copies in one datacenter, so it only protects against hardware failures. ZRS spreads three copies across availability zones in one region, so a whole zone can fail and the data still stays in that region. GRS and GZRS also copy the data to a paired region far away, which protects us against losing an entire region. GZRS uses zone redundancy at home, while GRS uses only local copies there. The RA- versions let us read the secondary copy at any time. Plain GRS does not, so we would need a failover first. The tradeoffs are cost and data loss. More distance costs more. The geo copy is asynchronous, so a regional failure can lose our most recent writes. And geo options move data out of the region, which may break residency rules.
rubricPoints: LRS keeps three copies in one datacenter and survives only hardware failure.
ZRS spreads copies across availability zones in one region and survives a zone outage.
GRS and GZRS add an asynchronous copy in a paired secondary region, and GZRS uses zone redundancy in the primary region.
Only the RA- variants allow reading the secondary region without a failover.
Asynchronous geo replication can lose recent writes, and geo options move data out of the region.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a redundancy level against simulated disk, zone and region failures, then seeing what survives and what data is lost, builds exactly the requirement-to-feature judgement this objective tests.

lessons.plain: Object replication is a way to have Azure automatically copy files (called blobs) from a folder-like container in one storage account into a container in another storage account, often in a different region. You choose which containers are paired, and you can limit copying to blobs whose names start with a certain text. The copy happens in the background a little after each change, not instantly. Think of it like a mail-forwarding service you set up yourself. You decide which mailbox forwards to which address, mail arrives a bit later, and nobody writes letters directly at the forwarding address.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company stores product images in a storage account in West Europe, but most customers are in Australia. Without copying the whole account, how might you get just the images container to a storage account near Australia, and what would you expect about how up to date that copy is?
lessons.teach:
Object replication is an Azure Blob Storage feature that copies block blobs (ordinary files stored as blobs) asynchronously from a source container to a destination container in a different storage account. Asynchronous means the copy runs in the background after the write succeeds, so the destination can lag behind for a while.

It works because Azure tracks every change. You must turn on blob versioning, which keeps a numbered version each time a blob changes, on both accounts. You must also turn on change feed, an ordered log of every create and update, on the source account. The replication process reads the change feed and copies the matching versions across. You define a replication policy on the destination account, then on the source. The policy contains rules, and each rule pairs one source container with one destination container. A rule can add a prefix filter, which copies only blobs whose names start with given text. It can also choose whether existing blobs are copied or only new ones. Only general-purpose v2 and premium block blob accounts are supported, and append or page blobs are not replicated.

Worked example: a rule pairs container invoices in account A (East US) with container invoices-copy in account B (West US), with prefix filter 2024/. Step 1, an app uploads 2024/jan.pdf to A. Step 2, versioning records a version, and change feed logs the write. Step 3, the replication process sees the entry, the name matches 2024/, so it copies the blob to B. Step 4, the blob appears in invoices-copy, where replicated blobs are read-only. An upload of 2023/dec.pdf would not be copied.

A common mistake is confusing this with geo-redundant storage (GRS). GRS copies the entire account to a Microsoft-chosen paired region, and you cannot pick containers or filters. Another mistake is treating object replication as a backup. Overwrites and bad changes flow to the destination too.

In a running system, readers in the destination region may briefly see older data, so object replication suits read-near-users and copy-for-processing scenarios rather than anything needing instant consistency.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm, Northwind Freight, stores scanned delivery photos in container scans in storage account FREIGHTSRC (North Europe). A team in West Europe needs copies for processing, so an administrator sets up object replication. Versioning is on in both accounts, change feed is on in the source, and one rule pairs container scans with container scans-proc in account FREIGHTDST (West Europe), with prefix filter depot7/. Trace two uploads. Step 1: a driver app uploads depot7/truck42.jpg to scans; versioning records a version and change feed logs the write. Step 2: the replication process reads the entry, sees the name starts with depot7/, and copies the blob to scans-proc, where it appears as read-only. Step 3: the app then uploads depot3/truck18.jpg to scans; versioning records a version and change feed logs the write. Step 4: ??? Which choice correctly completes Step 4?
choices: The replication process copies depot3/truck18.jpg to scans-proc, because a rule always copies every blob in its source container.
The replication process copies depot3/truck18.jpg to scans-proc and lets readers there edit it, since it falls outside the filter.
The replication process reads the entry, but the name does not start with depot7/, so depot3/truck18.jpg is not copied.
Azure copies depot3/truck18.jpg to the Microsoft-chosen paired region instead, because it did not match the rule.
questions.why: A prefix filter limits the rule to blobs whose names start with the given text, so depot3/truck18.jpg is logged but skipped.

questions.prompt: Contoso Health wants copies of only the blobs in its lab-results container, and only those whose names start with final/, sent to a storage account it chooses in Australia East. Which Azure Storage feature meets this requirement?
choices: Change feed alone, which keeps an ordered log of writes and copies each logged blob to another region
Object replication, using a rule that pairs the container with a destination container and applies the prefix filter final/
Geo-redundant storage (GRS), which copies the account to a region and lets you pick which containers are included
Blob versioning alone, which keeps a numbered version of each blob and sends it to a second account
questions.why: Object replication lets you pair specific containers in accounts you choose and filter by name prefix, while GRS copies the whole account to a Microsoft-chosen paired region with no container or filter choice.

questions.prompt: At Fabrikam Studios, an administrator set up an object replication rule from container renders in a general-purpose v2 account to a container in another general-purpose v2 account. Ordinary image files (block blobs) copy correctly, but a set of virtual disk files stored as page blobs in the same container never appear at the destination. What is the most likely reason?
choices: Versioning on the destination account blocks page blobs from being written there
The rule has no prefix filter, and page blobs are only copied when a filter is set
Change feed must be turned on in the destination account before any page blobs can be logged
Object replication copies only block blobs, so page blobs are never replicated
questions.why: Object replication works only on block blobs; append blobs and page blobs are not replicated, regardless of filters or settings.

questions.prompt: Tailspin Retail uses object replication to copy its price-lists container from an account in Central US to a second account in UK South. An employee accidentally overwrites prices/spring.csv in the source with a blank file. What happens at the destination, and what does this show?
choices: The blank file is also copied to the destination, showing object replication is not a backup
The destination instantly switches to the blank file, showing object replication gives immediate consistency
Nothing changes until the administrator approves the change in the replication policy on the source
The destination keeps the old file safe, because replicated blobs are read-only and ignore later source changes
questions.why: Overwrites and bad changes are replicated just like good ones (asynchronously, so with some delay), which is why object replication should not be treated as a backup.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what object replication does and what it needs turned on. Say when you would pick it over geo-redundant storage, and name one limitation they should plan around.
lessons.modelAnswer: Object replication copies block blobs in the background from a container in one storage account to a container in another account. That other account can be in a different region. We set a replication policy with rules, and each rule pairs a source container with a destination container. A rule can filter by name prefix and can include existing blobs or only new ones. It needs blob versioning on both accounts and change feed on the source, because the replication process reads that change log to know what to copy. I'd pick it over GRS when we want control: specific containers, a region we choose, and a destination we can actually read from. GRS just mirrors the whole account to a fixed paired region. Limitations: copies are asynchronous, so the destination can be slightly stale. Replicated blobs are read-only at the destination. Only block blobs are copied, and it isn't a backup, because bad overwrites replicate too.
rubricPoints: States it asynchronously copies block blobs between containers in different storage accounts.
Names the prerequisites: versioning on both accounts and change feed on the source.
Describes a policy of rules pairing containers, with optional prefix filters.
Contrasts it with GRS: chosen containers and regions versus a whole-account copy to a fixed pair.
Names a limit such as lag, read-only destination, block blobs only, or not being a backup.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing object replication over similar options like GRS for a stated requirement, so reasoning through scenario-style situations adds the most.

lessons.plain: Storage account encryption means Azure scrambles your data before it is written to disk and unscrambles it when an authorized request reads it back. It is always on and cannot be switched off. What you choose is who controls the key that does the scrambling. Think of a bank safe-deposit box. By default the bank holds the master key for you. You can instead bring your own master key, kept in your own key vault, so that if you take that key away, nobody can open the box, not even the bank.
lessons.guessPrompt: If your company insists it must be able to make stored data unreadable on demand, would you rather Microsoft hold the encryption key or your company hold it, and why?
lessons.teach:
Azure Storage service-side encryption (SSE) automatically encrypts every blob, file, queue and table with AES-256, a strong standard cipher, at rest. Encryption at rest means protection while the data sits on disk. You cannot disable it, and it adds no extra cost.

The setting you configure is key management. With Microsoft-managed keys, the default, Azure creates, stores and rotates the keys. With customer-managed keys (CMK), you keep a key in Azure Key Vault, a managed secret and key store, and the account uses it. This works by envelope encryption: data is encrypted with a data encryption key (DEK), and the DEK is itself encrypted, or wrapped, by your key encryption key (KEK) in Key Vault. Rotating the KEK only re-wraps the DEK, so the data does not need re-encrypting.

Worked example: you switch an account to CMK. First, the Key Vault must have soft delete and purge protection enabled, so a key cannot be destroyed by accident. Second, the storage account gets a managed identity, an Azure-issued identity for a resource. Third, you grant that identity permission to wrap and unwrap keys in the vault. Fourth, you point the account's encryption setting at the key, optionally with automatic version updates. Now every read asks Key Vault to unwrap the DEK.

Related options: infrastructure encryption adds a second layer of encryption with a separate key, and it can only be enabled when the account is created. Encryption scopes let different containers or blobs use different keys within one account. Customer-provided keys are supplied by the client on each Blob request rather than stored in Azure.

A common mistake is disabling or deleting the CMK, or removing the identity's vault access, during cleanup. The running consequence is that the account's data immediately becomes unreadable, and every application that reads it fails until access to the key is restored.

questions.prompt: Northwind Clinics' storage account 'nwpatients' holds 4 TB of blobs. It uses a customer-managed key (a key the organisation keeps in Azure Key Vault, a managed key store) with automatic version updates turned on. Policy requires rotating that key every 90 days. Trace of the day-90 rotation. Step 1: a new version of the key is created in Key Vault. Step 2: because automatic version updates is on, the storage account picks up the new key version. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: applications keep reading all 4 TB without interruption, and no bulk rewrite job ever runs. Which statement correctly fills Step 3?
choices: The account temporarily switches to Microsoft-managed keys until the rotation has finished.
The old key version is purged from the vault so that it can no longer unwrap anything.
Azure re-encrypts all 4 TB of blobs with the new key version, working through them one blob at a time.
The data encryption key is re-wrapped with the new key version, and the blobs themselves are left as they are.
questions.why: With envelope encryption the key in Key Vault only wraps the data encryption key, so rotating it re-wraps that one key and leaves the data alone, which is why no rewrite is needed.

questions.prompt: An engineer at Fabrikam asks you to turn off at-rest encryption on a 200 GB test storage account to save money. At-rest encryption protects data while it sits on disk. What is the correct response?
choices: Switch the account to Microsoft-managed keys, which turns encryption off and removes the charge.
Disable infrastructure encryption, because that is the setting that controls at-rest encryption.
Delete the customer-managed key, which leaves the stored data unencrypted and free of charge.
It cannot be done: service-side encryption is always on for the account and adds no extra cost.
questions.why: Azure Storage service-side encryption always encrypts the data with AES-256, cannot be disabled, and costs nothing extra, so there is nothing to turn off and nothing to save.

questions.prompt: Contoso Legal stores files for three client firms in three containers inside one storage account. Each client requires that its data be encrypted under its own separate key, and all three keys must stay in Contoso's Key Vault. Which feature meets this requirement?
choices: Customer-provided keys, which the client application sends with each Blob request
Encryption scopes, which let different containers in one account use different keys
A separate managed identity assigned to each container
Infrastructure encryption, which adds a second encryption layer to the account
questions.why: Encryption scopes allow different containers or blobs in one account to use different keys, while customer-provided keys are not stored in Azure and infrastructure encryption applies to the whole account.

questions.prompt: Tailspin's storage account uses a customer-managed key in Key Vault. At 02:00 a cleanup script removes the storage account's managed identity (the Azure-issued identity for the resource) from the vault's access permissions. What happens to the 14 applications that read from the account?
choices: They keep working, because Azure automatically falls back to Microsoft-managed keys for the account.
They keep working normally until the next scheduled key rotation, and only then do they start to fail.
Their reads fail right away, because the account can no longer unwrap its data key, until vault access is restored.
Only new writes fail; blobs that were already stored stay readable for the applications.
questions.why: Every read needs Key Vault to unwrap the data encryption key, so losing the identity's vault access makes the data unreadable immediately and the applications fail until access is restored.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between Microsoft-managed and customer-managed keys for a storage account, including one risk or tradeoff of choosing customer-managed keys.
lessons.modelAnswer: Every storage account is already encrypted at rest with AES-256, and that cannot be turned off. The choice is who controls the key. With Microsoft-managed keys, Azure handles creation and rotation and we do nothing. With customer-managed keys, we keep a key in Key Vault, give the storage account a managed identity, and grant it wrap and unwrap rights. Azure uses envelope encryption, so our key wraps the data encryption key, and rotating our key does not re-encrypt the data. The benefit is control: we can revoke access and own rotation for compliance. The tradeoff is operational risk. If someone deletes or disables the key or breaks the identity's access, all data in the account becomes unreadable. That is why the vault needs soft delete and purge protection. If we want double encryption, infrastructure encryption must be enabled when the account is created.
rubricPoints: States that encryption at rest with AES-256 is always on and cannot be disabled.
Distinguishes Microsoft-managed keys from customer-managed keys stored in Key Vault.
Mentions the managed identity and Key Vault permissions needed for customer-managed keys.
Explains that envelope encryption means key rotation re-wraps only the data key.
Names the risk that losing or disabling the key makes data unreadable.
Notes infrastructure encryption must be chosen at account creation, or mentions encryption scopes.

suggested.rationale: Wrapping a data key with a key encryption key, rotating it, and revoking it in a lab directly builds the intuition behind customer-managed keys.

lessons.plain: Azure Storage holds files in the cloud, and you need ways to move data in and out and look around. Azure Storage Explorer is a free desktop app with windows and folders: you sign in, browse your storage accounts, and drag files up or down, much like a file manager on your laptop. AzCopy is a small command-line program that does the same job by typed commands, so it suits big transfers, scripts and scheduled jobs. Think of Storage Explorer as carrying boxes by hand while you look at the shelves, and AzCopy as a delivery truck you can send on a timetable.
lessons.guessPrompt: You must copy 2 million files from an on-premises server to Azure every night at 2 a.m. with no one at a keyboard. Would you pick a point-and-click desktop app or a command-line tool, and why?
lessons.teach:
Azure Storage Explorer is a free graphical application (Windows, macOS, Linux) for browsing and managing Azure Storage. It shows storage accounts, blob containers (folders for unstructured objects called blobs), file shares (network drives in Azure Files), queues and tables. You can upload, download, rename, delete, set access tiers, create a shared access signature (SAS, a signed URL granting limited, time-bound access) and view properties. It connects by signing in with a Microsoft Entra ID account, an account key, a SAS, or a connection string. Notably, Storage Explorer uses AzCopy behind the scenes for its transfers.

AzCopy is a free command-line utility for copying data to, from and between storage accounts. It is fast because it runs many transfers in parallel, can resume a failed job, and can copy between accounts server-side without the data passing through your machine. It authenticates with Entra ID (azcopy login) or by appending a SAS to the URL. Key commands: azcopy copy (copy everything named), azcopy sync (copy only what is new or changed, comparing last-modified times), azcopy list, azcopy remove and azcopy make.

Worked example: a nightly backup of D:\reports to a container. Step 1, the script runs azcopy login with a managed identity or service principal. Step 2, it runs azcopy sync "D:\reports" "https://acct.blob.core.windows.net/reports" --recursive. Step 3, AzCopy lists both sides, sees 40 changed files out of 50,000, and uploads only those 40. Step 4, it writes a job log you can check if anything failed.

Common mistake: adding --delete-destination=true to sync without thinking. It makes the destination mirror the source, so a file accidentally deleted locally is also deleted in Azure, which defeats a backup. Another frequent slip is forgetting --recursive, so subfolders are skipped silently. Choose Storage Explorer for occasional, visual, ad-hoc work, and AzCopy for large, repeatable or automated transfers.

questions.prompt: A retail company is retiring an old storage account named oldinv and moving 7,500 archived invoice blobs into a container on a new account named newinv. An administrator runs the move from a laptop on a slow home connection. Step 1: she creates a shared access signature (SAS, a signed, time-limited URL) on the source container that allows read and list, and a second SAS on the destination container that allows write. Step 2: she runs azcopy copy "https://oldinv.blob.core.windows.net/invoices?<source-SAS>" "https://newinv.blob.core.windows.net/invoices?<dest-SAS>" --recursive. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: Wi-Fi drops after 3,000 blobs, so she resumes the AzCopy job and it carries on with the remaining blobs. Which statement correctly fills Step 3, describing what happens to the data during the copy?
choices: Because both ends are storage accounts, the copy happens server-side between them, so the invoice data does not pass through the laptop.
AzCopy deletes any blob in newinv that does not exist in oldinv so the two containers match exactly.
AzCopy copies only invoices whose last-modified time is newer on oldinv than on newinv, skipping the rest.
AzCopy downloads each invoice to the laptop and then uploads it to newinv, so the slow home connection sets the speed limit.
questions.why: When AzCopy copies between two storage accounts, the transfer runs server-side, so the data does not pass through the machine running the command.

questions.prompt: A marketing coordinator at a travel agency sometimes needs to look through a blob container of brochure images. A few times a month she renames a handful of files, and she gives an outside printer a link that works for three days. She is not comfortable with command lines. Which option fits her best?
choices: A scheduled azcopy sync job that runs every night against the container
Azure Storage Explorer, where she can browse, rename, and create a shared access signature from a graphical interface
The azcopy make command, run each time she needs a new link
A server-side azcopy copy from the container to a second storage account
questions.why: Storage Explorer is the free graphical tool for occasional, visual, ad-hoc work, and it can create a shared access signature, which is a time-limited link.

questions.prompt: A law firm backs up C:\contracts to Azure each night using azcopy sync with the --recursive and --delete-destination=true options. On Tuesday afternoon a paralegal accidentally deletes a local subfolder that holds 300 contracts. What happens to those 300 contracts in Azure after Tuesday night's run?
choices: They are moved to a separate recovery container that AzCopy creates automatically
They are kept in Azure, because sync only uploads new or changed files and never removes anything
They are deleted from Azure too, because the destination is made to mirror the source
The sync fails and writes an error to the job log, because files are missing on the source side
questions.why: With --delete-destination=true, sync makes the destination mirror the source, so a local deletion is copied to Azure. That defeats the purpose of a backup.

questions.prompt: An architecture studio runs azcopy copy "E:\designs" "https://studio.blob.core.windows.net/designs" with no other options. E:\designs holds 12 files directly inside it, plus subfolders for each project that hold about 900 more files. The command finishes without errors. What most likely ended up in the container?
choices: Nothing at all, because azcopy copy needs --recursive to upload any files
Only files changed since the last run, because azcopy copy compares last-modified times
Only the 12 top-level files, because without --recursive the subfolders were silently skipped
All 912 files, because azcopy copy always includes subfolders
questions.why: Leaving out --recursive means AzCopy skips subfolders without warning, so only the files sitting directly in the top folder are copied.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would use Azure Storage Explorer versus AzCopy, including one limit or risk of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both move data in and out of Azure Storage. Storage Explorer is a desktop app with a visual tree of accounts, containers and file shares; it is great for occasional jobs like checking a blob, uploading a few files, changing a tier or generating a SAS. Its limit is that someone has to sit at it, so it doesn't fit scheduled or scripted work. AzCopy is a command-line tool that transfers in parallel, can resume jobs and copy server-side between accounts, so it suits huge or nightly transfers in a script. You log in with Entra ID or append a SAS. Use copy to send everything and sync to send only changes. The risk is sync with delete-destination turned on: local deletions get mirrored to Azure, so a mistake can wipe your backup. Explorer actually uses AzCopy underneath for its transfers.
rubricPoints: Storage Explorer is a graphical desktop tool for browsing and ad-hoc management of blobs, files, queues and tables.
AzCopy is a command-line tool suited to large, scripted or scheduled transfers, including server-side copies between accounts.
AzCopy authenticates with Microsoft Entra ID login or a SAS appended to the URL.
copy transfers everything named while sync transfers only new or changed items.
Names a risk or limit, such as sync with delete-destination removing data or Explorer not being automatable.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine exercises these tools, and the exam tests choosing the right tool and command for a scenario, which reasoning through situations practises best.

lessons.plain: Azure Files gives you a shared network drive that lives in the cloud. A file share is one of those drives: a folder tree that several computers can open at the same time, just like a shared drive on an office server, except Microsoft runs the hardware. Programs use it with ordinary file paths, so nothing needs rewriting. Think of a storage account as a building and a file share as one shared filing cabinet in it: you choose its size limit, how fast it is, and who connects, and every desk in the office can reach the same drawers.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team already has an old app that reads and writes files on a mapped network drive like Z:. If you move that app to cloud virtual machines, would you rather give it blob storage (objects reached through a web address) or a cloud file share it can map as a drive? Why?
lessons.teach:
An Azure file share is a fully managed network file share inside a storage account (the top-level Azure container that holds storage services and has a unique name). Clients reach it with SMB (Server Message Block, the file-sharing protocol Windows uses, also supported on Linux and macOS) or NFS (Network File System, common on Linux). It works because the share behaves like a normal file server, so apps that expect paths, folders and file locks run unchanged.

When you create a share you set a few things. The name: lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens. The quota: the maximum size in GiB, which caps growth. The tier: on a standard account (hard-disk-backed) you choose transaction optimized, hot or cool, trading storage price against per-operation price; on a premium account (solid-state-backed, requiring the FileStorage account kind) you get low latency and pay for provisioned size. The protocol: NFS shares need a premium account and a private network path, while SMB works on both.

Worked example. A team needs a 100 GiB shared folder for Windows VMs with light, steady use. Step 1: in an existing standard general-purpose v2 account, create a share named team-docs. Step 2: set the quota to 100 GiB. Step 3: pick the hot tier for regular access. Step 4: use the portal's Connect button to get a mount script. Step 5: run it on a VM; it maps a drive letter to a path like \\accountname.file.core.windows.net\team-docs over SMB port 445.

A common mistake is forgetting that SMB uses TCP port 445, which many home internet providers and corporate firewalls block. The mount then fails with a vague network error even though the share is fine. In a running system this means on-premises users cannot connect until port 445 is opened, or traffic goes over a VPN or private connection. Another frequent error is choosing premium or NFS after creating a standard account, since the account kind cannot simply be switched later.

questions.prompt: A research lab runs Linux compute nodes that need a 2 TiB shared folder mounted with NFS, and the team wants low latency. An administrator plans the work as follows. Step 1: [missing]. Step 2: create a share named lab-results with a quota of 2048 GiB. Step 3: choose NFS as the protocol. Step 4: give the nodes a private network path to the account and mount the share. Which choice correctly fills Step 1?
choices: Create a standard general-purpose v2 account and pick the hot tier
Create a premium account of the FileStorage kind
Create a standard account now and switch it to premium once the share exists
Create a standard account and pick the transaction optimized tier
questions.why: NFS shares need a premium (solid-state) account, which requires the FileStorage account kind, and the account kind cannot simply be switched after creation.

questions.prompt: A legal firm wants to keep closed case files in an Azure file share on a standard (hard-disk-backed) storage account. The files are rarely opened, and the firm wants the lowest storage price, accepting higher per-operation prices. Which tier fits best?
choices: Transaction optimized
Premium provisioned
Cool
Hot
questions.why: On a standard account, cool trades a lower storage price for higher per-operation prices, which suits rarely accessed data.

questions.prompt: A retail company creates an SMB file share in Azure. Virtual machines in Azure mount it without problems, but staff in a store office get a vague network error when they try to map it, even though the share is healthy. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The share name contains uppercase letters
The store's network blocks TCP port 445, which SMB uses
The share's quota is set too low for the store's files
SMB only works on premium accounts, so the store needs NFS
questions.why: SMB uses TCP port 445, which many internet providers and corporate firewalls block, so on-premises users fail until the port is opened or traffic goes over a VPN or private connection.

questions.prompt: An administrator is creating an Azure file share for a payroll team. Which of these share names is valid?
choices: Payroll_Archive
payroll-archive-2024
PayrollArchive2024
payroll archive
questions.why: File share names may contain only lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens, so only payroll-archive-2024 meets the rule.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what an Azure file share is, how it differs from a blob container, and which settings you choose when creating one. Name at least one limit or tradeoff they should know before choosing.
lessons.modelAnswer: An Azure file share is a managed network drive inside a storage account. Unlike a blob container, which stores objects reached through a web address, a file share is mounted like a normal drive over SMB or NFS, so existing apps that use file paths and locks keep working. When creating one I choose a name, a quota that caps its size, and a tier. On a standard account the tiers are transaction optimized, hot and cool, which trade storage cost against per-operation cost. Premium shares need a FileStorage account and give lower latency, but you pay for the size you provision. NFS only works on premium shares over a private network path. A practical limit is that SMB uses port 445, which is often blocked, so on-premises clients may need a VPN or private connection to mount the share.
rubricPoints: Defines a file share as a managed network share inside a storage account, mounted over SMB or NFS.
Contrasts it with blob storage, which is object storage reached by web address rather than mounted as a drive.
Names the creation settings: share name, quota, and tier.
Distinguishes standard tiers from premium, including that premium needs the FileStorage account kind.
Mentions a limit such as SMB port 445 being blocked, or NFS requiring premium and private networking.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine creates file shares, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios that pick between tiers, protocols and blob versus file storage builds the comparison skill this unit tests.

lessons.plain: A container in Azure Blob Storage is a named folder-like bucket inside a storage account that holds blobs. A blob is any file stored as an object, such as an image, backup, or log. Think of the storage account as a warehouse, containers as labelled rooms inside it, and blobs as the boxes in each room. You create containers to group related files and to decide, room by room, who may walk in. The most important setting is whether anyone on the internet can read the files without signing in, or only people with credentials.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you put company invoices in a storage container, what do you think the safest default should be: anyone with the web address can read them, or only signed-in or authorised callers can? Why?
lessons.teach:
A container is the grouping layer between a storage account (the top-level Azure resource that owns your data and its address) and blobs (individual stored objects). Every blob lives in exactly one container, and an account can hold as many containers as you need. Each blob gets a web address built from all three: https://ACCOUNT.blob.core.windows.net/CONTAINER/BLOB.

Container names must be 3 to 63 characters, use only lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens, start with a letter or number, and contain no two hyphens in a row. They must be unique within the account, not globally.

The namespace (the way names are organised) is flat: there are no real subfolders. A slash in a blob name, such as reports/jan.csv, only creates a virtual directory that tools display as a folder.

The key container setting is the anonymous (public) access level. Private means every request needs authorisation. Blob means anyone can read a blob if they know its exact address, but cannot list contents. Container means anyone can read blobs and also list everything in the container. Anonymous access works only if the storage account itself allows it; newer accounts block it by default, which overrides the container setting. You can also attach metadata, meaning name-value labels such as department=finance.

Worked example: you create a container named invoices-2024 with Private access. You upload march/inv-001.pdf. Its address becomes https://contoso.blob.core.windows.net/invoices-2024/march/inv-001.pdf. An unauthenticated browser request is refused; an authorised user can read it, and the portal shows a virtual folder called march.

A common mistake is choosing Container level when Blob level was enough, or naming a container Invoices2024 with a capital letter, which is rejected. In a running system, an over-permissive level lets outsiders list and download every file, a real data leak, while a too-strict account setting makes a public website's images fail to load.

questions.prompt: Fabrikam runs an online shop. An administrator creates a container named catalog-photos in the storage account fabrikamweb and sets its anonymous access level to Blob. The account itself allows anonymous access. Step 1: she uploads a blob named shoes/red-01.jpg. Step 2: its address becomes https://fabrikamweb.blob.core.windows.net/catalog-photos/shoes/red-01.jpg. Step 3: a visitor who is not signed in opens that exact address and the image loads. Step 4 (missing): the same visitor, still not signed in, sends a request to list everything in catalog-photos. What happens?
choices: The request is refused, because Blob level allows reading a blob by its exact address but not listing.
The list is returned, because the account allows anonymous access and that overrides the Blob level.
The list is returned, because a visitor who can read one blob can also list the whole container.
Only the virtual folder shoes is listed, because Blob level shows folders but hides file names.
questions.why: Blob level lets anonymous users read a blob only when they know its exact address, so listing the container's contents is still refused.

questions.prompt: A team at Northwind wants a new container for its quarterly reports. Which proposed container name follows Azure's naming rules?
choices: -q3reports
q3-reports-2025
Q3-Reports
q3--reports
questions.why: q3-reports-2025 is all lowercase, uses only letters, numbers and single hyphens, starts with a letter, and is within 3 to 63 characters; the others use a capital letter, a double hyphen, or start with a hyphen.

questions.prompt: At Tailwind Traders, a container named brochures is set to the Container anonymous access level, but the storage account that holds it is a newer account that still blocks anonymous access by default. A visitor who is not signed in tries to open a brochure by its exact address. What happens?
choices: The brochure loads, but listing is refused, because the account setting reduces Container to Blob level.
The brochure loads, because a container's access level always takes priority over the account setting.
The brochure loads and the visitor can also list the container, because Container is the most open level.
The request is refused, because the account blocking anonymous access overrides the container setting.
questions.why: Anonymous access works only if the storage account allows it, so an account that blocks it overrides even the Container level and all unauthenticated requests are refused.

questions.prompt: In a container named diagnostics, an administrator uploads a blob named logs/2025/app.txt. The portal now shows folders called logs and 2025. Which statement is accurate?
choices: Azure created two real subfolders, logs and 2025, which must be deleted separately from the blob.
The upload creates two extra containers, logs and 2025, nested inside the diagnostics container.
There is a single blob whose name contains slashes; logs and 2025 are virtual directories shown by tools.
The slash is rejected, so the blob is stored under the name app.txt directly in diagnostics.
questions.why: Blob Storage has a flat namespace, so slashes in a blob name only create virtual directories that tools display as folders; no real subfolders or containers are created.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a Blob Storage container is, how its anonymous access levels differ, and name one limit or tradeoff they should watch for when configuring one.
lessons.modelAnswer: A container is a named grouping inside a storage account that holds blobs, which are our stored files. The blob's URL is the account address plus the container name plus the blob name. Names must be 3 to 63 lowercase letters, numbers, or single hyphens. Folders are not real; a slash in a blob name just makes a virtual directory. The main setting is anonymous access: Private requires authorisation for every request, Blob lets anyone read a file if they know its exact address, and Container also lets them list everything. The tradeoff is convenience versus exposure: Container level is easy for public content but reveals every file name. Also, the storage account can disallow anonymous access entirely, and that overrides whatever the container says, so a public setting may silently not work.
rubricPoints: Defines a container as the grouping of blobs inside a storage account and shows how it forms part of the blob URL.
States the naming rules: 3 to 63 characters, lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens.
Distinguishes Private, Blob, and Container anonymous access levels, including that only Container allows listing.
Notes that the account-level anonymous access setting overrides the container level.
Explains that folders are virtual because the namespace is flat.
Names a tradeoff such as public convenience versus data exposure.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine creates storage containers, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios that pick the correct access level and naming is the most useful practice.

lessons.plain: Azure Blob Storage, Microsoft's service for storing files as objects called blobs, lets you choose an access tier for each blob. The tier is a price-and-speed setting. Hot is for data you read often. Cool and Cold are for data you read less often. Archive is for data you almost never read. Think of a self-storage company. Hot is a locker by the front door: high rent, instant access. Archive is a sealed crate in a distant warehouse: very cheap, but you wait hours to get it back. Choosing the right tier means paying only for the access you actually need.
lessons.guessPrompt: You must keep scanned tax records for seven years, and you expect to open them perhaps once, during an audit. Would you pay more to store them or more to read them, and why?
lessons.teach:
An access tier is a setting on a block blob that trades storage cost against access cost and speed. A block blob is the ordinary blob type used for files such as documents, images, and backups. Azure offers four tiers. Hot has the highest storage price and the lowest read price. Cool and Cold charge progressively less to store data and more to read it. Archive is the cheapest to store and the most expensive to read, and its data is offline. Offline means you cannot read the blob until it is rehydrated. Rehydration is the process of moving the blob back to an online tier, either by changing its tier or by copying it to a new blob. Standard priority rehydration can take up to about 15 hours. High priority is faster but costs more.

Tiers work this way because data that is read rarely can sit on cheaper, slower storage. In return, Azure sets a minimum retention period: about 30 days for Cool, 90 for Cold, and 180 for Archive. If you delete a blob or move it to another tier before that period ends, you pay an early deletion charge for the days that remain.

Worked example: you upload a backup on day 0 and set it to Cool. On day 20 you delete it. Cool has a 30-day minimum, so you are billed as if it had stayed 10 more days. If you had expected to delete it within days, Hot would have been the cheaper choice.

A storage account, the container that holds your blobs and their settings, has a default access tier, either Hot or Cool. Blobs with no explicit tier inherit that default. Archive can only be set on individual blobs. Archive is also unavailable when the account uses zone-redundant replication, which keeps copies across separate datacenters in a region.

A common mistake is to confuse the access tier with the performance tier. Standard versus Premium is a separate choice about disk speed, and Premium block blob accounts do not use access tiers at all. Another mistake is archiving data that an application reads, which makes that application fail or stall for hours in production.

questions.prompt: A veterinary clinic uploads a set of scanned patient records on day 0 and sets them to the Cold tier. On day 60 the team decides it needs them often again and changes their tier to Hot. Work out the billing effect. Step 1: Changing a blob to another tier before its minimum retention period ends counts the same as deleting it early. Step 2: ______. Step 3: So the clinic pays an early deletion charge covering those remaining days, on top of normal storage costs. Which statement correctly fills Step 2?
choices: Cold has a 90-day minimum, so 60 days have been used and 60 days remain
Cold has a 90-day minimum, so 60 days have been used and 30 days remain
Cold has a 180-day minimum, so 60 days have been used and 120 days remain
Cold has a 30-day minimum, so the period is already over and nothing remains
questions.why: Cold's minimum retention is about 90 days, and 90 minus the 60 days already stored leaves 30 days to be billed as an early deletion charge.

questions.prompt: An online shop's website loads product photos directly from blob storage on every page view. To cut storage costs, an administrator moves all the photos to the Archive tier. What happens to the website?
choices: The photos cannot be read until they are rehydrated to an online tier, so the site fails or stalls, possibly for hours
Nothing changes for visitors, because Archive only affects how much the account is charged for storage
Pages load a little more slowly, but the photos still display because Archive is just a cheaper online tier
Azure automatically rehydrates each photo the moment a visitor requests it, so visitors notice no change
questions.why: Archive data is offline and must be rehydrated before it can be read, and standard priority rehydration can take up to about 15 hours, so an application that reads that data will fail or stall.

questions.prompt: A logistics company wants every new blob uploaded to a particular storage account to land in the Archive tier automatically, without anyone setting a tier on each blob. The account currently uses locally redundant replication. What should the administrator know?
choices: Set the storage account's default access tier to Archive and all new blobs will inherit it
Switch the account to zone-redundant replication first, because that is what enables an Archive default
Set the default to Cold, because blobs in Cold move to Archive by themselves after 90 days
An account's default tier can only be Hot or Cool, so Archive has to be set on individual blobs
questions.why: A storage account's default access tier can only be Hot or Cool, and Archive can only be applied to individual blobs (and zone-redundant replication makes Archive unavailable, not available).

questions.prompt: A media startup created a Premium block blob storage account for fast uploads. An engineer now tries to move rarely used video clips in that account to the Cool access tier to save money, but finds no access tier option. Why?
choices: The clips must first be rehydrated before any access tier option appears
Access tiers only appear after a blob has been stored for the 30-day minimum period
Cool is not available on Premium accounts, but Hot, Cold, and Archive are
Premium block blob accounts do not use access tiers at all; Standard versus Premium is a separate performance choice
questions.why: Performance tier (Standard or Premium) is a different setting from access tier, and Premium block blob accounts do not support access tiers, so tiering requires a Standard account.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between Hot, Cool, Cold, and Archive for a new dataset. Include at least one tradeoff or limit that could cost money or break an application.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by asking how often the data is read and how quickly we need it back. Hot is for frequently read data. It costs the most to store but the least to read. Cool and Cold are cheaper to store but charge more per read, and they carry minimum retention periods of roughly 30 and 90 days. If we delete or re-tier a blob early, we still pay for the remaining days. Archive is the cheapest to store, but it is offline. Before anyone can read an archived blob, it must be rehydrated, which can take hours unless we pay for high priority. So I would never archive anything an application reads directly. Also note that the account default can only be Hot or Cool, so Archive is set per blob. And access tiers are not the same thing as Standard versus Premium performance.
rubricPoints: Defines tiers as a tradeoff between storage cost and access cost and speed.
Names Hot, Cool, Cold, and Archive and orders them correctly by cost.
Explains that Archive is offline and needs rehydration, which can take hours.
Mentions minimum retention periods and early deletion charges.
Notes that the account default is Hot or Cool, while Archive is set per blob.
Distinguishes access tiers from the Standard versus Premium performance tier.

suggested.rationale: Tier choice is mainly a cost tradeoff, so pricing realistic access patterns, including early deletion and rehydration charges, in a cost model builds the judgment the exam tests.

lessons.plain: Soft delete is a safety net for files kept in Azure Blob Storage, Microsoft's service for storing large amounts of unstructured data such as images, backups and logs. When it is switched on, deleting something does not destroy it straight away. The item is hidden and kept for a number of days you choose, and you can bring it back during that window. Think of the recycle bin on a desktop computer that empties itself automatically after a set time. There are two separate safety nets: one for individual files (blobs) and one for whole folders of files (containers).
lessons.guessPrompt: If you turn on a recycle-bin style protection only for whole folders, and someone deletes a single file inside a folder that still exists, do you think that file can be recovered? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A blob is a single stored object, such as one file, in Azure Blob Storage. A container is a named grouping that holds blobs, similar to a top-level folder. Both live inside a storage account, the Azure resource that owns your storage settings. Soft delete keeps deleted data in a hidden, recoverable state for a retention period you set in days, from 1 to 365. When the period ends, the data is permanently removed.

Blob soft delete protects individual blobs. If a blob is deleted, it can be restored with an undelete action. It also helps when a blob is overwritten: the previous contents are kept as a soft-deleted snapshot, a read-only copy from an earlier point in time, so you can recover the older data.

Container soft delete protects whole containers. If a container is deleted, it and all the blobs it held can be restored together. It does nothing for a single blob deleted from a container that still exists. The two settings are separate and are switched on independently in the storage account's data protection settings, each with its own retention period.

Worked example: blob soft delete is on with 14 days retention. On day 1 a script deletes report.csv. The blob disappears from normal listings but is retained. On day 5 an admin lists deleted blobs, finds report.csv and undeletes it; it is active again. Had nobody noticed until day 16, it would be gone for good.

Common mistake: enabling only container soft delete and assuming individual files are covered. A user deletes one blob, and there is nothing to restore. Another trap: restoring a deleted container fails if a new container with the same name already exists.

In a running system, soft-deleted data is billed like active data, so long retention costs money. Soft delete also does not protect against deleting the storage account itself; that needs a separate safeguard such as a resource lock.

questions.prompt: A clinic stores scanned forms in a storage account. Blob soft delete is switched on with a 10-day retention period. On day 2 a faulty upload job overwrites intake-0098.pdf with an empty file. The trace so far: (1) The overwrite replaces the blob's current contents with the empty file. (2) ??? (3) On day 6 an admin looks at the blob's deleted data, finds the earlier version and uses it to recover the original scan. Which statement correctly fills step 2?
choices: The original contents are moved into a hidden container that container soft delete keeps for 10 days.
The original contents are kept forever, because overwritten data is not subject to the retention period.
The original contents are kept as a soft-deleted snapshot, a read-only copy from before the overwrite, for up to 10 days.
Nothing is kept, because soft delete only reacts to a delete action and an overwrite is not a delete.
questions.why: Blob soft delete also covers overwrites by keeping the previous contents as a soft-deleted snapshot for the set retention period, which is what allows the day 6 recovery.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm keeps shipment records in a container named manifests. Their requirement is that if someone deletes the whole manifests container, it and every blob inside it can be brought back together. Which setting meets this requirement?
choices: A resource lock on the storage account
Container soft delete
Blob soft delete only
A longer retention period on blob soft delete
questions.why: Container soft delete protects whole containers, so a deleted container can be restored together with all the blobs it held.

questions.prompt: A design studio turned on container soft delete with 60 days retention and left blob soft delete off. A designer deletes one file, logo-final.png, from the assets container, which still exists. The next day they ask for it back. What happens?
choices: There is nothing to restore, because container soft delete does not protect a single blob deleted from a container that still exists.
The file can be undeleted, because container soft delete covers every blob in the container.
The file can be restored by restoring the assets container from its soft-deleted state.
The file is kept as a snapshot for 60 days and can be recovered from there.
questions.why: Container soft delete only acts when a whole container is deleted; protecting individual blobs needs blob soft delete, which was off.

questions.prompt: A school has container soft delete on with 21 days retention. On Monday a teacher deletes the container named grades. On Tuesday, before anyone notices, a script creates a new, empty container also named grades. On Wednesday an admin tries to restore the deleted grades container. What is the most likely outcome?
choices: The restore fails, because a container with the same name already exists.
The restore fails, because the 21-day retention period has already ended.
The restore succeeds and silently replaces the new empty container.
The restore succeeds and merges the old blobs into the new container.
questions.why: Restoring a deleted container fails when a new container with the same name already exists, so the new one must be dealt with first.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between blob soft delete and container soft delete, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on soft delete.
lessons.modelAnswer: Soft delete means deleted data is hidden and kept for a retention period, between 1 and 365 days, instead of being destroyed immediately, so we can restore it if the delete was a mistake. There are two separate settings. Blob soft delete covers individual blobs: if someone deletes a single file, or overwrites it, we can undelete the blob or recover the earlier contents from a soft-deleted snapshot. Container soft delete covers whole containers: if a container is deleted, we can bring back the container and everything in it at once, but it does not help if one blob is deleted from a container that still exists. So for full coverage we usually turn on both. The tradeoffs: retained data is billed like normal data, so long retention costs more, once the period expires the data is gone for good, and neither setting protects against deleting the storage account itself.
rubricPoints: Soft delete keeps deleted data recoverable for a set retention period instead of destroying it at once.
Blob soft delete protects individual blobs, including recovering overwritten contents.
Container soft delete restores a whole deleted container with its blobs but not single blobs deleted from a live container.
The two settings are independent and each has its own retention period of 1 to 365 days.
Names a limit such as storage cost, permanent loss after expiry, or no protection against storage account deletion.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine exercises storage data protection directly, and the exam skill is reasoning through a deletion scenario to pick blob versus container soft delete, which an exam-style situation practises best.

lessons.plain: Azure Files is a managed network file share in the cloud. It offers two separate safety nets for mistakes. A snapshot is a frozen, read-only picture of the whole share at one moment. If someone ruins or deletes a file later, you copy the old version back out of the picture. Soft delete covers a bigger accident: if someone deletes the entire share, Azure keeps it hidden for a set number of days so you can bring it back. Think of snapshots as photos of your filing cabinet and soft delete as a holding room where a thrown-out cabinet waits before it is destroyed.
lessons.guessPrompt: A colleague accidentally deletes one spreadsheet inside an Azure file share, and a different colleague deletes a whole file share by mistake. Do you think the same protection feature would rescue both, or would you need two different ones?
lessons.teach:
A share snapshot is a read-only, point-in-time copy of an entire Azure file share. You take it at the share level, not per file. Snapshots are incremental: the first one records the share's state, and later ones store only data that changed, so they cost less than full copies. A share can hold up to 200 snapshots. To recover, you browse a snapshot and copy the file you need back into the live share. On Windows, the same snapshots can appear in a file's Previous Versions tab.

Soft delete for Azure Files is a recycle-bin setting for whole shares. You turn it on at the storage account level, the container that holds your shares, and it applies to every file share in that account. You choose a retention period between 1 and 365 days. When a share is deleted, it moves into a soft-deleted state instead of vanishing, and you can undelete it until the period ends. After that, it is permanently removed. Restoring a share also brings back the snapshots it held.

Worked example. Soft delete is set to 14 days, and a snapshot runs at 06:00 each day. At 15:00, a user deletes report.xlsx. Soft delete does nothing here, because the share still exists. You open the 06:00 snapshot, find report.xlsx, and copy it back. You lose only edits made after 06:00. The next week, an admin deletes the whole share. You list deleted shares, pick it, and undelete it within the 14 days. Its files and snapshots return.

The common mistake is assuming Azure Files soft delete works like blob soft delete and rescues single deleted files. It works only at the share level. If you rely on soft delete alone, a deleted file is simply gone unless a snapshot captured it. Both features live inside the same storage account, so they guard against mistakes, not against losing the account itself.

questions.prompt: A small architecture firm keeps drawings in an Azure file share (a managed network file share in the cloud) called projects. Soft delete, the recycle-bin setting for whole shares, is on with a 30-day retention period. A share snapshot, a read-only point-in-time copy of the whole share, is taken at 00:00, 08:00 and 16:00 every day. At 10:45 a designer deletes floorplan.dwg, which they had edited all morning. You start the recovery at 17:30. Step 1: Decide whether soft delete helps. It does not, because only a file was deleted and the share itself still exists. Step 2: ______. Step 3: Copy floorplan.dwg from that snapshot back into the live projects share. Edits made after the snapshot time are lost. Which choice correctly fills in Step 2 so that the least work is lost?
choices: Open the 16:00 snapshot, because it is the newest copy, and locate floorplan.dwg there
List the soft-deleted items for the storage account and undelete floorplan.dwg
Open the 08:00 snapshot, the latest one taken before the 10:45 deletion, and locate floorplan.dwg
Open the 00:00 snapshot, because the first snapshot of the day holds a full copy of the share
questions.why: The 08:00 snapshot is the most recent copy taken before the deletion, so it still contains the file and loses only the edits made after 08:00, while the 16:00 snapshot was taken after the file was gone.

questions.prompt: A hospital IT team wants deleted Azure file shares to be recoverable for 60 days. Where is Azure Files soft delete turned on, and what does it cover?
choices: On each folder inside a share, and it covers the files in that folder
On the share snapshot schedule, and it covers only shares that already have snapshots
On the storage account, and it covers every file share held in that account
On each individual file share, and it covers only the share where you enabled it
questions.why: Soft delete for Azure Files is a storage account setting, the account being the container that holds the shares, and it applies to all file shares in that account.

questions.prompt: A retailer set Azure Files soft delete to 10 days. An admin deleted a share called invoices, and nobody noticed until 12 days later. The share had 40 snapshots when it was deleted. What can the team recover now?
choices: Nothing from soft delete; the retention period has passed, so the share and its snapshots are permanently removed
The whole share and its snapshots, because undelete is always possible within the 200-snapshot limit
The share's 40 snapshots only, because snapshots are never deleted along with their share
The share's files but not its snapshots, because snapshots are kept separately for 365 days
questions.why: Once the soft delete retention period ends, a deleted share is permanently removed, and its snapshots went with it.

questions.prompt: A charity enabled Azure Files soft delete with a 90-day retention period but never set up share snapshots. A volunteer deletes budget.xlsx from a share that is still in use. What happens when the team tries to recover the file?
choices: They undelete the share, which brings back budget.xlsx even though the share was never deleted
They undelete budget.xlsx from the soft-deleted list, because the 90-day retention applies to every file
They open the Previous Versions tab in Windows, which always holds a copy even without snapshots
They cannot recover it from Azure Files, because soft delete only protects whole shares and no snapshot captured the file
