questions.why: Azure Files soft delete works only at the share level, so a single deleted file is gone unless a snapshot captured it, and Previous Versions shows only existing snapshots.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between share snapshots and soft delete for Azure Files, when each one saves you, and one limit of each.
lessons.modelAnswer:
They protect against different accidents. A share snapshot is a read-only, point-in-time copy of the whole file share. Snapshots are incremental, so each one only stores what changed, and a share can keep up to 200 of them. If someone deletes or corrupts a single file, we open an earlier snapshot and copy that file back. The limit is that we lose any changes made after the snapshot was taken, so snapshot frequency matters.

Soft delete is set on the storage account and covers every share in it. If a whole share is deleted, it stays recoverable for the retention period we choose, from 1 to 365 days, along with its snapshots. Its limit is that it does nothing for individual deleted files, and once retention ends the share is gone for good. Neither feature protects us if the storage account itself is lost.
rubricPoints: A snapshot is a read-only, point-in-time copy of the whole share, used to restore individual files.
Snapshots are incremental and limited to 200 per share, and changes made after the last snapshot are lost.
Soft delete is enabled at the storage account level and protects deleted whole shares for 1 to 365 days.
Soft delete for Azure Files does not recover individual deleted files, unlike blob soft delete.
Undeleting a share restores its snapshots, and after retention expires the share is permanently gone.

suggested.rationale: The exam skill is picking snapshots versus share soft delete for a described accident, which is best practised by reasoning through short recovery scenarios.

lessons.plain: Blob lifecycle management is a set of automatic housekeeping rules you attach to an Azure storage account. A blob is a single stored file, such as an image, backup or log. The rules say things like move files to a cheaper storage level once nobody has changed them for 30 days, and delete them after a year. Azure checks the rules about once a day and acts for you, so you are not moving or deleting files by hand. Think of a warehouse that moves boxes nobody has touched to cheaper back shelves, then throws them out after a set time.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team keeps application logs in blob storage. Logs are read often in the first month, almost never after that, and must be gone after one year. What would you want an automatic rule to do to a log file at day 30, and again at day 365?
lessons.teach:
Blob lifecycle management is a policy on a storage account. A policy is a JSON document holding one or more rules, and Azure applies it automatically. It works on general-purpose v2, Blob Storage and premium block blob accounts.

Each rule has three parts. A filter chooses which blobs the rule covers: the blob type (block blobs, or append blobs for some actions), a prefix match (a container name plus the start of a blob name, such as logs/), and optionally blob index tags (key-value labels you attach to blobs). A condition is an age test, measured in days since the blob was last modified, since it was created, or since it was last read. Testing the time since last read needs last access time tracking switched on for the account. An action is what happens when the condition is met: move to a cheaper access tier or delete. Access tiers are price levels. Hot costs the most to store and the least to read. Cool and cold cost less to store and more to read. Archive is cheapest to store but is offline. Rules can also target older versions and snapshots of a blob, not only the current blob.

Worked example. One rule uses the prefix logs/, measures days since last modification, moves blobs to cool after 30 days and to archive after 90, and deletes them after 365. A log written on 1 January and never changed stays hot until about 31 January, becomes cool, becomes archive around 1 April, and is deleted around 1 January the next year. If someone rewrites it in February, its age resets.

Why it works: Azure evaluates the policy roughly once a day and acts in the background, so a new or changed policy can take 24 hours or more to show any effect.

Common mistake: archiving data that people still need quickly. An archived blob must first be rehydrated, meaning copied back to an online tier, which can take hours. Moving data out of cool, cold or archive before their minimum storage periods also triggers early-deletion charges.

Lifecycle management changes tiers and deletes data. It is separate from soft delete and versioning, which protect data, and from object replication, which copies data.

questions.prompt: Harbor Point Clinic keeps scan images in a container called scans. Policy goal: move a scan to the cool tier once nobody has opened it for 60 days, and delete it 400 days after it was created. The administrator works through it like this. Step 1: confirm the storage account is general-purpose v2, which supports lifecycle management. Step 2: (missing). Step 3: write a rule whose filter is block blobs with the prefix scans/, whose condition is more than 60 days since last read, and whose action is move to cool. Step 4: add a second condition to the same rule, more than 400 days since creation, with the action delete. Step 5: save the policy and allow at least 24 hours before checking results. Which action belongs in Step 2?
choices: Switch on last access time tracking for the storage account
Move every scan to the archive tier first so the rule has a starting point
Turn on soft delete so that scans moved to cool can still be recovered later
Set up object replication so the scans are copied to a second account
questions.why: A condition that tests days since a blob was last read only works when last access time tracking is switched on for the account.

questions.prompt: A design studio stores project files in a container called projects. When a project ends, staff attach the blob index tag status=closed to its files. The studio wants only those closed files deleted after 180 days without changes, while open project files in the same container are left alone. Which part of the lifecycle rule should use the tag?
choices: The filter, by matching the blob index tag status=closed
The action, by choosing delete only for tagged blobs
The access tier, by placing tagged files in the cold tier
The condition, by counting days since the tag was added
questions.why: The filter decides which blobs a rule covers, and it can match blob index tags. The condition is only an age test and the action is only what happens.

questions.prompt: At 9 a.m. an administrator at a freight company saves a new lifecycle policy that should move invoices older than 45 days to the cool tier. At 3 p.m. the same day, old invoices are still in the hot tier. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Invoices must be rehydrated before any lifecycle rule can change their tier
Azure evaluates policies about once a day, so a new policy can take 24 hours or more to act
Lifecycle rules can only move blobs to the archive tier, never to cool
The policy failed, because lifecycle rules take effect within minutes of saving
questions.why: Lifecycle policies are run in the background roughly once a day, so no effect after a few hours is normal and not a sign of failure.

questions.prompt: A retailer has a lifecycle rule that moves sales reports to the archive tier 20 days after they were last modified. A manager now needs a 25-day-old report open within ten minutes for a meeting. What will happen?
choices: The report opens right away, because archive is simply the cheapest online tier
The report opens right away, but it costs more to read than a hot-tier report
The report must first be rehydrated to an online tier, which can take hours
The report has already been deleted, because archiving removes the blob
questions.why: Archive is offline. An archived blob has to be rehydrated, meaning copied back to an online tier, before anyone can read it, and that can take hours.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use blob lifecycle management to cut storage cost for logs, and name one limit or tradeoff they should know before turning it on.
lessons.modelAnswer: Lifecycle management is a policy on the storage account made of rules. Each rule has a filter, such as a prefix like logs/ or blob index tags, so it touches only the right blobs. It has an age condition, such as days since last modification, creation or last access. It has an action, such as moving the blob to the cool, cold or archive tier, or deleting it. For our logs I would move them to cool after 30 days, archive after 90 and delete after 365. Azure runs the policy about once a day, so nothing happens instantly. The tradeoff is retrieval. Archived blobs are offline and need hours of rehydration before anyone can read them. Cooler tiers also charge more to read and have early-deletion fees. Lifecycle management deletes data rather than protecting it, so it is not a substitute for soft delete or versioning.
rubricPoints: States that a lifecycle policy is a set of rules that change blob tiers or delete blobs automatically.
Names the filter, condition and action parts of a rule.
Mentions age conditions such as days since modification, creation or last access, and that last access needs tracking enabled.
Notes that the policy runs about once a day, so changes are not immediate.
Names a tradeoff, such as archive rehydration delay, higher read costs or early-deletion charges.
Distinguishes lifecycle management from data-protection features like soft delete or versioning.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing the right rule filter, condition and action for a stated retention or cost requirement, and no current mission or planned engine exercises blob tier rules directly, so reasoning through scenarios teaches it best.

lessons.plain: Blob versioning is a setting on an Azure storage account that makes the service keep an older copy of a file every time someone changes or deletes it. In Azure, a file stored in object storage is called a blob. Think of it like a document editor's version history: you keep working on the latest copy, but every earlier save is still there if you need it back. Versioning happens automatically, so nobody has to remember to make a backup first. The trade-off is that every kept copy takes up storage you pay for, so old versions need to be cleaned up on purpose.
lessons.guessPrompt: A colleague accidentally overwrites an important file in cloud storage with an empty one. If the storage quietly kept every earlier copy, what would you need to know to get the right one back, and what might it cost you to keep copies forever?
lessons.teach:
Blob versioning is an account-level feature of Azure Blob Storage, Azure's managed object store. A blob is one stored object, such as a file. When versioning is on, Azure automatically saves the previous state of a blob whenever that blob is overwritten or deleted. Each saved state is a version, labelled with a version ID, which is a timestamp the service assigns. The newest state is the current version. All the others are previous versions, and you cannot change them.

This works because the service handles every write. It records the old state before applying the new one, so no person or script has to remember to take a backup.

Here is a worked example. On Monday you upload report.csv, which creates version A as the current version. On Tuesday a script overwrites it. Version A becomes a previous version, and the new content becomes version B, now current. On Wednesday someone deletes report.csv. Version B becomes a previous version too, and now there is no current version, so the blob looks gone in a normal listing. To recover, you copy version A or version B back over the blob name, and the copy becomes the new current version.

Versioning is easy to confuse with two similar features. A snapshot is a read-only copy of a blob at one moment, and you create it yourself, by hand or with a script. Versioning creates copies for you on every change. Soft delete keeps deleted data recoverable for a retention period you set. Versioning has no built-in expiry. Microsoft recommends using versioning and soft delete together, and versioning must be on before you can use object replication.

A common mistake is turning on versioning for blobs that are overwritten often, such as logs or frequently refreshed exports, without a cleanup rule. Every overwrite adds another billed version, so storage costs grow quietly. The usual fix is a lifecycle management rule that deletes or moves versions after a set number of days. Versioning also cannot help if the whole storage account or container is deleted, so it is only one layer of protection.

questions.prompt: A small architecture firm has blob versioning turned on for its storage account. Trace what happens to one blob, site-plan.dwg. Step 1: In January a designer uploads site-plan.dwg, creating version P as the current version. Step 2: In February a sync tool overwrites it. P becomes a previous version, and the new content, version Q, is current. Step 3: In March a colleague overwrites it again. Q becomes a previous version, and version R is current. Step 4: In April an intern deletes site-plan.dwg. R becomes a previous version, there is no current version, and the file no longer appears in a normal listing. Step 5: The firm needs the February content back. What is Step 5?
choices: Wait for the soft delete retention period to end, after which Azure automatically restores the newest previous version, R, as current.
Edit version Q directly and mark it as the current version, because previous versions can be promoted in place.
Copy version Q back over the name site-plan.dwg, and that copy becomes the new current version of the blob.
Take a snapshot of site-plan.dwg now, because the snapshot will capture all of its previous versions, including Q.
questions.why: Previous versions cannot be changed, so you recover by copying the version you want back over the blob name, and that copy becomes the new current version.

questions.prompt: A finance team at a logistics company wants a read-only copy of a ledger blob taken only at moments they choose, just before each quarterly close, triggered by their own script. They do not want a copy made on every routine change. Which Azure Blob Storage feature matches this requirement?
choices: Object replication, because it copies blobs to another storage account
Blob versioning, because it saves a copy whenever the blob changes
Blob snapshots, because you create each read-only copy yourself when you decide to
Soft delete, because it keeps data recoverable for a retention period you set
questions.why: A snapshot is a read-only copy at one moment that you create yourself, while versioning makes copies automatically on every overwrite or delete.

questions.prompt: A retailer turned on blob versioning for a storage account that holds a sales export blob, which a job overwrites every 15 minutes. Two months later the storage bill has climbed steadily, although the export file itself has stayed about the same size. What is the usual fix?
choices: Delete the current version each day, because only the current version is billed
Switch to snapshots, because snapshots are free and never add to storage cost
Turn on soft delete, because it will replace versioning and stop new versions from being created
Add a lifecycle management rule that deletes or moves versions after a set number of days
questions.why: Each overwrite creates another billed version and versioning has no built-in expiry, so a lifecycle management rule is needed to delete or move old versions.

questions.prompt: At a clinic, blob versioning is on for a storage account. An administrator accidentally deletes an entire container that held 400 patient-letter blobs, each with several previous versions. Which statement is correct?
choices: Versioning can recover it, because every blob's previous versions are kept even after the container is gone.
Versioning can recover it only if snapshots were also taken of each blob.
Versioning can recover it, but only within its default 30-day retention period.
Versioning cannot recover this, because it does not protect against deleting a whole container or storage account.
questions.why: Versioning protects individual blobs from overwrites and deletes, but it cannot help if the whole container or storage account is deleted, so it is only one layer of protection.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what blob versioning does and how it differs from taking snapshots, including one limit or cost you would warn them about before they enable it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Blob versioning is a storage account setting. Once it's on, Azure automatically keeps the old state of a blob every time it's overwritten or deleted. Each old state is a read-only previous version with a timestamp ID, and the latest state is the current version. If someone overwrites or deletes a file, we copy a previous version back and it becomes current again. A snapshot is different because we have to create it ourselves at a chosen moment. Versioning captures every change without anyone remembering to do anything. The catch is cost. Versions never expire on their own, so a blob that gets overwritten hourly piles up billed copies, and we should add a lifecycle rule to delete old versions. Versioning also won't save us if someone deletes the whole container or account, so we should pair it with soft delete and other protections.
rubricPoints: Versioning is enabled at the storage account level and automatically keeps the prior state on every overwrite or delete.
Previous versions are read-only and identified by a version ID, separate from the current version.
Recovery means copying or restoring a previous version so it becomes the current version again.
Snapshots are created manually at a point in time, while versioning is automatic on every change.
Versions have no automatic expiry, so storage costs grow unless lifecycle management cleans them up.
Versioning does not protect against deleting the container or account, so it should be combined with soft delete.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing between versioning, snapshots and soft delete for a given recovery requirement, so reasoning through scenario questions adds more than any existing mission, since none of them touch Azure Storage.

lessons.plain: An Azure Resource Manager (ARM) template or a Bicep file is a written recipe for Azure infrastructure. Instead of clicking through the web portal to create a virtual machine, a network, and a storage account, you describe what you want in a text file, and Azure builds it to match. Reading one is like reading a building plan. You find the inputs the builder must supply, the measurements worked out from those inputs, the rooms to build, and what gets handed back at the end. Once you can read the plan, you can tell what will actually be created, where it will go, and in what order, before anything is built.
lessons.guessPrompt: A file says a storage account's name comes from an input called storageName, whose default value is 'stdev01'. The person deploying it types 'stprod01' for that input. Which name do you think the storage account will actually get in Azure, and why?
lessons.teach:
Azure Resource Manager (ARM) is the control layer that handles every create, change, or delete request in Azure. An ARM template is a JSON text file that declares the resources you want. Bicep is a shorter, friendlier language that compiles into that same JSON, so both describe identical things. Both are declarative: they state the end result, and ARM works out the steps itself.

To read either one, find four sections. Parameters are inputs supplied at deployment time. A parameter may have a default value, which is used only when the deployer supplies nothing, and it may list allowed values. Variables are values calculated inside the file, often by combining parameters. Resources are the things to build. Each resource has a type (for example Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts, which is a storage account), an apiVersion (the dated version of that resource's schema the file follows), a name, a location (the Azure region), and properties. Outputs are values returned after deployment, such as an IP address.

Order matters. ARM builds resources in parallel unless one depends on another. In JSON, a dependsOn list states this. In Bicep, the dependency is created automatically when one resource refers to another's symbolic name, which is the label used only inside the file and is different from the resource's real Azure name.

Worked example: a Bicep file has a location parameter defaulting to resourceGroup().location, meaning the region of the resource group (the container that holds related resources). It also has a vmSize parameter defaulting to Standard_B2s, a variable nicName built as the VM name plus '-nic', a network interface, and a VM whose properties use nic.id. Trace it in order. The region is the resource group's region. The size is B2s unless overridden. The network interface is named, say, web1-nic. Because the VM references the network interface, ARM builds the interface first.

Common mistake: assuming the default is what got deployed. A value passed in a parameter file or on the command line always replaces it. Misreading this can put a VM in the wrong region or size, raising cost or breaking the deployment.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm, Northwind Freight, deploys an ARM template (JSON). It declares a parameter storageSku with allowed values Standard_LRS, Standard_GRS and Standard_ZRS and a default value of Standard_LRS. It also declares a parameter prefix with no default. A variable accountName joins prefix with the text 'archive'. The resources are a storage account (type Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts) named from accountName, and a blob container whose dependsOn list names the storage account. One output returns the storage account's endpoint address. The deployer supplies a parameter file that sets prefix to 'nwf' and storageSku to 'Standard_ZRS'. Trace: Step 1: the storage account's name is nwfarchive. Step 2: ???. Step 3: ARM builds the storage account first and the container after it, because of dependsOn. Step 4: after deployment, the endpoint address is returned as an output. Which statement correctly completes Step 2?
choices: The SKU is Standard_LRS, because the default value in the template always takes priority over a parameter file.
The SKU is Standard_ZRS, because a value supplied in the parameter file replaces the default.
The SKU is Standard_GRS, because ARM picks the middle allowed value when a parameter has both a default and a supplied value.
The deployment is rejected, because a supplied value may not differ from the parameter's default.
questions.why: A default is used only when the deployer supplies nothing, and Standard_ZRS was supplied and is in the allowed list, so it replaces Standard_LRS.

questions.prompt: An engineer at Fabrikam reads this Bicep line: resource webPlan 'Microsoft.Web/serverfarms@2022-03-01' = { name: 'fab-prod-plan' ... }. What is webPlan?
choices: The real name the plan will have in Azure, as shown in the portal.
An output that returns the plan's identifier after deployment.
The symbolic name: a label used only inside the Bicep file so other resources can refer to it.
A parameter that the deployer must supply at deployment time.
questions.why: In Bicep the label after the word resource is the symbolic name used only inside the file, while the name property ('fab-prod-plan') is the resource's real Azure name.

questions.prompt: A Bicep file for a hospital analytics team declares two resources: a key vault (a managed store for secrets) and a log analytics workspace (a managed store for monitoring data). Neither resource refers to the other's symbolic name anywhere in the file, and there are no other dependencies. How will ARM order their creation?
choices: The key vault first, because it is listed first in the file.
The workspace first, because monitoring must exist before anything else.
ARM refuses to deploy until a dependsOn list is added to the Bicep file.
In parallel, because neither one depends on the other.
questions.why: ARM builds resources in parallel unless one depends on another, and in Bicep a dependency only exists when one resource refers to another's symbolic name.

questions.prompt: A template for a retail company's network contains a resource of type Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks (a virtual network) with an apiVersion of 2023-04-01. What does that apiVersion tell you?
choices: The dated version of the virtual network's resource schema that the file is written against.
The version of the Azure region where the virtual network will be placed.
The date after which the template expires and can no longer be deployed.
The date on which the virtual network will be created in Azure.
questions.why: The apiVersion identifies which dated version of that resource type's schema the file follows, which defines the properties it can use.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would read an unfamiliar ARM template or Bicep file to predict exactly what it will deploy. Include one limit of reading the file alone.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with parameters, because they are the inputs. I note each default but remember it only applies if nobody supplies a value, so I also check the parameter file or deployment command. Next come variables, the values the file calculates from those inputs, such as a name built from a prefix. Then I read each resource: its type tells me what it is, location tells me the region, name and properties tell me how it's configured, and apiVersion tells me which schema version it follows. For order, I look for dependsOn in JSON, or in Bicep for one resource referencing another's symbolic name. Anything without a dependency can be built in parallel. Outputs show what comes back afterward. The limit is that the file alone doesn't show the final values. Overridden parameters, or functions like resourceGroup().location, only resolve at deployment, so I can't be fully certain without the actual inputs.
rubricPoints: Names the four sections: parameters, variables, resources, outputs.
States that defaults apply only when no value is supplied at deployment.
Reads each resource's type, name, location, apiVersion and properties.
Explains deployment order through dependsOn or Bicep symbolic references.
Notes that Bicep compiles to the same ARM JSON.
Names a limit, such as values that only resolve at deployment time.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine has the learner read infrastructure files, so tracing short exam-style template snippets to predict names, regions, sizes and build order builds this skill best.

lessons.plain: An Azure Resource Manager (ARM) template is a JSON file that describes the Azure resources you want, such as a virtual machine, a storage account or a network, so Azure can build them the same way every time. Modifying an existing template means editing that file to change what gets built. You might add a parameter so the VM size can be chosen at deploy time, add a second resource, or change a setting. Think of it like editing a recipe card: you swap an ingredient, or leave a blank for the cook to fill in, and every future meal follows the new card.
lessons.guessPrompt: A template has the VM size written directly inside the virtual machine resource as a fixed value. Your team wants to pick a different size each time they deploy, without editing the file again. What would you change in the template to make that possible?
lessons.teach:
An ARM template is a declarative JSON document: it states the end result you want, and Azure Resource Manager (the Azure deployment and management service) works out how to create it. Its main sections are parameters (values supplied at deploy time), variables (values computed inside the template), resources (the things to create, each with a type, an apiVersion, a name, a location and properties) and outputs (values returned after deployment). Modifying a template almost always means touching one or more of these sections. Because the file is declarative, an edit only needs to describe the new desired state.

Worked example. A template creates a storage account with the name hard-coded as "stdemo001". Step 1: add a parameter named storageName of type string, so each deployment can supply a unique name. Step 2: in the resource, replace the fixed name with the expression [parameters('storageName')]. Square brackets tell Resource Manager to evaluate an expression rather than treat the text literally. Step 3: add a parameter skuName with allowedValues of Standard_LRS and Standard_GRS and a defaultValue of Standard_LRS. allowedValues rejects typos before anything is built. Step 4: point the resource's sku name at [parameters('skuName')]. Step 5: add an output that returns the account's endpoint. Redeploying in incremental mode, the default mode that adds or updates resources and leaves unlisted ones alone, applies the change.

When one new resource needs another, such as a network interface that needs a virtual network, add a dependsOn entry that references the other resource with the resourceId() function. This ensures the network exists before the interface is created.

A common mistake is referencing a parameter that was never declared, or misspelling its name. Validation then fails before anything is created. Another mistake is redeploying in complete mode, which deletes resources in the resource group that the template does not list. On a running system that can remove production resources, so check the mode before redeploying.

questions.prompt: Northwind Logistics has an ARM template that creates a public IP address (a fixed, internet-reachable address for a resource). The name is hard-coded as "pip-gateway-07", and the team wants each deployment to supply its own name. Step 1: add a parameter named ipName of type string to the parameters section. Step 2: (missing). Step 3: add an output that returns the public IP address's ID after deployment. Step 4: redeploy in incremental mode, so this resource is added or updated and other resources in the group are left alone. What is Step 2?
choices: In the variables section, add a variable ipName with the value pip-gateway-07
Redeploy in complete mode first so the old hard-coded name is cleared out
In the resource, replace the fixed name with the expression [parameters('ipName')]
In the resource, set the name to parameters('ipName') with no square brackets around it
questions.why: The resource has to reference the new parameter, and the square brackets tell Resource Manager to evaluate the expression rather than use the text literally.

questions.prompt: In an ARM template, which section holds values that are computed inside the template itself, rather than supplied by the person running the deployment?
choices: variables
parameters
outputs
resources
questions.why: Variables are values calculated within the template. Parameters are supplied at deploy time, and outputs are values returned after deployment.

questions.prompt: Fabrikam edits a template to add a virtual network named vnet-app and a network interface (the virtual network card a VM uses to join a network) that attaches to that virtual network. On deployment, Resource Manager sometimes tries to create the interface before the virtual network exists. What edit fixes this?
choices: Add a parameter that holds the virtual network's name
Add a dependsOn entry to the interface that references the virtual network using resourceId()
Move the network interface below the virtual network in the JSON file
Return the virtual network's ID in the outputs section
questions.why: A dependsOn entry that references the virtual network with resourceId() makes Resource Manager create the virtual network before the interface.

questions.prompt: A resource group at Tailspin Toys holds five running resources. An administrator edits a template that lists only two of them and redeploys it to that group in complete mode. What happens to the other three resources?
choices: They are left unchanged, because the template does not mention them
They are only updated to match the two listed resources' settings
Validation fails and nothing is deployed
They are deleted, because complete mode removes resources the template does not list
questions.why: Complete mode deletes resources in the resource group that the template does not list, which is why you should check the mode before redeploying to a live system.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would change an existing ARM template so a hard-coded setting becomes something chosen at deploy time. Name one risk or tradeoff to watch for when you redeploy it.
lessons.modelAnswer: An ARM template is a JSON file that declares the resources we want. To make a hard-coded value adjustable, I first declare a parameter in the parameters section, giving it a type and, where it helps, allowedValues and a defaultValue. Then I replace the literal value inside the resource with an expression like [parameters('name')], so Resource Manager reads the value at deploy time. If I add a resource that relies on another, I add dependsOn so the order is right. The tradeoff is that every new parameter is one more thing someone must supply correctly, so defaults and allowed lists keep it safe. The main risk is the deployment mode. Incremental mode, the default, only adds or updates resources. Complete mode deletes anything in the resource group that the template does not list. That could wipe out live resources, so I confirm the mode before redeploying.
rubricPoints: Identifies the template sections: parameters, variables, resources and outputs.
Declares a new parameter and references it with a bracket expression in the resource.
Mentions defaultValue or allowedValues to guard input.
Uses dependsOn when a new resource relies on another.
Names the incremental versus complete mode risk, or the undeclared-parameter error.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine edits ARM templates, so reading a traced example of the template sections and edits is the best fit here.

lessons.plain: A Bicep file is a text recipe that tells Azure which cloud resources to build and how to set them up. Modifying one means editing that recipe, for example making a hard-coded setting adjustable, adding a label, or adding a related resource, so the next deployment produces what you now need. Think of a house blueprint. You can mark a window size as 'choose at build time' or add a porch attached to the house, and the builder updates the existing house rather than starting over. The one thing you must not casually change is the house's address, because a new address means a whole new house.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a recipe file names a storage account 'shopdata01', and you change that name to 'shopdata02' and run it again. Do you think Azure renames the existing account, or does something else happen?
lessons.teach:
Modifying a Bicep file means editing its declarations so the next deployment produces the infrastructure you now want. Bicep is a language for describing Azure resources as text. It compiles to an Azure Resource Manager (ARM) template, which is the JSON format that Azure's deployment service reads.

A file has four main building blocks. A parameter (param) is a value supplied at deploy time, and it can have a default. A variable (var) is a value worked out inside the file. A resource declaration (resource) has three parts: a symbolic name that is used only inside the file, a type with an API version (for example Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts@2023-01-01), and a body of properties. An output returns a value after deployment. Decorators such as @allowed or @minLength sit above a parameter and restrict what callers may pass.

Edits like these are safe because deployment is declarative. Azure compares the file with what already exists and changes only the differences. Redeploying an edited file therefore updates resources in place.

Here is a worked example. A file hard-codes sku: { name: 'Standard_LRS' } on a storage account whose symbolic name is stg. The new requirement is to let each environment choose its redundancy.

Step 1: add param storageSku string = 'Standard_LRS' and put @allowed(['Standard_LRS','Standard_GRS']) above it.
Step 2: replace the literal value with sku: { name: storageSku }.
Step 3: add tags: { env: 'prod' } to the resource body.
Step 4: add a blob service as a new resource and set parent: stg. This uses the symbolic name instead of a typed resource ID, and Bicep infers the dependency so the account is built first.
Step 5: redeploy with storageSku set to Standard_GRS. Azure updates the existing account rather than creating another one.

A common mistake is editing the name property to 'rename' a resource. The name property identifies the real Azure resource, so a new name makes Azure create a second resource. Under the default incremental mode, the old one is left running and still billing. You can change the symbolic name freely, but treat the name property as the resource's identity. Some properties also cannot be changed after creation, and changing them makes the deployment fail.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's Bicep file declares a virtual network (a private network space in Azure) with the symbolic name vnet and the name property 'corpVnet'. The team must add a subnet whose address range can differ per environment. Step 1: add param subnetPrefix string = '10.20.1.0/24'. Step 2: declare a new resource of type Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks/subnets@2023-04-01 with a body that sets addressPrefix: subnetPrefix. Step 3: (missing). Step 4: redeploy. Azure leaves the existing network in place and adds only the subnet, building the network first. What is Step 3?
choices: Change the network's name property to 'corpVnet-subnet1' so Azure knows the network now holds a subnet
Add an output that returns subnetPrefix so the subnet can find its network after deployment
In the subnet's body, set parent: vnet so it attaches to the network through the symbolic name
Turn subnetPrefix into a var instead of a param so the subnet attaches to the network
questions.why: Setting parent to the network's symbolic name links the child to the right resource without a typed ID, and Bicep infers that the network must be built first.

questions.prompt: An engineer at a clinic tidies a Bicep file. She changes a key vault's symbolic name from kv to clinicVault and updates every reference to it in the file. The name property stays 'clinic-kv-01'. What happens when the file is redeployed?
choices: The existing key vault is kept, and nothing about it changes because of this edit
Azure deletes clinic-kv-01 and recreates it under the new symbolic name
The deployment fails because a symbolic name cannot be changed after the resource is created
Azure creates a second key vault called clinicVault and leaves the first one running
questions.why: The symbolic name is used only inside the file, so changing it does not change which real Azure resource is identified by the name property.

questions.prompt: A retail team wants to rename a storage account from 'retaildata01' to 'retailarchive01'. They edit the name property in their Bicep file and redeploy using the default incremental mode. What is the result?
choices: The existing account is renamed in place, and its data stays where it was
Azure moves the data into retailarchive01 and then deletes retaildata01
A new account retailarchive01 is created, and retaildata01 is left running and still billing
The deployment fails because storage accounts cannot be updated once they exist
questions.why: The name property is the resource's identity, so a new value makes Azure create another resource, and incremental mode leaves the old one in place.

questions.prompt: A Bicep file has param vmSize string = 'Standard_B2s'. Callers must only be able to pass either 'Standard_B2s' or 'Standard_D2s_v5'. What edit enforces this?
choices: Put @minLength(12) above the vmSize parameter so short values are rejected
Add an output that returns vmSize so callers can see which value was used
Put @allowed(['Standard_B2s','Standard_D2s_v5']) directly above the vmSize parameter
Replace the parameter with var vmSize = 'Standard_D2s_v5' inside the file
questions.why: The @allowed decorator sits above a parameter and limits callers to the listed values, while @minLength only checks length.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would change a hard-coded setting in an existing Bicep file into something each environment can choose, and add a child resource. Name one change that looks harmless but is not.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd add a parameter for the setting, say param storageSku string with a sensible default. I'd put an @allowed decorator above it so nobody passes an invalid value. Then I'd replace the hard-coded literal in the resource body with the parameter name. For the child resource, I'd declare a new resource and set parent to the existing resource's symbolic name. That avoids typing resource IDs, and Bicep works out the deployment order for me. When I redeploy, Azure compares the file with what exists and updates the resource in place. The trap is the name property. It's the real resource's identity, so changing it creates a brand-new resource, and in incremental mode the old one keeps running and costing money. The symbolic name is only internal, so renaming that is fine. Also, a few properties can't change after creation, and the deployment will fail if you edit them.
rubricPoints: Replaces a hard-coded value with a parameter, optionally restricted by a decorator such as @allowed.
Adds a related resource using parent or a symbolic-name reference so the dependency is inferred.
States that redeploying is declarative and updates existing resources in place.
Distinguishes the internal symbolic name from the name property that identifies the real resource.
Warns that changing the name property creates a new resource and leaves the old one under incremental mode.
Notes that some properties are fixed after creation and editing them causes a failed deployment.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine edits Bicep, so reasoning through exam-style snippets and choosing the correct edit, such as parameterising a value versus changing the name property, builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Deploying with a template means describing the Azure resources you want in a file, then handing that file to Azure and letting it build them for you. Azure Resource Manager (ARM) is the service that receives every request to create or change something in Azure. An ARM template is a JSON file listing the resources you want; Bicep is a shorter, friendlier language that turns into that same JSON. It is like giving a builder a blueprint instead of shouting instructions one brick at a time: the result is the same every time, and you can reuse the blueprint for another site.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you send Azure the same template twice, describing one storage account that already exists from the first run, what do you think happens the second time: an error, a duplicate account, or nothing much?
lessons.teach:
A template deployment is a request to Azure Resource Manager (ARM), the control layer every create or change request goes through, to make your environment match a file. The file is either an ARM template (JSON) or a Bicep file (a simpler language that is compiled, meaning automatically translated, into ARM JSON before deployment). Templates are declarative: you state the end result, not the steps, and ARM works out the order and dependencies.

Every deployment has a scope, the level it targets: a resource group (a container for related resources), a subscription, a management group, or the tenant. Most resources go to a resource group, and that group must already exist. Parameters are inputs, such as a name or location, that you supply at deploy time, often from a separate parameters file so one template serves dev and production.

You can deploy from the Azure CLI with az deployment group create --resource-group rg-app --template-file main.bicep --parameters storageName=stapp01, from PowerShell with New-AzResourceGroupDeployment, or in the portal through Deploy a custom template. Adding what-if (az deployment group what-if) previews changes without making them.

Worked example: main.bicep declares one storage account. First run: ARM sees it is missing and creates it. Second run, unchanged: ARM sees it already matches, so nothing changes. This repeat-safe behaviour is called idempotency. Third run with the SKU changed: ARM updates only that property.

Deployment mode decides what happens to resources in the group that the template does not mention. Incremental, the default, leaves them alone. Complete deletes them.

The common mistake is choosing complete mode against a shared resource group. Any virtual machine or database a colleague added by hand that is not in your file gets deleted, causing an outage and possible data loss. Run what-if first and keep complete mode for groups the template fully owns.

questions.prompt:
A payroll team has a Bicep file that declares a key vault and an app service plan, the hosting capacity for web apps. They will deploy it to the resource group rg-payroll, which also holds a virtual machine a colleague built by hand. That VM is not in the file. Their steps:

Step 1: Confirm rg-payroll already exists.
Step 2: Run what-if with complete mode selected. The preview shows the key vault and plan would be created and the hand-built VM would be deleted.
Step 3: ?
Step 4: Run the real deployment. The key vault and plan are created, and the VM keeps running untouched.

Which action belongs in Step 3?
choices: Translate the Bicep file into ARM JSON, since only JSON templates leave unlisted resources alone
Run the complete-mode deployment twice, so idempotency brings the VM back on the second run
Keep complete mode, because what-if already showed the changes and nothing was actually deleted
Switch the deployment to incremental mode, which leaves resources the file does not mention alone
questions.why: Incremental mode, the default, leaves resources that are not in the template alone, so the hand-built VM survives while the new resources are created.

questions.prompt: An engineer at a travel agency runs az deployment group create --resource-group rg-bookings-test --template-file web.bicep. Nobody has created rg-bookings-test yet. What happens?
choices: The resources are placed at subscription scope instead, since the group is missing
what-if mode is turned on automatically, so nothing is deployed and no error appears
The deployment fails, because a resource-group deployment needs a resource group that already exists
Resource Manager creates rg-bookings-test automatically and then deploys the web resources into it
questions.why: A resource group is the deployment's target scope and must already exist before you deploy into it.

questions.prompt: A hospital's pipeline deploys the same unchanged Bicep file every night. The file declares two virtual networks and one storage account, and all three were created on the first night. In incremental mode, what does the deployment do on the 30th night?
choices: It fails, because those resources already exist in the group
It makes no changes, because the resources already match the file
It deletes the three resources and recreates them from the file
It creates a second copy of each of the three resources
questions.why: Deployments are idempotent: when the environment already matches the declared end result, Resource Manager changes nothing.

questions.prompt: A retailer needs the same set of resources in a development environment and a production environment. Only the names and the region differ between the two. Which approach fits template deployments best?
choices: Write two separate Bicep files and edit the names and regions inside each file by hand
Keep one template and supply the names and region at deploy time from a separate parameters file for each environment
Deploy production in complete mode and development in incremental mode, so the two copies stay different
Deploy at tenant scope, so a single deployment covers both environments at once
questions.why: Parameters are deploy-time inputs, often kept in a separate file, so one template can serve both dev and production.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how deploying a Bicep file or ARM template to a resource group works, including what happens on a repeat run, and name the main risk or tradeoff around deployment mode.
lessons.modelAnswer: Azure Resource Manager is the layer that handles every create or change in Azure. A template, written in JSON or in Bicep (which compiles to JSON), declares the resources we want, and ARM makes the target scope match it. For most work the scope is an existing resource group. We pass parameters, often from a parameters file, and deploy with az deployment group create, New-AzResourceGroupDeployment, or the portal's custom template page. Because it is declarative and idempotent, running the same file again changes nothing, and editing a property updates only that property. The tradeoff is deployment mode. Incremental, the default, ignores resources not in the file. Complete deletes them, so it is dangerous on a shared group where people added things by hand. I would run what-if before deploying to preview exactly what will be created, changed or deleted.
rubricPoints: ARM is the control layer that processes deployments, and Bicep compiles to ARM JSON.
Templates are declarative and target a scope, usually an existing resource group.
Parameters or a parameters file let one template serve several environments.
Redeploying the same template is idempotent and changes only what differs.
Incremental mode leaves unlisted resources alone, but complete mode deletes them.
Running what-if previews changes before deploying.

suggested.rationale: No OpsForge mission or planned engine runs Azure template deployments, so the most useful practice is reasoning through exam-style scenarios about scope, parameters, deployment mode and what-if.

lessons.plain: Azure keeps a description of everything you build. Exporting a deployment means asking Azure to write that description out as a template. The template is a file listing your resources and their settings, so you can rebuild them later or somewhere else. An ARM template is that file in JSON format. JSON is a structured text format of braces and key-value pairs, and it is wordy. Bicep is a shorter, friendlier language that says the same thing. Converting to Bicep rewrites the JSON in that cleaner form. It is like photographing a finished room and turning the photo into a floor plan. The plan is useful, but you still tidy it before building from it.
lessons.guessPrompt: You built a storage account and a virtual network by clicking through the Azure portal, and now you ask Azure to export them as a template. Do you think the file will be ready to deploy again unchanged into another environment, or will you need to edit it first? Why?
lessons.teach:
Azure Resource Manager (ARM) is the control layer that creates and updates every Azure resource. An ARM template is a JSON file that declares which resources should exist and how they are configured. Bicep is a domain-specific language, meaning a small language built for one job. Bicep describes the same resources with less syntax, and the Bicep tooling compiles it back into ARM JSON before deployment.

There are two main export routes. First, open a resource group or a single resource and choose Export template. This captures the resources as they exist right now, and the portal can show the result as JSON or as Bicep. The same capture is available from the command line with az group export or Export-AzResourceGroup. Second, open the resource group's Deployments history and pick a past deployment. This gives you the exact template and parameters that were used at the time, even if the resources changed afterwards.

To convert an existing JSON template to Bicep, run az bicep decompile --file main.json. This writes a file named main.bicep. Decompiling is best effort, so it may produce warnings or awkward code that you must fix.

Worked example. You built a storage account by hand. You open its resource group and choose Export template. The output hard-codes the account name and region and adds no parameters. You save it as main.json and run az bicep decompile --file main.json. You then review main.bicep and replace the fixed name and region with parameters. Finally, you run az bicep build to confirm that it compiles cleanly.

A common mistake is to treat an export as a finished, reusable template. Exports often hard-code values and include read-only or default properties. Some resource types cannot be exported at all, and an export is limited in how many resources it can include. If you deploy an unedited export, it can fail on name conflicts, or it can quietly recreate settings you never meant to copy. Always review and parameterize an export before you rely on it.

questions.prompt: A logistics company deployed an App Service plan (a managed hosting plan for web apps) from a template three weeks ago, with the pricing tier set to S1. Last week an engineer manually raised the tier to P1v3 in the portal. An auditor now asks for the exact template and parameter values that were used in the original deployment, delivered as Bicep. Step 1: The admin notes that the live plan no longer matches what was originally deployed. Step 2: ______. Step 3: The admin saves that template as plan.json and runs az bicep decompile --file plan.json, which writes plan.bicep. Step 4: The admin reviews plan.bicep, fixes any warnings, and hands it over. Which action belongs in Step 2?
choices: Open the resource group, choose Export template, and save the result, since the portal can show it as JSON or as Bicep
Run az bicep build against the live App Service plan to regenerate the JSON that was originally deployed
Open the resource group's Deployments history, select the deployment from three weeks ago, and take its template and parameters
Run az group export on the resource group, then edit the output by hand so the tier reads S1 again
questions.why: Deployments history keeps the exact template and parameters used at deployment time, whereas Export template and az group export capture the plan as it is now, with the P1v3 tier.

questions.prompt: A developer at a design studio writes infrastructure in Bicep instead of ARM JSON. What happens to the Bicep file before Azure Resource Manager deploys the resources?
choices: It is uploaded to the resource group's Deployments history and stored there as Bicep only
Azure Resource Manager reads the Bicep file directly, so no JSON is ever produced
The Bicep tooling compiles it into an ARM JSON template, which is what gets deployed
It must first be decompiled with az bicep decompile so that Azure can understand it
questions.why: Bicep is a shorter language for describing the same resources, and its tooling compiles it back into ARM JSON before deployment.

questions.prompt: An admin at a regional bank exports a resource group that holds a web app named bank-portal-01 and a database server. Without editing the file, the admin deploys it to a second resource group to create a test copy, and the deployment fails. What is the most likely reason?
choices: The export must be converted to Bicep before Azure Resource Manager will accept it
An export cannot include more than one resource, so the database server was left out
Exported templates can only be deployed back into the resource group they came from
The export hard-coded resource names such as bank-portal-01, which clash with the existing resources
questions.why: Exports often hard-code values such as names, so an unedited export can fail on name conflicts until those values are replaced with parameters.

questions.prompt: An engineer at a university runs az bicep decompile --file campus-network.json. A file named campus-network.bicep appears, but the command also prints several warnings, and some of the code looks awkward. What should the engineer conclude?
choices: The JSON file is corrupt, and the engineer must re-export it before decompiling again
Warnings mean the conversion failed, so campus-network.bicep is empty and should be deleted
The warnings can be ignored, because a decompiled file is always ready to deploy unchanged
This is expected, because decompiling is best effort, so the engineer should review and fix the Bicep code before relying on it
questions.why: Decompiling is best effort and can produce warnings or awkward code, which you are expected to review and correct.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would turn resources someone built by hand in the portal into a reusable Bicep file. Cover the export options and the limits of what export and decompile give you.
lessons.modelAnswer: There are two ways to get a template out of Azure. Export template on a resource group or resource captures the current state. Deployment history gives the exact template and parameters from an earlier deployment, even if things changed since. The portal can show the export as Bicep directly. If I only have JSON, I run az bicep decompile to produce a .bicep file. Neither step gives a finished product. Exports hard-code names, regions and IDs, and they can include read-only properties. Some resource types are not exported at all. Decompiling is best effort, so warnings and clumsy code are normal. I would therefore review the file and replace fixed values with parameters. Then I would run az bicep build to confirm it compiles before anyone deploys it. The tradeoff is that export saves typing, but it takes careful cleanup before the file is truly reusable.
rubricPoints: Names Export template on a resource group or resource as a capture of current state.
Names deployment history as the source of the exact template used in a past deployment.
States that az bicep decompile converts ARM JSON into a Bicep file.
Notes that exports hard-code values, may include extra or read-only properties, and may skip some resource types.
Says decompile output is best effort and must be reviewed, parameterized and built before reuse.

suggested.rationale: This objective is about knowing the portal and CLI export and decompile steps and their limits, and no current mission or planned engine exercises Azure templates.

lessons.plain: Creating a virtual machine (VM) means renting a computer that lives inside a cloud provider's data center. You never touch the hardware. Instead, you fill in a form or run a command that tells Azure what you want, and Azure builds it in minutes. You choose where it lives, which operating system it starts with, how much processing power and memory it gets, how you will log in, and how it connects to the network. Think of ordering a custom laptop online: you pick the model, the specs and the accessories, and it arrives ready to switch on. The difference is that this one arrives in minutes and is billed by the hour.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you asked a cloud provider to build you a server in their data center, what three or four things would you have to tell them before they could build it?
lessons.teach:
Creating an Azure virtual machine asks Azure to carve a software-defined computer out of its physical servers. A VM is never one object, because Azure builds several linked resources. You can create one in the portal's Create a virtual machine wizard, with the Azure CLI command az vm create, with the PowerShell cmdlet New-AzVM, or from a template. All of them ask the same questions.

You must choose a subscription (the billing account) and a resource group (a container for related resources). You also pick a region (the data-center location) and an image (the starting operating system, such as Ubuntu or Windows Server). The size is the bundle of CPU cores and memory, such as Standard_B2s, and it sets the hourly price. The administrator login is either a username plus an SSH key pair (you keep the private half) for Linux, or a username and password for Windows. Finally you set the inbound port rules.

Azure also creates an OS disk (a managed disk holding the operating system) and a network interface, or NIC (the VM's virtual network card). It places the NIC in a subnet of a virtual network, or VNet (a private network you control). It can optionally add a public IP address and a network security group, or NSG (a list of firewall rules).

Worked example: a Linux test web server. Step 1: create resource group rg-web-test in East US. Step 2: pick image Ubuntu Server and size Standard_B2s. Step 3: choose SSH public key with username azureuser. Step 4: allow port 80 for web traffic and port 22 only from your office IP. Step 5: accept a new VNet, subnet, public IP and NSG. Step 6: Review + create validates the settings and deploys them, and you then SSH to the public IP.

A common mistake is opening SSH (22) or RDP (3389) to the whole internet. Bots find these ports within minutes and guess weak passwords. Use keys, restrict source addresses, or use Azure Bastion, a managed jump service. Also, deleting a VM can leave its disk, NIC and public IP behind, and those keep billing unless you delete them too.

questions.prompt: Ledgerline, a small accounting firm, needs a Windows Server virtual machine (VM) to run its bookkeeping app. A VM is a software-defined computer that Azure carves out of its physical servers. Here is the admin's plan. Step 1: create resource group rg-ledger-prod (a container for related resources) in West Europe. Step 2: pick image Windows Server (the starting operating system) and size Standard_D2s_v3 (the bundle of CPU cores and memory that sets the hourly price). Step 3: ???. Step 4: add an inbound port rule that allows RDP (port 3389) only from the office IP address 203.0.113.10. Step 5: accept a new virtual network (VNet), subnet, public IP address and network security group (NSG, a list of firewall rules). Step 6: select Review + create, then connect over RDP. What belongs in Step 3?
choices: Set the administrator login as a username, such as ledgeradmin, plus a strong password
Choose which subnet the OS disk should be placed in
Open port 3389 to every internet address so staff can also log in from home
Upload the private half of an SSH key pair to Azure and set the username ledgeradmin
questions.why: A Windows VM's administrator login is a username and password, and this step is still missing because the image, size, ports and network are already covered by the other steps.

questions.prompt: An administrator at Contoso Bakery is creating a VM. They want more CPU cores and more memory and accept that this will cost more per hour. Which VM creation setting should they change?
choices: The image
The size
The region
The resource group
questions.why: The size is the bundle of CPU cores and memory, and it sets the VM's hourly price.

questions.prompt: Fabrikam Labs deleted a VM named vm-analytics-07 last month. This month the bill still shows charges linked to that VM's project. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Deleting a VM only pauses it, so the CPU cores and memory are still charged every hour
Linked resources that Azure created with the VM, such as its managed OS disk, network interface (NIC) and public IP, were left behind and keep billing
Azure charges a monthly fee to keep storing the SSH public key that was used at creation
The resource group itself has an hourly charge that continues after its VMs are deleted
questions.why: A VM is several linked resources, and deleting the VM can leave its disk, NIC and public IP behind, which keep billing until you delete them too.

questions.prompt: Northwind Traders runs a Linux VM. Its network security group (NSG) allows SSH on port 22 from any internet address, and the logs show thousands of failed login attempts from unknown addresses. What is the best response?
choices: Add a second network interface (NIC) to the VM so that the login attempts are spread across two network cards
Restrict port 22 to the team's own IP addresses or use Azure Bastion, and log in with SSH keys
Switch the image to Windows Server and open RDP port 3389 to the internet instead of port 22
Move the VM to a different region, because bots only target well-known data-center locations
questions.why: Bots quickly find SSH or RDP ports that are open to the whole internet, so the fix is to limit the source addresses or use the managed jump service Azure Bastion, and to use keys instead of guessable passwords.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what actually gets created when you create an Azure VM and which choices you must make, and name one security or cost tradeoff they should watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: Creating a VM isn't one thing, it's a bundle. I pick a subscription and resource group, a region, an image for the operating system, and a size that sets the cores, memory and hourly cost. I also choose how the admin logs in: an SSH key for Linux or a password for Windows. Azure then builds an OS disk, a network interface sitting in a subnet of a virtual network, and optionally a public IP and a network security group that acts as a firewall. The portal wizard, az vm create, New-AzVM and templates all ask these same questions. The tradeoff is that opening SSH or RDP to the internet makes connecting easy but invites brute-force attacks, so restrict the source IPs or use Bastion. Also, deleting the VM may leave the disk, NIC and public IP still costing money.
rubricPoints: States that a VM is several linked resources: OS disk, NIC, VNet/subnet, and optional public IP and NSG.
Names the core choices: resource group, region, image, size, and admin authentication.
Notes the size drives CPU, memory and hourly cost.
Mentions that portal, CLI, PowerShell and templates all create the same thing.
Identifies the risk of exposing SSH/RDP publicly and a mitigation.
Mentions that leftover disks, NICs or public IPs can keep billing after VM deletion.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine provisions a VM, so reasoning through an exam-style scenario that picks the image, size, authentication and port rules for a given workload builds the most useful skill.

lessons.plain: Encryption at host is a virtual machine setting that scrambles data while it sits on the physical server running your VM, not just once it reaches the storage service. Azure already encrypts managed disks (the virtual hard drives) in storage by default, but some data never makes it there: the temporary disk and the disk caches live on the host machine itself. Turning on encryption at host covers those too. Think of a bank vault that is locked, but the cash counted on the teller's desk is not. This setting locks the desk drawer as well.
lessons.guessPrompt: Azure already encrypts a VM's managed disks in storage. Which pieces of a VM's data might still sit unencrypted somewhere, and where would they be?
lessons.teach:
Encryption at host is a VM option that encrypts data at rest on the physical host server. That covers the temporary disk (scratch space attached to the VM, lost when it moves hosts) and the OS and data disk caches (copies of recent reads and writes kept on the host for speed). Data then travels to the storage service already encrypted. This matters because server-side encryption (SSE), which Azure applies to all managed disks by default, only protects data once it lands in storage. It does not cover the temp disk or the caches.

It works at the host layer, so the VM's guest operating system does nothing and spends no CPU on it. That differs from Azure Disk Encryption (ADE), which runs BitLocker (Windows) or DM-Crypt (Linux) inside the guest. You cannot use ADE and encryption at host on the same VM. Keys can be platform-managed (Azure's keys) or customer-managed (your keys in a key vault, linked through a disk encryption set, a resource that points disks at a key).

Worked example, an existing VM. Step 1: register the feature once per subscription, for example with az feature register --namespace Microsoft.Compute --name EncryptionAtHost. Step 2: confirm the VM size supports it. Step 3: stop (deallocate) the VM. Step 4: enable it in the portal on the VM's Disks blade, or in an ARM template or Bicep file set securityProfile.encryptionAtHost to true. Step 5: start the VM. For a new VM, tick the option on the Disks tab during creation.

A common mistake is trying to flip the setting on a running VM, or skipping the feature registration. Either way the change fails. Another mistake is assuming SSE is enough. In a running system that leaves page files and scratch data on the temp disk unencrypted, which is a gap auditors will flag.

questions.prompt: An auditor at Brightwater Insurance flags VM bw-claims-07. Its Windows page file sits on the temporary disk, and the auditor says that data is unencrypted. The admin answers that every managed disk already has server-side encryption (SSE). Trace the reasoning. Step 1: SSE protects managed disk data once that data lands in the storage service. Step 2: ???. Step 3: So the page file can sit unencrypted on the physical host, and the auditor's finding is valid. Step 4: The fix is to enable encryption at host on bw-claims-07, which encrypts data on the host before it travels to storage. Which statement belongs in Step 2?
choices: SSE only applies to data disks, so the OS disk and the temp disk are both left unprotected on the host
The temporary disk and the disk caches live on the host server, not in the storage service, so SSE never covers them
SSE needs customer-managed keys in a key vault before it covers the temp disk, and this VM uses platform-managed keys
The page file is encrypted by SSE, but the auditor's tooling cannot read Azure's platform-managed keys to confirm it
questions.why: SSE protects data only once it is in storage, and the temp disk and caches stay on the host, so they fall outside SSE's coverage.

questions.prompt: A VM's managed disks already use server-side encryption (SSE) by default. Which data does turning on encryption at host additionally protect?
choices: Only the OS disk, which SSE skips so that the VM can still boot
Network traffic between the VM and other VMs in the same virtual network
Snapshots and backups of the data disks kept in a separate storage account
The temporary disk and the OS and data disk caches held on the physical host
questions.why: Encryption at host covers the temp disk and the disk caches on the host, which SSE does not cover.

questions.prompt: At Kestrel Analytics, a Linux VM already encrypts its disks with Azure Disk Encryption (ADE), which runs DM-Crypt inside the guest operating system. The security lead now asks the team to also enable encryption at host on the same VM. What should the team understand?
choices: Both work together only if the VM uses customer-managed keys through a disk encryption set
ADE and encryption at host cannot be used on the same VM, so the team has to pick one
Both can run together, but the guest will spend double the CPU because each layer encrypts the data
Encryption at host replaces DM-Crypt automatically the next time the VM is restarted
questions.why: Using ADE and encryption at host on the same VM is not allowed, so the team must choose one of them.

questions.prompt: At Tidewell Retail, the subscription is already registered for the EncryptionAtHost feature, and the VM size of tw-web-03 supports it. An admin redeploys a Bicep file that sets securityProfile.encryptionAtHost to true while tw-web-03 is running, and the change fails. What is the most likely fix?
choices: Stop (deallocate) tw-web-03, apply the change, then start the VM again
Install an encryption agent inside the guest OS so the setting has a component to talk to
Create a disk encryption set, because encryption at host cannot use platform-managed keys
Register the EncryptionAtHost feature again, because registration must be repeated for each VM
questions.why: Encryption at host cannot be switched on for a running VM, so the VM must be deallocated before the change and started afterwards.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what encryption at host adds beyond default disk encryption, how you would enable it on an existing VM, and one limit or tradeoff.
lessons.modelAnswer: By default, Azure encrypts managed disks with server-side encryption, but only once the data is in the storage service. The VM's temporary disk and its OS and data disk caches live on the physical host, so SSE doesn't cover them. Encryption at host encrypts that host-side data too, so the data is encrypted from the host all the way to storage. It runs at the host, not inside the guest OS, so the VM spends no CPU on it. To enable it on an existing VM, register the EncryptionAtHost feature in the subscription and check that the VM size supports it. Then deallocate the VM, set encryption at host on the Disks blade or set securityProfile.encryptionAtHost to true in the template, and start the VM. Tradeoffs: it needs downtime to enable on an existing VM, only some sizes support it, and you can't combine it with Azure Disk Encryption on the same VM.
rubricPoints: Default SSE protects disks in storage but not the temp disk or host caches.
Encryption at host encrypts temp disk and caches on the physical host, without using guest CPU.
The subscription feature must be registered and the VM size must support it.
An existing VM must be deallocated before enabling, via the portal Disks blade or securityProfile.encryptionAtHost.
It cannot be combined with Azure Disk Encryption on the same VM.
Keys can be platform-managed or customer-managed through a disk encryption set.

suggested.rationale: The core exam skill is reasoning through a scenario to choose between default SSE, encryption at host and Azure Disk Encryption, and to recall the deallocate-and-enable steps, and no current mission or planned engine exercises this VM setting directly.

lessons.plain: Moving a virtual machine means changing where it lives in Azure without rebuilding it by hand. Azure organises things in layers. A region is the physical datacenter area. A subscription is the billing and access boundary. A resource group is a labelled folder of related resources. Shifting a VM to another folder or subscription is like relabelling a box on the same shelf: quick, and the box stays put. Shifting it to another region is like shipping the box to a different warehouse. A copy is made there and the original is then removed.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you move a virtual machine from a resource group called rg-test to one called rg-prod, do you think the VM ends up in a different datacenter region? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A VM can be moved in two very different ways, depending on the destination.

Moving to another resource group or subscription uses the Azure Resource Manager move operation. Azure Resource Manager (ARM) is the management layer that tracks every resource. A resource group is a logical container, and a subscription is the billing and permission boundary above it. The move only changes this bookkeeping, so the VM keeps its region and normally keeps running. What does change is its resource ID, the full path that names the resource, because that path includes the subscription and resource group. Permissions inherited from the old group stop applying, and the new group's permissions take over. For a subscription move, both subscriptions must sit in the same Microsoft Entra tenant (the directory of users), and the target subscription must have the needed resource providers registered.

Moving to another region is not a move in that sense. ARM cannot change a resource's location. Instead you use Azure Resource Mover, a service that copies resources to a target region. For VMs it relies on Azure Site Recovery replication, a disaster-recovery service that keeps a copy of disks in sync. You add resources, resolve dependencies, prepare, initiate the move, then commit. The source VM is deleted only when you choose to delete it. There is a short outage at cutover, and the copy gets new IDs.

Worked example: you move vm-web01 from rg-test to rg-prod. Step one, in the portal you select the VM together with its OS disk, data disk, network interface and public IP. Step two, Azure validates the move, and both resource groups are locked against changes while it runs. Step three, the IDs change from .../resourceGroups/rg-test/... to .../resourceGroups/rg-prod/... and the location stays East US.

A common mistake is selecting only the VM and leaving out its dependent disks and network interface, which makes validation fail. Afterwards, any scripts or alerts that hard-coded the old resource ID will break until you update them.

questions.prompt: Fabrikam Health wants to move a VM named vm-sql02 (in West Europe) from its subscription Sub-Dev to its subscription Sub-Prod, keeping it in a resource group called rg-data. Here is the plan. Step 1: confirm that Sub-Dev and Sub-Prod belong to the same Microsoft Entra tenant (the shared directory of users). Step 2: ??? Step 3: in the portal, select vm-sql02 together with its OS disk, its two data disks, its network interface and its public IP, then let Azure validate the move. Step 4: after the move, confirm that the location still reads West Europe and that the resource ID now contains Sub-Prod, then update a monitoring alert that pointed at the old ID. What belongs in Step 2?
choices: Enable Azure Site Recovery replication from Sub-Dev to Sub-Prod so that the disks stay in sync during the move
Stop and deallocate vm-sql02, because a subscription move always requires the VM to be shut down first
Change the VM's location to the default region of Sub-Prod so that the move validation can succeed
Confirm that Sub-Prod has the needed resource providers registered for the resources being moved
questions.why: A subscription move needs both subscriptions in the same tenant and the target subscription to have the required resource providers registered, while the VM normally keeps running and keeps its region.

questions.prompt: Northwind Traders runs a VM named vm-app07 in East US and must relocate it to North Europe so it sits closer to its customers. Which approach fits this requirement?
choices: Edit the VM's location property from East US to North Europe and save the change
Move the VM into a different subscription whose billing is based in North Europe
Use Azure Resource Mover, which copies the VM to the target region using Azure Site Recovery replication
Use the Azure Resource Manager move operation to move the VM into a resource group created in North Europe
questions.why: Azure Resource Manager cannot change a resource's location, so a region change needs Azure Resource Mover, which copies the VM to the new region rather than moving it in place.

questions.prompt: An administrator at Tailspin Toys tries to move a VM named vm-batch3 from rg-staging to rg-live. In the portal they select only the VM itself and start the move, and validation fails. What is the most likely reason?
