choices: Resource group moves only work between two different subscriptions, not inside one
The two resource groups are in different regions, so the move needs Azure Resource Mover
The VM's dependent resources, such as its disks and network interface, were not selected along with it
The VM was still running, and VMs must be stopped before any resource group move
questions.why: A VM has to move together with its dependent disks, network interface and similar resources, and leaving them out makes the move validation fail.

questions.prompt: At Wingtip Bikes, an engineer has a role that was granted on the resource group rg-sandbox and nothing else. A VM named vm-tools4 is moved from rg-sandbox to rg-core, where the engineer has no role. What happens to the engineer's access to vm-tools4?
choices: Access stays the same, because the permissions travel with the VM to its new resource group
Access stays the same until the VM is restarted, and then the permissions of rg-core apply
The engineer loses that inherited access, because the permissions of rg-core now apply to the VM instead
The engineer loses access only if the move also changed the VM's region
questions.why: Permissions inherited from the old resource group stop applying after the move, and the new resource group's permissions take over straight away.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between moving a VM to another resource group or subscription and moving it to another region. Name at least one limit or tradeoff of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: Moving a VM to another resource group or subscription is a metadata change in Azure Resource Manager. The VM stays in the same region and usually keeps running. Its resource ID changes, though, so scripts, alerts or anything else pointing at the old ID must be updated. Permissions now come from the new group. We have to move its disks, network interface and public IP with it, or validation fails. A subscription move also needs both subscriptions in the same Entra tenant and the right providers registered in the target. Moving to another region is really a copy. Azure Resource Mover, using Site Recovery replication, builds the VM in the new region, and we commit and then delete the source. The tradeoff is a cutover outage, new resource IDs, and more steps, plus a brief window where the source still exists and costs money until deleted.
rubricPoints: A resource group or subscription move keeps the VM in the same region.
The resource ID changes, so references to the old ID need updating.
Dependent resources such as disks and the network interface must move together.
A subscription move requires the same Microsoft Entra tenant and registered providers in the target.
A region move is a copy using Azure Resource Mover or Site Recovery, with prepare, move, commit and source-deletion steps.
A region move involves cutover downtime, while a resource group move normally does not.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine performs Azure moves, so the learner gains most from reasoning through exam-style scenarios about which kind of move, tool and dependencies each situation needs.

lessons.plain: A virtual machine size is the fixed bundle of computing power you rent for one cloud server: how many processors, how much memory, how many disks it can attach, and how much network it gets. Managing sizes means picking the right bundle and changing it later when needs change. Think of renting a moving van. Small, medium and large vans come in fixed shapes, and you cannot add an extra metre to one. If your load grows, you swap to a bigger van, and the swap means stopping briefly to move your things across.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your cloud server keeps running out of memory, so you decide to switch it to a bigger size. Do you think it can keep running without interruption during the change, or will it need to restart? Why?
lessons.teach:
A virtual machine (VM) size is a fixed bundle of resources Azure sells as one unit. It sets the number of virtual CPUs (vCPUs, which are slices of a physical processor), the memory (RAM), a temporary local disk, the maximum number of data disks you can attach, and the network bandwidth. Sizes are grouped into families by shape. B is burstable: it is cheap, saves up CPU credits while idle and spends them during spikes. D is general purpose, E is memory-optimised, F is compute-optimised, L is storage-optimised, and N has GPUs (graphics processors). The name tells you the shape. Standard_D4s_v5 means the D family, 4 vCPUs, s for able to use premium SSD disks, and v5 for the hardware generation.

Resizing changes the size of an existing VM. This is called scaling up or down, or vertical scaling. Scaling out is different: it means adding more VMs. You can resize in the portal on the VM's Size page, with the Azure CLI command az vm resize, with PowerShell Update-AzVM, or by changing the vmSize property in a template. A resize always restarts the VM, because the VM has to land on hardware that can supply the new bundle. If the target size is offered on the cluster (the group of physical hosts) already running the VM, the resize works while the VM is running, but it still reboots. If the size is not offered there, it does not appear in the list until you stop and deallocate the VM, which releases its hardware. After that, every size in the region becomes available.

Worked example: a D2s_v5 web server (2 vCPU, 8 GiB) runs out of memory. Step 1: confirm the shortage is memory, not CPU, and choose E2s_v5 (2 vCPU, 16 GiB). Step 2: check that the regional vCPU quota for that family has room. Step 3: open the Size page. E2s_v5 is not listed, so deallocate the VM. Step 4: select E2s_v5 and resize. Step 5: start the VM, which now boots with 16 GiB.

A common mistake is picking a size without the s, or with fewer data-disk slots, for a VM that uses premium disks or many data disks. That resize fails. Also, data on the temporary disk is lost when the VM is deallocated or moved, so never keep important data there. A single VM is down during any resize, so schedule resizes in a maintenance window.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs its route-planning service on a Standard_B2s VM (2 vCPU, burstable). The CPU now stays near 100% all day, so the VM's saved CPU credits run out and it slows down. Step 1: the admin confirms the problem is sustained CPU load, not a short spike, and picks Standard_D4s_v5 (general purpose, 4 vCPU, premium-disk capable). Step 2: the admin checks that the region's vCPU quota for the D family has room for 4 more vCPUs. Step 3: on the VM's Size page, Standard_D4s_v5 already appears in the list while the VM is running. Step 4: ??? Step 5: after the VM comes back up, the admin confirms it now shows 4 vCPUs. Which choice correctly completes Step 4?
choices: Select Standard_D4s_v5 and resize while the VM is running, inside a maintenance window, expecting the VM to reboot.
Add a second Standard_B2s VM so the two VMs share the CPU load, which is how a VM's size is increased.
Stop and deallocate the VM first, because Azure only allows a resize after the VM has released its hardware.
Select Standard_D4s_v5 and resize. Expect no restart, because the size is offered on the current cluster.
questions.why: The size is listed, so it is offered on the current cluster and the resize can run without deallocating, but every resize still restarts the VM, so it belongs in a maintenance window.

questions.prompt: An admin sees a VM size called Standard_E8s_v4 in a deployment template. Based on how Azure size names are built, what does this name tell the admin?
choices: Memory-optimised family, 8 vCPUs, able to use premium SSD disks, hardware generation 4
Compute-optimised family, 8 GiB of memory, s for a small temporary disk, generation 4
General-purpose family, 8 vCPUs, s for scale-set ready, 4 GPUs
Memory-optimised family, 8 data-disk slots, s for standard HDD only, version 4 of the template
questions.why: E is the memory-optimised family, 8 is the vCPU count, s means the size can use premium SSD disks, and v4 is the hardware generation.

questions.prompt: An online ticketing team expects heavy traffic for a concert sale. Their plan is to keep their existing Standard_D2s_v5 VMs exactly as they are and add four more identical VMs to share the load. What is this approach called?
choices: Scaling up, also called vertical scaling
Scaling down to burstable sizes
Resizing, done with az vm resize
Scaling out, which means adding more VMs instead of changing the size of existing ones
questions.why: Adding more VMs is scaling out. Changing the size of an existing VM is scaling up or down, also called vertical scaling.

questions.prompt: A clinic's records VM is Standard_F8s_v2 and has several premium SSD data disks attached. To save money, an admin tries to resize it to a similar size whose name has no s, for example Standard_F8_v2. What is the most likely result?
choices: The resize succeeds, and Azure converts the premium disks to standard disks during the reboot.
The resize succeeds without a reboot, because both sizes are in the same F family.
The resize succeeds, but only the temporary disk is lost and the data disks stay unchanged.
The resize fails, because the target size cannot use the premium disks the VM depends on.
questions.why: A size without the s cannot use premium SSD disks, so resizing a VM that relies on premium disks to that size fails.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would resize a production Azure VM that needs more memory, and name at least one limit or tradeoff they must plan for.
lessons.modelAnswer: A VM size is a fixed bundle of vCPUs, memory, temporary disk, data-disk slots and network bandwidth, and the family tells you the shape. Since we need memory, I'd move to the memory-optimised E family rather than simply buying more CPUs. First I'd check that the new size keeps the s for premium disks and has enough data-disk slots, and that our regional vCPU quota has room. Then I'd open the VM's Size page or run az vm resize. If the size isn't listed, the current hardware cluster can't host it, so I'd deallocate the VM to see every size in the region. The big tradeoff is downtime: a resize always reboots a single VM, so we schedule a maintenance window. Anything on the temporary disk is lost if we deallocate. Resizing is vertical scaling, and it has a ceiling, so adding more VMs may be the better long-term answer.
rubricPoints: Defines a VM size as a fixed bundle of vCPU, memory, disk limits and bandwidth, with families for different shapes.
Matches the family to the bottleneck, for example memory-optimised for memory shortages.
States that a resize reboots the VM, and that deallocating may be needed to see sizes the current cluster cannot host.
Checks compatibility: premium-storage support, data-disk count and regional vCPU quota.
Warns that temporary-disk data is lost and that a single VM is down during a resize.
Distinguishes vertical scaling (resize) from scaling out (more VMs).

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or engine has the learner resize an Azure VM, and the exam tests this as situation-based reasoning, so working through scenarios about which family to pick, whether to deallocate and what downtime to expect adds the most.

lessons.plain: A virtual machine in Azure stores everything on virtual disks, which act like hard drives you rent from Azure instead of drives screwed into a server. Every machine has an operating system disk that boots it. Most also have a temporary scratch disk that can be wiped. You can add more data disks for your files and databases. Managing disks means choosing how fast they are, adding or removing them, making them bigger, and taking copies for safety. Think of it like adding, swapping and upgrading drives in a home PC, except you do it with a few settings changes rather than a screwdriver.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your database server keeps its data on a 128 GiB virtual disk that is almost full, so you make the disk 256 GiB in Azure. When you log in to the server, it still shows only 128 GiB of usable space. What do you think still needs doing?
lessons.teach:
Managing virtual machine disks means picking the type, size and caching of the disks behind a VM and changing them safely over time. Azure mostly uses managed disks, which are block storage volumes that Azure stores and replicates for you, so you never handle the underlying storage account. A VM has three kinds of disk. The OS disk holds the operating system and boots the machine. The temporary disk is local scratch space on the physical host and can be erased during maintenance or a redeploy. Data disks are extra managed disks you attach for application data.

Disk types trade cost against speed. Standard HDD is cheap and slow. Standard SSD suits light workloads. Premium SSD gives steady low latency for production. Premium SSD v2 and Ultra Disk let you tune performance separately from size for heavy databases. Host caching (None, ReadOnly or ReadWrite) controls whether reads and writes are cached on the host. ReadOnly often helps read-heavy data disks, and None is usual for write-heavy log disks. A snapshot is a point-in-time copy of one disk, which you can use for backup or to build a new disk.

Worked example. A data disk is 128 GiB and full. Step 1: in the portal, open the VM, go to Disks, select the data disk and raise its size to 256 GiB. Many data disks can grow while the VM runs, but some cases need the VM deallocated (stopped so it releases its host) first. Step 2: Azure now reports 256 GiB. Step 3: inside the guest operating system, extend the partition and file system, for example with Disk Management on Windows or the growpart and resize tools on Linux. Only after this step does the space become usable.

Common mistake: skipping step 3, or trying to shrink a disk. Azure does not support shrinking a managed disk. A second mistake is putting real data on the temporary disk, because that data can vanish after a host move. Changing a disk's type usually requires deallocating the VM, which means planned downtime for a running service.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm runs its billing app on a VM whose 64 GiB data disk is Standard SSD. Month-end reports are slow, so the administrator moves that disk to Premium SSD, a faster disk type that gives steady low latency. Step 1: tell staff the billing app will be offline for a short window that evening. Step 2: ____. Step 3: in the portal, open the VM's Disks page, select the data disk and change its type from Standard SSD to Premium SSD. Step 4: start the VM again and confirm the app works. What is Step 2?
choices: Take a snapshot of the temporary disk so the billing data can be restored if the type change fails
Set host caching on the data disk to ReadWrite so the type change can happen while the VM keeps running
Deallocate the VM, which stops it and releases its physical host, so the disk type can be changed
Inside the guest operating system, extend the partition and file system so it can use the faster disk
questions.why: Changing a managed disk's type usually requires the VM to be deallocated first, which is why the downtime window was planned in Step 1.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's warehouse VM lets users upload delivery photos, and the app saves them to the VM's temporary disk because it is fast. After Azure moves the VM to a different physical host during maintenance, all the photos are gone. What is the best explanation and fix?
choices: The OS disk ran out of space and deleted older files, so the OS disk should be made larger
The temporary disk is local scratch space on the host and can be erased, so the photos should go on an attached data disk
Standard HDD disks lose data during maintenance, so the temporary disk should be upgraded to Premium SSD
Host caching was set to None, which discards writes, so caching should be changed to ReadOnly
questions.why: The temporary disk lives on the physical host and can be wiped during maintenance or a host move, so real data belongs on a managed data disk.

questions.prompt: A hospital's database VM has a separate data disk that holds only the transaction log, which is written to constantly and rarely read back. Host caching controls whether reads and writes to a disk are cached on the physical host. Which host caching setting is the usual choice for this log disk?
choices: ReadOnly, because caching reads always speeds up any database disk
The setting does not matter for data disks; caching only applies to the temporary disk
ReadWrite, because a disk that is written to constantly needs write caching
None, because caching is usually turned off for write-heavy log disks
questions.why: For write-heavy log disks, None is the usual host caching setting, while ReadOnly tends to suit read-heavy data disks.

questions.prompt: A marketing agency attached a 1 TiB managed disk to a VM, but only about 150 GiB is in use. To cut costs, a junior admin wants to change that disk to 256 GiB. Which statement is accurate?
choices: Azure does not support shrinking a managed disk, so the 1 TiB disk cannot simply be reduced to 256 GiB
Deallocate the VM first, then lower the size in the portal; shrinking only needs the VM stopped
Shrink the partition inside the guest operating system and Azure will reduce the disk to match
Reduce the size in the portal while the VM runs; Azure shrinks managed disks online
questions.why: Managed disks can grow but Azure does not support shrinking them, whether the VM is running, deallocated or resized inside the guest.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would give a running VM more and faster disk space in Azure, including what has to happen inside the operating system, and name at least one limit or tradeoff they should plan around.
lessons.modelAnswer: Azure VMs use managed disks: an OS disk that boots the machine, data disks for application data, and a temporary disk that is scratch space and can be wiped, so nothing important belongs there. To get more space, I would open the VM's Disks blade and raise the data disk's size. Many data disks can grow while the VM is running, but some cases need the VM deallocated. Azure then sees the bigger disk, but I still have to extend the partition and file system inside the guest OS before the space is usable. To make it faster, I would switch the type, for example Standard SSD to Premium SSD, which normally means deallocating the VM and planning a short outage. I would also check host caching: ReadOnly suits read-heavy data, and None suits write-heavy logs. The limits are that disks cannot be shrunk and faster tiers cost more, so I would take a snapshot before making changes.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes the OS disk, data disks and the temporary disk, and warns that the temporary disk can lose data.
States that growing a disk in Azure must be followed by extending the partition inside the guest OS.
Notes that managed disks can be expanded but not shrunk.
Explains that disk types trade cost against performance and that changing type usually needs a deallocated VM.
Mentions host caching choices or taking a snapshot before changes.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests whether you can pick the right disk type, caching setting and resize steps for a described workload, so reasoning through realistic scenarios builds that judgment best.

lessons.plain: When you run important software on virtual machines, you do not want one broken power supply or one maintenance reboot to take everything down. Azure gives you two ways to spread copies of a virtual machine (a rented computer running in Microsoft's datacenter) so they do not all fail together. An availability zone is a separate building, or group of buildings, inside one region, with its own power and cooling. An availability set spreads machines across different racks and maintenance batches inside one datacenter. Think of storing spare house keys: different drawers in one house (set) versus different houses in one town (zones).
lessons.guessPrompt: You run two copies of a website on two virtual machines. Which would protect you better if a whole datacenter building lost power: putting both machines on different racks in the same building, or putting them in different buildings in the same city? Why?
lessons.teach:
An availability zone is a physically separate location inside an Azure region, with independent power, cooling and networking. Zones are numbered 1, 2 and 3. Deploying a VM to a zone pins it there. Two or more VMs spread across two or more zones carry a 99.99% uptime commitment (an SLA, or service level agreement).

An availability set is a logical grouping inside one datacenter. It uses fault domains, which are groups of hardware sharing a power source and network switch (up to 3), and update domains, which are groups Azure reboots together during planned maintenance (up to 20, default 5). Two or more VMs in a set carry a 99.95% SLA. Sets protect against rack failures and maintenance, not a whole building outage.

Worked example: four web VMs in a set with 2 fault domains and 5 update domains. Azure places VM1 in fault domain 0 and update domain 0, VM2 in fault domain 1 and update domain 1, VM3 in fault domain 0 and update domain 2, VM4 in fault domain 1 and update domain 3. A rack fails in fault domain 0: VM1 and VM3 stop, VM2 and VM4 keep serving. During maintenance, only one update domain reboots at a time, so three VMs stay up.

How you provision it: in the portal, the Basics tab of VM creation has an Availability options choice (zone, set, or none). In ARM or Bicep, a VM gets a zones property such as ['1'], or an availabilitySet property pointing to a Microsoft.Compute/availabilitySets resource that defines its fault and update domain counts. A VM uses one or the other, never both.

Common mistake: trying to add an existing VM to a set or zone later. Placement is chosen at creation; changing it means recreating the VM from its disks. Another trap is deploying one VM and expecting high availability; you need at least two, usually behind a load balancer (a service that spreads traffic across healthy machines), or the outage still reaches users.

questions.prompt: A payroll company runs six API VMs in one availability set configured with 3 fault domains and 5 update domains. Azure has placed them like this: VM1 in fault domain 0 and update domain 0, VM2 in fault domain 1 and update domain 1, VM3 in fault domain 2 and update domain 2, VM4 in fault domain 0 and update domain 3, VM5 in fault domain 1 and update domain 4, and VM6 in fault domain 2 and update domain 0. Step 1: During planned maintenance on update domain 0, Azure reboots VM1 and VM6 together, and the other four keep serving. Step 2 (missing): A rack failure hits fault domain 2. What happens?
choices: All six VMs stop, because an availability set lives inside one datacenter.
Only VM3 stops, because each fault domain holds a single VM.
VM3 and VM6 stop. VM1, VM2, VM4 and VM5 keep serving.
VM3, VM6 and VM1 stop, because VM1 shares an update domain with VM6.
questions.why: A fault domain is a group of hardware sharing power and a network switch, so a rack failure there stops only the VMs placed in fault domain 2 (VM3 and VM6), while the VMs in fault domains 0 and 1 keep running.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm must keep its order-tracking VMs running even if an entire datacenter building in the region loses power. Which deployment meets this need?
choices: Two VMs in one availability set with 3 fault domains
Two VMs in one availability set with 20 update domains
Two or more VMs spread across two or more availability zones
One VM pinned to availability zone 2
questions.why: Availability zones are physically separate locations with independent power, cooling and networking, so spreading VMs across zones survives a building outage, while an availability set only protects against rack failures and maintenance inside one datacenter.

questions.prompt: An administrator built a single reporting VM last month with Availability options set to none. Now the team wants it inside an existing availability set. What must the administrator do?
choices: Edit the VM's availabilitySet property in place and restart it
Add a zones property such as ['1'] so Azure can then attach the set
Move the VM into the set from its Availability blade without downtime
Recreate the VM from its disks, choosing the availability set at creation
questions.why: A VM's placement in a set or zone is chosen only at creation, so changing it means recreating the VM from its disks.

questions.prompt: A retailer deploys three web VMs in Bicep, each with the property zones: ['1'], behind a load balancer. They expect the 99.99% availability-zone SLA. Is that expectation correct?
choices: No, they would also need an availabilitySet property on each VM.
Yes, because the load balancer spreads traffic across healthy machines.
Yes, three VMs is more than the two-VM minimum.
No, all three are pinned to the same zone; they must span two or more zones.
questions.why: The 99.99% commitment requires two or more VMs spread across two or more zones, and pinning all three to zone 1 leaves them exposed to a single-zone outage.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between deploying VMs to availability zones and to an availability set, when you would pick each, and one limit or tradeoff of the choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both spread copies of a workload so one failure does not take it all down. An availability set keeps VMs in one datacenter but places them on different fault domains, meaning separate racks with their own power and network, and different update domains, meaning separate maintenance reboot batches. That gives a 99.95% SLA with two or more VMs. Availability zones put VMs in physically separate buildings within the region, so even a whole-building outage leaves copies running, and two or more VMs across zones get 99.99%. I would choose zones for critical workloads where the region supports them, and a set where zones are not available or I need everything in one location. Tradeoffs: placement is decided at creation, so moving later means recreating the VM; a VM cannot use both; and traffic between zones crosses buildings, adding a little latency. Either way I need at least two VMs behind a load balancer.
rubricPoints: An availability zone is a physically separate location in a region; zones protect against a whole datacenter outage.
An availability set spreads VMs across fault domains (shared power and network) and update domains (maintenance batches) in one datacenter.
States the SLA difference: 99.99% across zones versus 99.95% in a set, both needing two or more VMs.
Notes placement is chosen at VM creation and an existing VM cannot simply be added later.
Notes a VM uses either a zone or a set, not both, and needs a load balancer and multiple VMs to benefit.

suggested.rationale: The core exam skill is reasoning through a workload scenario to pick zones or a set and the matching portal or template setting, which an exam-style situation exercises better than any current mission.

lessons.plain: A virtual machine scale set is a way to run many identical virtual computers in the cloud as one group, instead of building and babysitting each one by hand. You describe one machine once, its size, operating system image and network, and the platform stamps out as many copies as you ask for. It can also add copies when the machines get busy and remove them when things calm down. Think of a bakery that uses one recipe card: on a busy morning it bakes more identical loaves, and in the quiet afternoon it bakes fewer, without rewriting the recipe.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a group of identical web servers is set to add one server whenever average processor use stays above 70 percent, what should also be set so the group does not grow forever and keep paying for idle machines after traffic drops?
lessons.teach:
An Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set (VMSS) is a resource that manages a group of virtual machines (VMs, rented virtual computers) built from one shared definition called the model: the VM size, the image (a saved operating-system template), disks and network settings. Each VM in the set is an instance. Because every instance comes from the same model, you scale by changing a number, the instance count, rather than building servers one by one.

Key settings when deploying, whether in the portal or in an ARM template or Bicep file: the orchestration mode, either Uniform (all instances identical, managed as a block) or Flexible (instances can differ and mix with standalone VMs, now the recommended default); availability zones (separate datacenters within a region) to spread instances; a load balancer (a component that spreads incoming traffic across instances); and the upgrade policy, which decides how model changes reach existing instances. Manual means you must update instances yourself, Automatic updates them all at once, and Rolling updates them in small batches.

Autoscale adds or removes instances using rules you write. You set a minimum, maximum and default count, then scale-out and scale-in rules based on a metric such as average CPU, plus a cooldown, a waiting period after any change before another one.

Worked example: minimum 2, maximum 6, scale out by 1 when average CPU is above 70 percent for 10 minutes, scale in by 1 when below 30 percent for 10 minutes, cooldown 5 minutes. Traffic surges and CPU sits at 85 percent: the set goes 2 to 3, waits 5 minutes, still hot, goes to 4. Load drops to 20 percent: it steps 4 to 3 to 2 and stops at the minimum.

Common mistake: writing only a scale-out rule. The set grows during a spike and never shrinks, so you keep paying for idle machines. A second trap is changing the image with the Manual upgrade policy and assuming running instances changed; they keep the old model until you upgrade them.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking company runs its checkout service on a Virtual Machine Scale Set (a group of identical virtual machines built from one shared definition). Its autoscale settings (rules that add or remove instances automatically) are: minimum 3, maximum 9, default 3. Scale out by 2 instances when average CPU is above 75 percent for 5 minutes. Scale in by 1 instance when average CPU is below 25 percent for 15 minutes. Cooldown (the wait after any change before another change) is 10 minutes. Trace: Step 1, a concert goes on sale and CPU sits at 90 percent, so the set grows from 3 to 5. Step 2, it waits 10 minutes, CPU is still 90 percent, so it grows from 5 to 7. Step 3, sales end and CPU falls to 15 percent and stays there. Step 4 is missing. What happens in Step 4?
choices: The set drops from 7 to 5 at once, because scale-in mirrors the 2-instance scale-out step, and then keeps dropping 2 at a time to 3.
After each cooldown and 15 minutes below 25 percent, the set removes 1 instance at a time, 7 to 6 to 5 to 4 to 3, and stops at the minimum of 3.
The set drops straight from 7 to the minimum of 3 in a single change, because CPU is far below the 25 percent threshold.
The set keeps removing 1 instance at a time until it reaches 0, because CPU never rises back above 25 percent.
questions.why: The scale-in rule removes 1 instance per action, each action is separated by the cooldown, and autoscale never goes below the configured minimum of 3.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs 10 instances in a scale set behind a load balancer (a component that spreads incoming traffic across instances). They plan a new image (a saved operating-system template) and want the change to reach existing instances automatically, but never take all instances offline at the same time. Which upgrade policy fits?
choices: Rolling
Automatic
Uniform
Manual
questions.why: Rolling updates existing instances in small batches, so the change is applied automatically while the rest keep serving traffic; Automatic updates them all at once, Manual needs you to do it, and Uniform is an orchestration mode, not an upgrade policy.

questions.prompt: An online bakery set up autoscale on its scale set with minimum 2, maximum 10, and one rule: add 1 instance when average CPU is above 65 percent for 10 minutes. After a holiday rush, CPU has sat near 5 percent for two weeks, yet the monthly bill is still high. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The cooldown period is too long, so autoscale has not had time to react yet.
There is no scale-in rule, so the set grew during the rush and never shrank back.
The minimum count of 2 forces the set to keep all 10 instances running.
The upgrade policy is set to Manual, which blocks autoscale from changing the instance count.
questions.why: With only a scale-out rule, nothing ever removes instances, so the set stays at its peak size and you keep paying for idle machines.

questions.prompt: A school district runs its grading portal on a scale set whose model (the shared definition of VM size, image, disks and network settings) produces every instance. Demand doubles during exam week. In a scale set, what does an administrator change to add capacity?
choices: The orchestration mode, switching from Flexible to Uniform to get more machines
The instance count, so more instances are created from the same model
The image in the model, so each existing instance becomes larger
Each VM one by one, building and configuring new servers by hand
questions.why: Because every instance comes from one shared model, you scale a scale set simply by raising the instance count rather than building servers individually.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a virtual machine scale set is and how its autoscale rules decide when to add or remove instances, and name one limit or tradeoff, such as the upgrade policy choice or missing a scale-in rule.
lessons.modelAnswer: A scale set is one Azure resource that runs a group of identical VMs from a single model: size, image, disks and network. We change capacity by changing the instance count instead of building servers. Autoscale does that for us: we set a minimum, maximum and default, then pair a scale-out rule, say add one when average CPU stays above 70 percent for 10 minutes, with a scale-in rule, say remove one below 30 percent. A cooldown stops it from flapping. We also put a load balancer in front and spread instances across zones. The tradeoff is the upgrade policy: Automatic updates every instance at once, which is fast but risky; Rolling updates in batches, which is safer but slower; Manual leaves old instances on the old model until we upgrade them. And if we forget the scale-in rule, the set grows during spikes and never shrinks, so we pay for idle VMs.
rubricPoints: A scale set manages many identical VM instances built from one shared model.
Capacity changes by adjusting instance count, manually or with autoscale.
Autoscale needs minimum, maximum and default counts plus paired scale-out and scale-in rules on a metric.
A cooldown period prevents rapid back-and-forth scaling.
The upgrade policy (Manual, Automatic, Rolling) controls how model changes reach existing instances.
Names a tradeoff, such as a missing scale-in rule causing cost or Automatic upgrades risking all instances at once.

suggested.rationale: Writing and tuning scale-out and scale-in rules with minimums, maximums and cooldowns, then watching instance counts respond to load, is exactly what a planned autoscaling-policy engine would let the learner practise.

lessons.plain: Azure Container Registry is Microsoft's managed private storage for container images. A container image is a packaged, ready-to-run copy of an application together with everything it needs. Think of a registry as a private warehouse with your company's name on the door. Builders drop off finished, labelled boxes (images), and approved delivery trucks (container services and virtual machines) collect them by label. Microsoft runs the warehouse for you. You decide its size and features, who may drop boxes off, and who may pick them up. Because it is private, your images are not exposed on a public site.
lessons.guessPrompt: A registry stores labelled container images that other services download. Should a service that only runs those images be allowed to upload or delete images, or only to download them? Why?
lessons.teach:
Azure Container Registry (ACR) is a managed, private registry. A registry is a service that stores and serves container images. An image is identified by repository:tag: the repository is a named collection of related images, and the tag is a version label such as v1.

To create one, you choose a resource group, which is a folder for related Azure resources. You also choose a region, a registry name and a SKU, which is a pricing tier. The name must be globally unique, 5 to 50 characters, and letters and numbers only. It becomes the login server, name.azurecr.io.

There are three SKUs. Basic suits learning. Standard adds storage and throughput. Premium adds geo-replication, which keeps copies of the registry in several regions. Premium also adds private endpoints, which give the registry a private address inside your virtual network. You can create the registry in the portal, with az acr create --resource-group rg1 --name contosoreg --sku Standard, or as a Microsoft.ContainerRegistry/registries resource in an ARM template or Bicep file.

Access uses Microsoft Entra ID, Azure's identity service, together with role-based access control (RBAC), which grants rights through roles. The AcrPush role lets an identity upload images, and AcrPull lets it only download them. A managed identity is an identity Azure creates and manages for a resource. Giving a workload's managed identity AcrPull lets it fetch images without any stored password. The admin user is a single shared username and password. It is off by default and is best left off.

Here is a worked example of pushing an image. First, az acr login --name contosoreg signs your local tools in. Second, tag the image with the full address: docker tag web:v1 contosoreg.azurecr.io/web:v1. Third, docker push contosoreg.azurecr.io/web:v1 uploads it. Alternatively, ACR Tasks can build the image in Azure with az acr build. Either way, the image ends up as repository web with tag v1.

A common mistake is pushing an image without the login-server prefix. The push then goes to the public Docker Hub or fails. Another mistake is forgetting the AcrPull role, so the running service cannot fetch the image and deployments fail with an authorization error.

questions.prompt: Northwind Traders needs a new private registry for its order-processing images. The registry must keep copies in two regions, and it must have a private address inside the company's virtual network. Here is the plan, worked step by step. Step 1: choose the resource group rg-northwind-orders and the primary region. Step 2: choose the registry name northwindorders77. It has 17 characters and uses only letters and numbers, so it meets the naming rule, as long as no one else already uses it. Step 3: (missing). Step 4: once the registry is created, the login server is northwindorders77.azurecr.io, and images will be pushed to addresses that start with that prefix. Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Choose the Basic SKU now to save money, then turn on geo-replication and private endpoints later without changing the SKU.
Choose any SKU, because the region chosen in Step 1 already decides whether copies are kept in other regions.
Choose the Premium SKU, because only Premium offers geo-replication and private endpoints.
Choose the Standard SKU, because it adds more storage and throughput than Basic, and that covers multi-region copies.
questions.why: Geo-replication (copies in several regions) and private endpoints (a private address in your virtual network) are both Premium-only features, so the SKU, or pricing tier, must be Premium.

questions.prompt: Tailspin Toys is creating an Azure Container Registry. A registry is a service that stores and serves container images. Which proposed registry name meets the naming rules?
choices: tailspinreg01
acr1
tail-spin-reg
Tailspin_Registry
questions.why: A registry name must be 5 to 50 characters and use only letters and numbers. tailspinreg01 qualifies, while the others contain a hyphen, are too short (4 characters), or contain an underscore.

questions.prompt: Contoso Pharma runs a web app that has a managed identity. A managed identity is an identity that Azure creates and manages for a resource. The app must download images from the registry pharmaimages, without any stored password and without being able to upload images. What should the administrator do?
choices: Copy the images to the public Docker Hub so the web app needs no permissions.
Assign the AcrPull role on the registry to the web app's managed identity.
Enable the registry's admin user and save its username and password in the web app's settings.
Assign the AcrPush role on the registry to the web app's managed identity.
questions.why: AcrPull only allows downloading images. Granting it to the managed identity through role-based access control means no password is stored, and the app cannot upload images.

questions.prompt: An engineer at Woodgrove Bank runs az acr login --name woodgrovereg. She then runs docker tag ledger:4.2 ledger:4.2, followed by docker push ledger:4.2. What is the most likely result?
choices: The image is stored in woodgrovereg as repository ledger with tag 4.2, because she signed in first.
The push goes to the public Docker Hub or fails, because the image name lacks the woodgrovereg.azurecr.io login-server prefix.
The push fails with an AcrPull authorization error, because pulling rights are missing.
Azure adds the woodgrovereg.azurecr.io prefix automatically, so the push succeeds into the private registry.
questions.why: Docker uses the image name to decide where to push. Without the login-server prefix, the push does not go to the Azure registry: it is sent to the public Docker Hub or fails.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would set up a container registry so that an app can pull images securely, and name one tradeoff you face when choosing the SKU.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd create an Azure Container Registry in our resource group. Its name must be globally unique and alphanumeric, and that name becomes the login server, name.azurecr.io. Developers or the pipeline get the AcrPush role to upload images. Images are tagged with the full login-server address, like name.azurecr.io/web:v1, before pushing, or built in Azure with ACR Tasks. The app that runs containers uses a managed identity with only the AcrPull role, so no password is stored anywhere. I'd leave the admin user disabled because it is a single shared credential. The SKU choice is a cost-versus-features tradeoff. Basic is cheapest but limited. Standard gives more storage and throughput. Only Premium offers geo-replication and private endpoints, so if we need the registry reachable privately or copied to other regions, we have to pay for Premium.
rubricPoints: Defines the registry as a managed private store for container images identified by repository and tag.
States that the name is globally unique and forms the name.azurecr.io login server.
Uses Entra ID roles with least privilege, AcrPush for publishers and AcrPull for consumers, ideally via managed identity.
Notes that the admin user is a shared credential that should stay disabled.
Names a SKU tradeoff: geo-replication and private endpoints require Premium at higher cost.
Mentions tagging with the login-server prefix before pushing.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine provisions a registry, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios on SKU choice, naming and pull permissions builds the judgement the exam tests.

lessons.plain: Azure Container Instances (ACI) is a way to run a container in Azure without building or managing any server or cluster yourself. A container is a packaged application together with everything it needs to run. You tell ACI which container image to run, how much processor and memory it needs, and whether it should be reachable from the internet. Azure then starts it within seconds and bills you only while it runs. Think of it like hailing a taxi instead of buying a car: you state where you are going, ride, and pay for that trip only.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have a small script packaged as a container that processes one file and then exits. If Azure is told to restart the container every time it stops, what do you think will happen after the script finishes?
lessons.teach:
Azure Container Instances (ACI) is a managed service that runs containers on demand, with no virtual machine or orchestrator for you to maintain. The unit you create is a container group: one or more containers that share a host, a lifecycle, a network address and storage. Most single-app deployments are a group holding one container.

When provisioning, through the portal's Create container instance page, a template, or the command line, you set a few things. The image is the packaged app plus its registry, such as Docker Hub or Azure Container Registry. A private registry needs a username and password, or a managed identity, so ACI can pull the image. The OS type is Linux or Windows. Size is the CPU cores and memory reserved for the group. Networking is either public, meaning a public IP with an optional DNS name label that gives a friendly address and must be unique in that region, or private, meaning the group is placed inside a virtual network. You also list the ports to open. The restart policy can be Always, OnFailure or Never. Environment variables pass settings into the container, and secure environment variables hide values such as keys from view. Volumes, for example an Azure Files share, give the container storage that outlives it.

Worked example: run a public web demo. First, choose the image nginx from a public registry, so no credentials are needed. Second, pick Linux, 1 core and 1.5 GB. Third, select Public networking, set the DNS label demo-web42 and open port 80. Fourth, keep restart policy Always, because a web server should stay up. Fifth, create it. ACI pulls the image, starts it, and the site answers at the DNS address.

A common mistake is leaving Always on a run-once batch job. The job finishes, ACI restarts it, and it reprocesses the same work in a loop, billing you continuously. Batch work should use OnFailure or Never.

questions.prompt: Larkspur Logistics wants a nightly job that parses invoices with Azure Container Instances (ACI), the managed service that runs containers without a virtual machine for you to maintain. An admin builds the container group (the unit ACI creates: one or more containers sharing a host, lifecycle, address and storage) like this. Step 1: choose the image invoiceparser:2.1, stored in the company's private Azure Container Registry, a private image store called larkspuracr. Step 2: ???. Step 3: pick Linux, 2 CPU cores and 4 GB of memory. Step 4: select Private networking so the group sits inside the company's virtual network, with no public IP. Step 5: set the restart policy to Never, because the job should run once and stop. Step 6: add a secure environment variable, a setting whose value is hidden from view, for the database key. Step 7: create it. What belongs in Step 2?
choices: Set a DNS name label that is unique in the region so ACI can locate the private registry
Supply registry credentials (a username and password) or a managed identity so ACI can pull the image
Mount an Azure Files share that holds a copy of the image for the container to start from
Switch the restart policy to Always so ACI keeps retrying until the image pull succeeds
questions.why: The image sits in a private registry, so ACI needs either a username and password or a managed identity to pull it. A public registry would need neither.

questions.prompt: A team at Brightwater Media deploys an Azure Container Instances container group that holds two containers: a web app and a small helper that refreshes its cache. Which statement correctly describes what those two containers share?
choices: The same host, lifecycle, network address and storage
A dedicated virtual machine that the team must patch and maintain
Only the container image, while each container gets its own IP address and storage
Nothing at runtime, because the group is just a label used for billing reports
questions.why: A container group is one or more containers that share a host, a lifecycle, a network address and storage, and ACI gives you no virtual machine to maintain.

questions.prompt: Fennick Research runs a monthly reporting container in Azure Container Instances. The container writes PDF reports, and the analysts need those files to still be there after the container stops. Which provisioning setting meets this need?
choices: Add secure environment variables that hold the report contents
Set the restart policy to Always so the container and its files never go away
Increase the memory reserved for the group so the files fit
Attach a volume, such as an Azure Files share, and write the reports to it
questions.why: A volume such as an Azure Files share gives the container storage that outlives it. Environment variables, restart policy and memory size don't keep files after the container stops.

questions.prompt: An admin at Corvel Bakeries creates a public Azure Container Instances group in the West Europe region and enters the DNS name label 'shop', which would give the group a friendly web address. The deployment is rejected because the label is unavailable. What is the most likely cause?
choices: DNS name labels can only be used when the group is placed inside a virtual network
The group was given too little CPU and memory to be assigned a DNS name
The restart policy must be set to OnFailure before a DNS name label is accepted
Another deployment in West Europe already uses the 'shop' label, and labels must be unique within a region
questions.why: A DNS name label on a public container group must be unique in that region, so a label someone else already uses there is refused.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what you must decide when provisioning a container in Azure Container Instances, and name one limit or tradeoff of choosing ACI over a fuller platform.
lessons.modelAnswer: ACI lets us run a container without managing servers. We create a container group, which is one or more containers sharing a host, an IP and a lifecycle. We pick the image and registry, adding credentials if the registry is private. We choose Linux or Windows, and the CPU and memory. Networking is either public, with an IP, a DNS label that must be unique in the region and open ports, or private inside a virtual network. We also set environment variables, using secure ones for secrets, and mount volumes like Azure Files if data must persist. The restart policy matters: Always suits long-running services, while OnFailure or Never suits batch jobs so they do not loop forever and keep billing. The tradeoff is that ACI is simple and fast but gives few built-in features for scaling or traffic routing, so bigger multi-service apps usually belong on a fuller platform.
rubricPoints: Describes ACI as serverless container hosting where the container group is the deployed unit.
Names the image, the registry and its credentials as required inputs.
Mentions CPU, memory and OS type as provisioning choices.
Explains public networking with a DNS label and ports versus deployment into a virtual network.
Matches the restart policy to the workload, with Always for services and OnFailure or Never for batch jobs.
States a limit, such as little built-in scaling or orchestration compared with fuller platforms.

suggested.rationale: No OpsForge mission or planned engine provisions ACI, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios that pick the image, networking and restart policy is the most useful practice.

lessons.plain: Azure Container Apps is a managed service that runs your packaged application, called a container, without you looking after any servers or a cluster. A container is a sealed bundle of an app plus everything it needs to run. You hand Azure the container image, which is the saved template of that bundle, and say how much CPU and memory it needs and whether the internet may reach it. Azure then starts it, gives it a web address and restarts it if it crashes. Think of renting a furnished flat in a managed building. You bring your belongings and the landlord handles the plumbing, power and security.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your app inside a container listens on port 8080, but when you set up the container app you tell Azure the app's port is 80. What do you think happens when someone opens the app's web address?
lessons.teach:
Provisioning a container with Azure Container Apps means creating two things. The first is a Container Apps environment, which is a shared, secure boundary that one or more apps live in. Apps in the same environment share a virtual network and send their logs to a Log Analytics workspace, which is a store for logs that you can search. The second is the container app itself. That is the resource that runs your image.

In the portal you choose Create a resource, then Container App. On the Basics tab you pick a subscription, a resource group (a folder for related resources), a name, a region, and an existing or new environment. On the Container tab you point at the image source. That can be a registry, which is a store for images such as Azure Container Registry or Docker Hub. You also give the image name and tag (its version label), the CPU and memory, and any environment variables, which are settings the app reads when it starts. On the Ingress tab you decide whether traffic can reach the app. External ingress means it is reachable from the internet. Internal ingress means only traffic from inside the environment can reach it. Here you also set the target port, which is the port your app actually listens on. The command-line equivalent is az containerapp create with options for the environment, image, target port and ingress.

Each deployment creates a revision, which is an unchangeable snapshot of the app's settings and image.

Worked example. You have an API image called orders:v1 in your private registry, and it listens on 8080. First, create the environment env-prod in the resource group rg-orders. Second, create the container app orders-api in env-prod. Third, choose your registry and the image orders:v1, and let the app pull it using a managed identity, which is an Azure-issued identity, or using registry credentials. Fourth, give it 0.5 vCPU and 1 GiB of memory. Fifth, enable external ingress with target port 8080. Azure creates revision one and gives you a public address ending in azurecontainerapps.io.

A common mistake is a target port that does not match the port the app listens on. When that happens, Azure cannot reach the app. Its health checks fail, the revision is marked unhealthy, and users get errors even though the image itself is fine.

questions.prompt: Larkfield Clinic has an image called billing-worker:2.3 in its Azure Container Registry. The app inside listens on port 5000. It should be called only by other container apps in the same environment, never from the internet. Here is the provisioning so far. Step A: the Container Apps environment env-clinic already exists in the resource group rg-clinic. Step B: the admin creates a container app called billing-svc in env-clinic. Step C: the admin points it at billing-worker:2.3 and lets it pull the image with a managed identity. Step D: the admin gives it 1 vCPU and 2 GiB of memory. Step E is missing. Which Ingress tab setting should the admin choose so the app is reachable correctly?
choices: Internal ingress with target port 80
External ingress with target port 5000
Turn ingress off and add PORT=5000 as an environment variable
Internal ingress with target port 5000
questions.why: Internal ingress limits traffic to callers inside the environment, and the target port must match the port the app actually listens on, which is 5000.

questions.prompt: In Azure Container Apps, each deployment of a container app creates a revision. What is a revision?
choices: The shared, secure boundary that several apps live inside
A searchable store that collects the app's logs
The version label attached to an image in a registry
An unchangeable snapshot of the app's settings and image
questions.why: A revision is a fixed snapshot of the app's settings and image that is created on each deployment; the other choices describe a tag, an environment and a Log Analytics workspace.

questions.prompt: A logistics company is deploying two container apps, route-planner and driver-portal. It wants them to share one virtual network and to send their logs to the same Log Analytics workspace. What is the simplest way to get this?
choices: Turn on external ingress for both apps
Use the same target port for both apps
Create both apps in the same Container Apps environment
Give both apps the same image tag
questions.why: Apps in the same Container Apps environment share a virtual network and send their logs to that environment's Log Analytics workspace.

questions.prompt: A team deploys a container app from the image quotes:4.1, which listens on port 3000. On the Ingress tab they enable external ingress but set the target port to 80. The image itself has no bugs. What is the most likely result?
choices: Health checks fail, the revision is marked unhealthy, and users get errors
The deployment is blocked and no revision is created
The app works normally because Azure detects port 3000 on its own
The app is reachable only from inside its environment
questions.why: When the target port does not match the port the app listens on, Azure cannot reach the app, so its health checks fail and the revision is marked unhealthy even though the image is fine.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what you have to create and configure to get a container running on Azure Container Apps. Name one limit or tradeoff compared with running the container on a virtual machine you manage yourself.
lessons.modelAnswer: First you need a Container Apps environment. It is the shared boundary for one or more apps, with a common network and a Log Analytics workspace for logs. Inside it you create the container app. You point it at an image in a registry such as Azure Container Registry and give it a way to pull that image, either a managed identity or registry credentials. You also set CPU and memory, plus any environment variables. Then you configure ingress: external if the internet should reach it, internal if only the environment should. The target port has to match the port the app really listens on, or health checks fail. Every deployment creates a revision, which is a fixed snapshot. The tradeoff versus a VM is less control. You can't log into or tune the host operating system, and you work within the service's CPU and memory options. In return you don't patch servers or run a cluster.
rubricPoints: States that a Container Apps environment must exist and holds one or more apps with shared networking and logging.
Says the container app needs an image from a registry and permission to pull it.
Mentions setting CPU, memory and optional environment variables.
Explains external versus internal ingress and that the target port must match the app's listening port.
Notes that each deployment creates a revision.
Names a real tradeoff, such as no access to the host operating system or limited sizing choices, in exchange for not managing servers.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine provisions a container app. The skill being tested is picking the right environment, image, ingress and port settings from a workload description, so an exam-style scenario to reason through teaches it best.

lessons.plain: Sizing and scaling decide how much computing muscle a containerized app gets and how many copies of it run. A container is a packaged app that runs the same way anywhere. Azure Container Instances (ACI) runs containers on demand with a fixed size you choose, like renting one food truck of a set size. Azure Container Apps is a managed container platform that can add or remove identical copies automatically as demand changes, like a restaurant that opens or closes extra serving counters as the queue grows. Sizing sets how big each copy is. Scaling sets how many copies run.
lessons.guessPrompt: Each copy of a web app can comfortably handle 10 requests at the same moment. If 35 requests arrive at once and the platform may run at most 5 copies, how many copies would you expect it to start?
lessons.teach:
Sizing means choosing the CPU (processor cores, counted in vCPUs, virtual CPUs) and memory (in GB) each container gets. Scaling means changing how many copies, called replicas or instances, run at once.

In Azure Container Instances, the unit you deploy is a container group: one or more containers that share a host, network and lifetime. You set CPU and memory per container, and the group's total is the sum. ACI has no built-in autoscaler. To give a container more power you redeploy the group with new values, and its containers restart. To handle more load you run more container groups yourself, for example from a script or another service.

Azure Container Apps sizes each container from a set of allowed CPU and memory pairings, with memory growing in step with CPU. Scaling is automatic and built in. You set a minimum replica count, a maximum replica count, and scale rules. A scale rule is a trigger that says when to add replicas. Common triggers are HTTP concurrency (simultaneous requests per replica), TCP connections, CPU or memory use, and custom event sources such as the length of a message queue. Changing size or scale settings creates a new revision, which is a numbered, unchangeable snapshot of the app's configuration.

Worked example: a Container App has an HTTP rule of 10 concurrent requests per replica, minimum 1, maximum 5. At 35 simultaneous requests, the platform divides 35 by 10 and rounds up to 4 replicas. At 80 requests it wants 8 replicas but stops at the maximum of 5, so each replica carries more load and responses slow. When traffic falls, it removes replicas down to the minimum of 1.

A common mistake is setting the minimum to 0 for a user-facing app. Scaling to zero saves money when idle, but the first request after a quiet period waits for a replica to start, called a cold start. Another mistake is expecting ACI to scale itself; it will not, so a traffic surge simply overloads the fixed group.

questions.prompt: Fernhill Tickets runs a booking API as an Azure Container App. Its HTTP scale rule targets 15 concurrent requests per replica, with a minimum of 1 replica and a maximum of 6. During a flash sale, 100 requests arrive at the same moment. Step 1: the platform divides 100 by 15, giving about 6.67. Step 2: it rounds up, so it wants 7 replicas. Step 3: ??? Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: It runs 7 replicas, because live demand overrides the configured maximum during a surge.
It drops back to the minimum of 1 replica until the surge passes.
It runs 6 replicas, the maximum, so each replica carries more than 15 requests and responses slow down.
It runs 6 replicas and rejects the 10 requests that exceed 6 times 15.
questions.why: The maximum replica count is a hard ceiling, so the app stops at 6 replicas and the extra load is spread across them, which slows responses rather than adding replicas or dropping requests.

questions.prompt: A lab team deploys one Azure Container Instances container group with three containers: a web container with 1 vCPU and 1.5 GB of memory, a worker with 2 vCPUs and 3 GB, and a log shipper with 0.5 vCPU and 1 GB. What total CPU and memory does the container group use?
choices: 1 vCPU and 1.5 GB, the size of the first container
1.17 vCPUs and 1.83 GB, the average of the three
3.5 vCPUs and 5.5 GB
2 vCPUs and 3 GB, the size of the largest container
questions.why: In ACI you set CPU and memory per container and the group's total is the sum: 1 + 2 + 0.5 = 3.5 vCPUs and 1.5 + 3 + 1 = 5.5 GB.

questions.prompt: Brightwell Clinics runs its appointment-reminder service as a single Azure Container Instances container group. A seasonal campaign triples the number of reminders it must send. Nobody changes the deployment. What happens, and what would actually add capacity?
choices: ACI's built-in autoscaler adds container groups automatically, so nothing needs to change.
ACI moves the group to a larger host without restarting it, so it absorbs the load.
The fixed group becomes overloaded; to add capacity you must run more container groups yourself, for example from a script or another service.
ACI creates a new revision with more replicas, keeping the old revision as a fallback.
questions.why: ACI has no built-in autoscaler, so a surge simply overloads the fixed group, and extra capacity comes only from running additional container groups yourself (or redeploying with more CPU and memory, which restarts the containers).

questions.prompt: Quayside Bank hosts a customer-facing balance-checking app in Azure Container Apps with a minimum replica count of 0 and a maximum of 8. Customers report that the first request each morning takes noticeably longer than later ones. What is the most likely cause, and which change addresses it?
choices: The maximum of 8 is too low; raising it to 20 removes the morning delay.
Each morning request creates a new revision, and revisions take time to build; turning off revisions fixes it.
A cold start: after a quiet night the app scaled to zero, so the first request waits for a replica to start; setting the minimum to at least 1 keeps a replica ready.
The app's CPU and memory pairing is too small; any app sized below 2 vCPUs is always slow on its first request.
questions.why: With a minimum of 0 the app scales to zero when idle, so the first request after a quiet period must wait for a replica to start (a cold start), and keeping at least one replica running avoids that wait at some extra cost.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would size and scale a bursty web API on Azure Container Instances versus Azure Container Apps, and name one tradeoff of the settings you would choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: Sizing is how much CPU and memory each container gets; scaling is how many copies run. On Azure Container Instances I set CPU and memory per container in the container group, and the group total is their sum. ACI does not autoscale, so to resize I redeploy with new values, which restarts the containers, and to absorb more load I would have to launch extra groups myself. For a bursty API, Azure Container Apps fits better: I pick a CPU and memory pairing per container, then set minimum and maximum replicas and an HTTP concurrency rule, say 10 requests per replica. The platform adds replicas as concurrency rises, up to the maximum, and removes them as it falls. Size and scale changes produce a new revision. The tradeoff: a minimum of 0 saves cost when idle but causes cold-start delays, and a low maximum caps cost but lets responses slow during a surge.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes sizing (CPU and memory per container) from scaling (number of replicas).
States that ACI sizes per container in a container group and has no built-in autoscaling.
Notes that resizing ACI means redeploying the group, which restarts containers.
Describes Container Apps minimum replicas, maximum replicas and scale rules such as HTTP concurrency or queue length.
Names a tradeoff such as scale-to-zero cold starts or a low maximum limiting capacity under load.

suggested.rationale: Setting minimum and maximum replicas and a concurrency rule, then watching replica counts respond to load, is best learned by doing it in an autoscaling policy lab.

lessons.plain: An App Service plan is the rented set of servers that your web apps run on in Azure's managed web hosting service, called App Service. You do not manage the servers yourself. You choose where they live (the region), which operating system they run (Windows or Linux), how powerful they are and which features they unlock (the pricing tier), and how many copies of the server you want. Think of it like leasing an apartment: the plan is the apartment, and each web app is a roommate. Roommates share the space, and the rent is the same whether one person lives there or five.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you put three small websites into one App Service plan instead of giving each its own plan, do you expect your bill to roughly triple, stay about the same, or drop? Why?
lessons.teach:
An App Service plan is the compute container for Azure App Service, which is Azure's managed platform for hosting web apps and APIs. The plan, not the app, is what you pay for. In ARM templates and Bicep, which are text files that describe Azure resources, the resource type for a plan is Microsoft.Web/serverfarms.

When you provision a plan, you set four things. The region is the Azure datacenter location, and every app in the plan runs there. The operating system is Windows or Linux, and it cannot be changed after the plan is created. The pricing tier, also called the SKU, sets CPU, memory and features. Free and Shared tiers run on servers shared with other customers and have tight limits. Basic gives you dedicated servers. Standard adds features such as autoscale and deployment slots. Premium adds more power and more instances. Isolated runs inside a private, single-tenant environment. The instance count is how many identical workers, meaning server copies, run every app in the plan.

This works because every app in a plan runs on every instance and shares its CPU and memory. Adding an app does not add servers or cost. Adding instances or moving to a bigger tier does.

Here is a worked example. A team needs a Linux API with a staging slot in West Europe. Step one: create or pick a resource group, which is the folder that holds related resources. Step two: in the portal, choose Create an App Service plan, or in Bicep declare a Microsoft.Web/serverfarms resource. Step three: set the location to westeurope. Step four: choose Linux. In Bicep you do this with kind 'linux' and the property reserved: true. Step five: choose sku S1, because slots need Standard or higher. Step six: start with one instance.

A common mistake is crowding a busy app into a plan with other apps. It competes with them for the same CPU and memory, so one noisy app can slow or crash its neighbours. Another mistake is picking the Free tier and later finding that features you need are missing. The plan's tier and OS set what every app in it can do.

questions.prompt: A charity, Harbour Aid, needs a Windows web app for donations in East US. During fundraising events traffic spikes, so the app must scale out automatically, and it should normally run on two instances. Their admin is provisioning the App Service plan. Step 1: use the existing resource group rg-donations, the folder that holds related resources. Step 2: declare a Microsoft.Web/serverfarms resource in Bicep, the resource type for an App Service plan. Step 3: set the location to eastus. Step 4: choose Windows as the operating system. Step 5: ??? Step 6: set the instance count to 2. Which choice correctly completes Step 5?
choices: Choose a Standard tier SKU such as S1, because autoscale needs Standard or higher
Choose a Shared tier SKU, because shared servers grow automatically with traffic
Choose a Basic tier SKU, because dedicated servers are all that autoscale needs
Choose a Free tier SKU, because the app is small and autoscale can be added to it later
questions.why: Autoscale is a feature that arrives with the Standard tier, so the plan must be Standard or higher; Free, Shared and Basic lack it.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm, Northline, runs three web apps for its depots in a single App Service plan. Their finance team asks which resource actually determines the hosting bill, and what its resource type is in a Bicep file (a text file that describes Azure resources). What is the correct answer?
choices: Each web app is billed separately, declared as Microsoft.Web/sites
The App Service plan is billed, declared as Microsoft.Web/serverfarms
The resource group is billed, declared as Microsoft.Web/serverfarms
The App Service plan is billed, declared as Microsoft.Compute/plans
questions.why: The plan is the compute container you pay for, and its ARM/Bicep resource type is Microsoft.Web/serverfarms.

questions.prompt: A bakery chain, Crumb & Co, has a Standard tier App Service plan in UK South running 2 instances and hosting one ordering app. They deploy a second, lightly used loyalty app into the same plan. What happens?
choices: The loyalty app runs on only one of the two instances to save resources
The loyalty app runs on both instances, sharing their CPU and memory, with no added cost
A third instance is added automatically for the new app, raising cost
The loyalty app gets its own separate CPU and memory reserved for it
questions.why: Every app in a plan runs on every instance and shares its resources, so adding an app adds neither servers nor cost.

questions.prompt: A clinic network, Medway Health, created a Windows App Service plan in North Europe last month. Their developers now want to host a Linux-only container app on that same plan. What should the administrator do?
choices: Create a new App Service plan with Linux as its operating system
Move the existing plan to a Premium tier, which allows mixed operating systems
Add more instances to the existing plan so one can run Linux
Edit the existing plan and switch its operating system to Linux
questions.why: A plan's operating system is fixed when it is created and cannot be changed, so a Linux app needs a new Linux plan.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what an App Service plan is and what you must decide when provisioning one. Include one tradeoff of putting several apps in the same plan.
lessons.modelAnswer: An App Service plan is the pool of managed servers that App Service apps run on. It is the thing we are billed for, not the individual apps. When we create one, we pick the region, the operating system, the pricing tier and the instance count. The OS is Windows or Linux and is permanent. The tier sets CPU, memory and which features are available; for example, deployment slots and autoscale need Standard or above. The instance count is how many workers run every app. In Bicep, a plan is a Microsoft.Web/serverfarms resource, and Linux is set with kind 'linux' and reserved: true. Putting several apps in one plan is cheaper because they share the same servers. The tradeoff is that they also share CPU and memory, so one heavy app can starve the others. All of them also scale together and are limited by the same tier and OS.
rubricPoints: Defines the plan as the shared compute that hosts App Service apps and is the unit of billing.
Names the region, operating system, pricing tier and instance count as the provisioning choices.
Notes that the OS is fixed at creation and the tier controls features such as slots and autoscale.
States that apps in one plan share resources, which saves cost but risks noisy-neighbour contention.

suggested.rationale: The skill tested is reasoning from a workload's needs to the right region, OS, tier and plan sharing choice, which a scenario to work through practises best.

lessons.plain: An App Service plan is the set of rented servers that your web apps run on in Azure, a managed web-hosting service. Scaling the plan means changing how much computing power those apps get. You can make each server bigger, which is called scaling up, or add more copies of the server, which is called scaling out. Think of a restaurant kitchen: scaling up is buying a bigger stove, and scaling out is hiring more cooks who all follow the same recipes. Azure can add and remove cooks for you automatically, based on rules you write about how busy the kitchen is.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your website slows down every weekday at 9 a.m. when hundreds of staff log in, then sits nearly idle overnight. Would you rather buy one much bigger server permanently, or have extra identical servers added only during the busy hours? Why?
lessons.teach:
An App Service plan is the pool of virtual machines (rented servers) that hosts one or more App Service web apps. Every app in the plan runs on every instance, meaning every server copy, so scaling the plan affects all of its apps together.

Scale up (vertical scaling) means moving the plan to a different pricing tier, such as Basic, Standard or Premium. A higher tier gives each instance more CPU and memory and unlocks features. Scale out (horizontal scaling) means changing the instance count. The tier sets the limits. Free and Shared tiers cannot scale out. Basic allows only manual scale-out to a few instances. Standard and above allow autoscale, which means Azure changes the instance count for you based on rules.

An autoscale setting has a minimum, maximum and default instance count. It also has rules. A metric rule watches a measurement such as average CPU percentage over a time window. A schedule rule sets counts for set times. Each rule has a cooldown, a waiting period after a scaling action before the next one can happen. This works because load is spread across identical instances by a built-in load balancer, so extra copies share the traffic.

Worked example: min 2, max 5, default 2. The scale-out rule is CPU above 70% averaged over 10 minutes, add 1 instance, cooldown 5 minutes. The scale-in rule is CPU below 30% over 10 minutes, remove 1. At 9:00 the CPU averages 85%, so the count goes from 2 to 3. At 9:05, after the cooldown, the CPU is still 75%, so it goes to 4. By noon the CPU averages 25%, so it steps back down. It never drops below 2 or rises above 5.

A common mistake is writing a scale-out rule with no matching scale-in rule. Another is setting thresholds too close together, such as 60% out and 55% in. The first keeps you paying for idle instances indefinitely. The second causes flapping, where instances are added and removed over and over. Remember that scale-up briefly restarts the apps, while scale-out does not.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking company runs its web apps on an App Service plan in the Standard tier. Autoscale is set to minimum 3, maximum 8, default 3. The scale-out rule is: average memory above 80% over 15 minutes, add 2 instances, cooldown 10 minutes. The scale-in rule is: average memory below 35% over 15 minutes, remove 1 instance. Trace a busy afternoon. Step 1: at 14:00 memory averages 90%, so the count goes from 3 to 5. Step 2: at 14:04 memory is 88%, but the 10-minute cooldown has not finished, so the count stays at 5. Step 3: at 14:10 the cooldown has ended and memory is still 86%, so the count goes from 5 to 7. Step 4: at 14:20 the cooldown has ended again and memory is still 84%. What is the instance count after Step 4, and why?
choices: 8, because the rule tries to add 2 but the count cannot rise above the maximum of 8
3, because the count resets to the default once the maximum is approached
9, because the rule adds 2 instances each time the threshold is crossed after a cooldown
7, because a second cooldown must pass before any further scale-out is allowed
