questions.why: The scale-out rule asks for 2 more instances, but autoscale never goes above the configured maximum, so 7 plus 2 is capped at 8.

questions.prompt: A small charity hosts its donation site on an App Service plan (the pool of rented servers that runs its web apps) in the Basic tier. They want Azure to add instances automatically whenever average CPU gets high. What must they do first?
choices: Scale the plan up to the Standard tier or higher, then configure autoscale rules
Add a CPU-based metric rule to the plan while it stays in the Basic tier
Manually set the instance count to the Basic maximum so autoscale is switched on
Move the plan to the Shared tier, which is designed for automatic scaling
questions.why: Autoscale is only available in Standard and higher tiers, so the plan must be scaled up to a supporting tier before autoscale rules can be added.

questions.prompt: An engineer configures autoscale on a Premium-tier App Service plan with a scale-out rule at average CPU above 50% and a scale-in rule at average CPU below 47%. Over the next day, monitoring shows instances being added and removed again and again. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The plan's tier is too low to support metric rules, so autoscale behaves randomly
There is no scale-in rule, so instances pile up until the maximum is reached
The cooldown is too long, which forces repeated scaling actions
The scale-out and scale-in thresholds are too close together, causing flapping
questions.why: With only a 3-point gap between the thresholds, small changes in CPU keep triggering opposite actions, which is called flapping.

questions.prompt: A news site's App Service plan is in the Standard tier with 2 instances, and a sudden traffic spike arrives during business hours. The team needs more capacity right now without even a brief restart of the apps. Which action fits?
choices: Scale up by moving the plan to the Basic tier to free up resources
Create a second plan in the Free tier and move half the apps into it
Scale up by moving the plan from Standard to Premium
Scale out by raising the instance count, for example from 2 to 4
questions.why: Scale-out adds identical instances behind the built-in load balancer without restarting the apps, whereas scale-up (changing tier) briefly restarts them.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between scaling up and scaling out an App Service plan, how an autoscale rule decides when to add instances, and one limit or tradeoff they should watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: An App Service plan is the group of servers our web apps run on, and every app in the plan runs on every instance. Scaling up means changing the pricing tier so each instance gets more CPU and memory. That briefly restarts the apps and is limited by the biggest tier. Scaling out means adding more identical instances behind a load balancer. With Standard tier or higher, autoscale does this for us. We set a minimum, maximum and default count, then rules like 'if average CPU is above 70% for 10 minutes, add one instance', with a cooldown so it waits before acting again. We need a matching scale-in rule, or we pay for idle instances forever. The two thresholds also need a wide gap between them, or the count flaps up and down. One more tradeoff: scaling the plan scales every app in it, including quiet ones.
rubricPoints: Scale up changes the pricing tier to give each instance more power; scale out changes the number of instances.
Autoscale needs Standard tier or higher; Free and Shared cannot scale out, and Basic is manual only.
An autoscale setting has minimum, maximum and default counts plus metric or schedule rules.
A cooldown stops repeated scaling actions from firing too quickly.
Every scale-out rule needs a scale-in rule, and the two thresholds need a wide gap to avoid flapping.
Scaling the plan affects all apps hosted in it.

suggested.rationale: Tuning thresholds, cooldowns and min/max counts against a simulated load curve builds the rule-writing judgment this objective tests.

lessons.plain: An App Service is Azure's managed home for web applications and APIs. You hand it your code (or a container image) and Azure runs it on servers it looks after, handling the operating system, patching and the web server software for you. Think of renting a furnished apartment instead of building a house: you bring your belongings (the app), the landlord maintains the building. Each app you create is called a web app, and it lives inside an App Service plan, which is the actual pool of computing power you pay for. Creating an App Service means filling in a short form that tells Azure what your app needs.
lessons.guessPrompt: If Azure gives every new web app a public address ending in azurewebsites.net, what do you think has to be true about the name you pick for your app, and why?
lessons.teach:
Azure App Service is a platform-as-a-service (PaaS) offering, meaning Azure manages the servers, operating system and web server while you manage only your application. A web app is one application hosted in App Service. Every web app must run inside an App Service plan, which defines the region, operating system (Windows or Linux), size of the underlying machines and therefore the price. Billing is on the plan, not on each app, so several apps can share one plan and its compute.

To create a web app in the portal you supply: a subscription and resource group (a resource group is a folder that holds related Azure resources); a name, which becomes the default address name.azurewebsites.net and so must be unique across all of Azure; a publish model, either Code or Container (a packaged image of the app and its dependencies); a runtime stack, the language and version such as .NET 8, Node 20 or Python 3.12; the operating system; the region; and an existing or new plan. In a template, the same thing is a resource of type Microsoft.Web/sites whose serverFarmId property points at the plan.

Worked example: a team needs a Python API. Step 1, choose resource group rg-api. Step 2, name it contoso-orders-api; the portal confirms it is free. Step 3, publish model Code, runtime Python 3.12, which only runs on Linux, so OS is Linux. Step 4, region East US. Step 5, pick plan asp-linux-eastus. Step 6, review and create. The app is reachable at contoso-orders-api.azurewebsites.net.

A common mistake is trying to place a web app on a plan in a different region or with a different operating system. The plan list simply will not offer it, because an app runs on its plan's machines. The consequence in a running system: apps sharing a plan share its CPU and memory, so one busy app can slow the others.

questions.prompt: Northwind Bakery wants to host its online ordering site, written in Node 20, in App Service. Its administrator works through the portal like this. Resource group: rg-bakery-web. Name: northwind-orders, which the portal confirms is free, so the site will be at northwind-orders.azurewebsites.net. Publish model: Code. Runtime stack: Node 20. Operating system: Linux. Region: West Europe. Next the administrator must pick an App Service plan. An App Service plan is the set of machines an app runs on, and it fixes the region, operating system, size and price. The subscription has three existing plans: asp-win-westeurope (Windows, West Europe), asp-linux-centralus (Linux, Central US) and asp-linux-westeurope (Linux, West Europe). After the plan is chosen, the administrator reviews and creates the app. Which choice completes the plan step correctly?
choices: Pick asp-linux-centralus, because the operating system matches and the app can still be served from West Europe.
Skip the existing plans and create a new one, because each web app is billed on its own and needs a plan of its own.
Pick asp-win-westeurope, because the region matches and the app's operating system is set separately from the plan.
Pick asp-linux-westeurope, because the plan must match both the app's region and its operating system.
questions.why: A web app runs on its plan's machines, so the plan must be in the same region and have the same operating system as the app, and only asp-linux-westeurope meets both conditions.

questions.prompt: An administrator at Adatum is writing a template instead of using the portal. The template defines a web app, which is a resource of type Microsoft.Web/sites. Which property tells Azure which App Service plan the web app runs on?
choices: runtimeStack
resourceGroup
publishModel
serverFarmId
questions.why: In a template, the web app's serverFarmId property points at the App Service plan, which is the set of machines the app will run on.

questions.prompt: An administrator at Litware tries to create a web app named tailwind-booking. The portal reports that the name is already in use. The name belongs to a different company, in a subscription Litware has no access to. What does this mean?
choices: Litware can reuse the name by choosing a different region for its app.
Litware must choose another name, because the name becomes name.azurewebsites.net and has to be unique across all of Azure.
Litware can reuse the name as long as its app runs on a different operating system.
Litware can reuse the name by putting its app in a different resource group.
questions.why: The web app name forms the default address name.azurewebsites.net, so it must be unique across all of Azure, regardless of subscription, resource group, region or operating system.

questions.prompt: A retailer runs four web apps on a single App Service plan. During a sale, the checkout app gets very busy. The other three apps on the same plan become slow, even though their own traffic has not changed. What is the most likely cause?
choices: All four apps share the plan's CPU and memory, so the busy app is using compute the others need.
Each app has its own separate machines, so the slowdown must come from the apps' own code.
Azure throttles every app in a resource group whenever one app in that group is busy.
The other apps are slow because they use a different runtime stack from the checkout app.
questions.why: Apps on the same App Service plan run on that plan's machines and share its CPU and memory, so one busy app can slow down the others.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what you must decide when creating an Azure web app, and name one tradeoff of putting several web apps on the same App Service plan.
lessons.modelAnswer: App Service is Azure's managed hosting for web apps and APIs: Azure looks after the servers and OS, we just bring code or a container. When creating a web app we pick a resource group, a globally unique name that becomes name.azurewebsites.net, whether we publish code or a container, the runtime stack and version, the operating system, the region, and the App Service plan it runs on. The plan is the real compute and the thing we pay for, and the app must match the plan's region and OS; some runtimes like Python need Linux. The tradeoff of sharing a plan is cost versus isolation: several apps on one plan cost no extra, but they compete for the same CPU and memory, so a busy or misbehaving app can slow the others, and they all scale together.
rubricPoints: States that App Service is managed PaaS hosting where Azure runs the servers and OS.
Lists the key creation choices: name, publish model, runtime stack, OS, region, plan.
Notes the name must be globally unique because it forms the azurewebsites.net address.
Explains the web app runs on and is billed through an App Service plan whose region and OS must match.
Names the shared-plan tradeoff: lower cost but apps compete for the same compute.

suggested.rationale: Creating a web app is mostly a set of portal and template choices to know, and no current mission or planned engine has the learner provision App Service.

lessons.plain: When people visit a website, the address bar padlock means the connection is encrypted and the site has proven its identity. That proof is a certificate, a digital ID card for a web address issued by a trusted authority. Transport Layer Security (TLS) is the set of rules that uses that ID card to set up an encrypted connection. Azure App Service is a managed service that hosts web apps for you. Configuring TLS there means giving your app the right ID card for its custom name, attaching it, and refusing unsafe, unencrypted visitors. It works like a hotel desk that checks your passport before handing over a key.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web app answers at shop.contoso.com, but browsers show a 'not secure' warning. What two things do you think the app needs: something that proves who it is, and what else?
lessons.teach:
Configuring TLS for an App Service means getting a certificate for your custom domain, binding it to that domain, and setting the app's security options. A certificate is a file that ties a domain name to a public key and is signed by a trusted certificate authority. The matching private key is the secret half that only the server holds; without it the certificate cannot be used to encrypt traffic. A binding is the link that tells App Service which certificate to present for which hostname.

App Service offers four sources for a certificate. A free App Service managed certificate is created and renewed for you, but it cannot cover wildcard names like *.contoso.com and cannot be exported. You can import one stored in Azure Key Vault, a managed secret store. You can upload your own as a PFX file, a password-protected file that contains both the certificate and its private key. Or you can buy an App Service certificate through Azure. Custom-domain TLS requires the Basic pricing tier or higher, and the custom domain must already be mapped to the app.

When you add the binding, choose SNI SSL in most cases. Server Name Indication (SNI) lets the client name the site it wants, so many certificates can share one IP address. IP-based SSL gives the domain its own dedicated address instead.

Worked example for shop.contoso.com: first, confirm the plan is Basic or above. Second, confirm the custom domain is mapped. Third, create a managed certificate for that domain. Fourth, add a TLS/SSL binding of type SNI SSL. Fifth, turn on HTTPS Only, which redirects plain HTTP to HTTPS. Sixth, set the minimum TLS version to 1.2 so older, weaker versions are refused. Optionally, you can require client certificates, known as mutual TLS, where callers must also present their own certificate.

A common mistake is uploading a .cer file. That file holds only the public certificate and no private key, so App Service rejects it. Another is skipping HTTPS Only. Visitors can then still reach the app over unencrypted HTTP, and their logins travel in clear text.

questions.prompt: Northwind Health runs a patient portal on an App Service plan in the Standard tier. They want TLS for every subdomain under the wildcard name *.northwindhealth.net. Their own certificate authority has issued a wildcard certificate, which the admin received as a password-protected PFX file. Step 1: The admin confirms Standard is at or above Basic, so custom-domain TLS is allowed. Step 2: The admin confirms portal.northwindhealth.net is already mapped to the app. Step 3: ??? Step 4: The admin adds a TLS/SSL binding of type SNI SSL for portal.northwindhealth.net. Step 5: The admin turns on HTTPS Only and sets the minimum TLS version to 1.2. What is the correct Step 3?
choices: Export the public part to a .cer file and upload that, keeping the private key off the server
Switch the binding plan to IP-based SSL first, because wildcard certificates cannot share an IP address
Create a free App Service managed certificate for *.northwindhealth.net, so that it renews automatically
Upload the PFX file to the app and enter its password, so App Service gets the certificate and private key
questions.why: A managed certificate cannot cover wildcard names and a .cer file has no private key, so uploading the PFX, which holds both the certificate and its private key, is the step that works.

questions.prompt: An App Service hosts three customer sites. Each site has its own certificate, and all three share a single IP address. Which binding type makes this possible, and why?
choices: Mutual TLS, because each client sends its own certificate, which tells the server which site to serve
HTTPS Only, because the redirect to HTTPS carries the hostname that selects the correct certificate
SNI SSL, because the client names the site it wants, so the server can pick the matching certificate
IP-based SSL, because each certificate is tied to the shared address and the server rotates between them
questions.why: Server Name Indication lets the client state the hostname it is asking for, so many certificates can share one IP address.

questions.prompt: A developer at Tailwind Traders mapped the custom domain orders.tailwindtraders.io to an app running on the Free (F1) App Service plan. When she tries to add a TLS binding for that domain, she cannot complete it. What is the most likely fix?
choices: Turn on client certificates so mutual TLS is enabled first
Scale the App Service plan up to the Basic tier or higher
Set the minimum TLS version to 1.0 so the binding is accepted
Upload the certificate as a .cer file instead of a PFX file
questions.why: Custom-domain TLS requires the Basic pricing tier or higher, so a Free-tier app must be scaled up before the binding can be added.

questions.prompt: An auditor at Contoso Pharma finds that the internal app at hr.contosopharma.com has a valid certificate and an SNI SSL binding. However, staff who type http://hr.contosopharma.com still load the login page over plain HTTP. What setting is missing, and what is the risk?
choices: Minimum TLS version 1.2 is missing, and older TLS versions let attackers read the HTTP page
HTTPS Only is off, so plain HTTP is not redirected and logins can travel in clear text
Client certificates are not required, so any caller can reach the app over unencrypted HTTP
IP-based SSL is not used, so the shared address falls back to HTTP for some visitors
questions.why: HTTPS Only is the setting that redirects plain HTTP to HTTPS, and without it users can still send their logins unencrypted.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would secure a custom-domain App Service with TLS, which certificate source you would pick and why, and one limit or tradeoff of that choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I make sure the App Service plan is Basic or higher and that the custom domain is already mapped, because TLS binds to that name. Then I get a certificate, which is a signed file linking the domain to a key pair. For a single name like shop.contoso.com, I'd use the free App Service managed certificate, since Azure issues and renews it for me. The tradeoffs are that it can't do wildcards and can't be exported. If we needed *.contoso.com, I'd import a certificate from Key Vault or upload a PFX that includes the private key. Next I add an SNI SSL binding so the app presents the right certificate on a shared IP. Finally I turn on HTTPS Only and set the minimum TLS version to 1.2, so nobody connects unencrypted or with a weak protocol.
rubricPoints: States that the custom domain must be mapped and the plan must be Basic tier or higher.
Names a certificate source and gives a matching limit, such as managed certificates having no wildcard and no export.
Explains that an uploaded certificate must include the private key, as in a PFX file.
Describes adding a binding, normally SNI SSL, that links the certificate to the hostname.
Mentions enforcing HTTPS Only and a minimum TLS version of 1.2.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine configures App Service TLS, so the most useful practice is reasoning through exam-style scenarios, such as picking a certificate source for a wildcard domain or diagnosing a rejected upload.

lessons.plain: Every Azure App Service web app gets a free address that ends in azurewebsites.net. A custom DNS name is your own address, such as www.contoso.com, pointing at that same app. Mapping it takes two halves. At your domain provider you create DNS records, the internet's phone-book entries, that send visitors to the app and prove you own the name. In App Service you tell the app to accept that name. It is like having mail forwarded: the post office redirects letters, but the new building must also agree to accept them.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you own contoso.com and want www.contoso.com to open your Azure web app, what two things do you think must happen: one at your domain provider and one inside Azure?
lessons.teach:
Mapping a custom DNS name means making a domain you already own, such as www.contoso.com, serve an App Service app. App Service is Azure's managed web hosting. Every app gets a default hostname like contoso-web.azurewebsites.net. DNS (Domain Name System) is the internet's directory that turns names into destinations, and your registrar or DNS host is wherever those records live.

Two record types can point the name at the app. A CNAME record is an alias from one name to another name. Use it for a subdomain, for example www pointing to contoso-web.azurewebsites.net. An A record maps a name straight to an IP address. Use it for the apex, also called the root domain (contoso.com with nothing in front), because DNS rules forbid a CNAME there. The A record targets the app's inbound IP address, shown on the app's Custom domains page.

Azure also needs proof of ownership. You add a TXT record (a free-text DNS entry) named asuid.<subdomain> whose value is the app's Custom Domain Verification ID. Without it, Azure will not bind the name, which stops anyone from claiming a domain they do not control.

Worked example. First, confirm the App Service plan is Shared tier or higher, because the Free tier cannot use custom domains. Second, open the app's Custom domains page, choose Add custom domain, and copy the verification ID. Third, at the DNS host create a CNAME from www to contoso-web.azurewebsites.net and a TXT record asuid.www holding the ID. Fourth, back in Azure, run validation. When both checks pass, add the domain. Browsers can now reach www.contoso.com, although HTTPS needs a separate certificate binding.

A common mistake is creating the DNS records but never adding the hostname in App Service. Visitors reach Azure's front end, and Azure has no app registered for that name, so they see an error page instead of your site. DNS changes can also take time to spread, so an early validation failure may succeed later.

questions.prompt: Northwind Traders hosts its website on an App Service app named nw-store, whose default hostname is nw-store.azurewebsites.net. The App Service plan is on the Basic tier. They want visitors who type northwind-traders.org (the apex, with nothing in front) to reach the app. Worked so far: Step 1, they confirmed Basic is above the Free tier, so custom domains are allowed. Step 2, on the app's Custom domains page they chose Add custom domain, copied the Custom Domain Verification ID and noted the app's inbound IP address, 20.51.7.88. Step 3 (missing): at the DNS host, create the record that points northwind-traders.org at the app. Step 4, add the TXT verification record holding the ID. Step 5, run validation in Azure and, when both checks pass, add the domain. What belongs in Step 3?
choices: Create an A record from northwind-traders.org to 20.51.7.88
Skip a pointing record, because the TXT verification record also routes traffic
Create a CNAME record from northwind-traders.org to nw-store.azurewebsites.net
Create an A record from northwind-traders.org to nw-store.azurewebsites.net
questions.why: The apex cannot hold a CNAME, so it needs an A record, and an A record must target an IP address, which here is the app's inbound IP 20.51.7.88.

questions.prompt: Tailspin Toys wants blog.tailspintoys.com to serve their App Service app tt-blog.azurewebsites.net. They have created a CNAME from blog to tt-blog.azurewebsites.net. Which name should the TXT record that proves domain ownership use?
choices: blog
verify.tt-blog
asuid.blog
asuid.azurewebsites.net
questions.why: The ownership TXT record is named asuid followed by the subdomain being mapped, so for blog it is asuid.blog, and its value is the app's Custom Domain Verification ID.

questions.prompt: An administrator at Woodgrove Clinic created a CNAME from portal.woodgroveclinic.com to wg-portal.azurewebsites.net and the matching asuid.portal TXT record. Days later, visitors to portal.woodgroveclinic.com still see an Azure error page instead of the clinic's site. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The CNAME should have been an A record because portal is a subdomain
DNS changes always take at least a week to spread
The TXT record value must be the app's inbound IP address
The hostname was never added on the app's Custom domains page
questions.why: Traffic reaches Azure's front end, but if the hostname was never added in App Service, Azure has no app registered for that name and returns an error page.

questions.prompt: Fourth Coffee's App Service app runs on a Free tier plan. When an engineer tries to map menu.fourthcoffee.com to it, Azure will not allow the custom domain. What change fixes this?
choices: Bind an HTTPS certificate to the app before adding the domain
Rename the app so its default hostname matches the custom domain
Move the app to a plan on the Shared tier or higher
Replace the CNAME with an A record pointing to the app's inbound IP
questions.why: The Free tier cannot use custom domains, so the plan must be Shared tier or higher before any custom name can be bound.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would map both contoso.com and www.contoso.com to an existing App Service app, including which DNS record each name needs and one limit or tradeoff to watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: Mapping a custom name takes work in two places: DNS records at the domain host, and the hostname added to the app. For www.contoso.com I'd create a CNAME alias pointing at the app's azurewebsites.net name. For the apex, contoso.com, a CNAME isn't allowed, so I'd create an A record pointing at the app's inbound IP. For each name I'd also add a TXT record, asuid or asuid.www, containing the app's Custom Domain Verification ID, because Azure uses it to confirm we own the domain. Then I'd validate and add each domain on the app's Custom domains page. Limits: the plan must be Shared tier or above, since Free can't host custom domains. An A record is tied to an IP rather than a name, so it is more fragile than a CNAME. DNS propagation can delay validation. TLS is a separate step.
rubricPoints: States that DNS records at the provider and adding the hostname in App Service are both required.
Uses a CNAME to the azurewebsites.net name for a subdomain.
Uses an A record to the app's inbound IP for the apex, because a CNAME is not allowed there.
Mentions the asuid TXT record with the verification ID as proof of ownership.
Notes a limit, such as the Free tier not supporting custom domains, DNS propagation delay, or A-record IP fragility.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine covers DNS mapping, so working through exam-style cases, such as choosing between a CNAME and an A record or diagnosing a failed validation, builds the most useful skill.

lessons.plain: Backing up an App Service means taking a saved copy of a hosted web app at a point in time so you can bring it back after a bad change, accidental deletion, or corruption. App Service is Azure's managed web hosting: you hand it your code, and it runs the servers for you. A backup captures the app's files, its configuration, and optionally a connected database. Think of it like a save point in a video game. If things go wrong, you reload the last good save instead of starting from zero. You decide how often saves happen and how long they are kept.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you schedule a web app backup once a day and keep each copy for 7 days, roughly how many backups exist at any moment, and what happens to the oldest one?
lessons.teach:
An App Service backup is a point-in-time copy of a web app. It contains the app's content (the files under its site folder), its configuration (app settings and connection strings), and, if you choose, a database the app connects to. A restore is the reverse: you write a backup back onto the same app, onto a different app, or onto a deployment slot.

There are two kinds. Automatic backups are taken by Azure on its own schedule (about hourly), kept for a fixed period, and stored by Azure, so there is nothing to set up. They do not include databases. Custom backups are the ones you configure. You supply a storage account, which is Azure's general-purpose file and blob storage, and a container, which is a folder-like bucket inside it. You also set a schedule, such as every 1 day, and a retention period in days, after which old copies are deleted. You can tick an option to include a linked database. Backup only works on paid dedicated tiers of the App Service plan, which is the set of servers your app runs on. Free and Shared tiers cannot be backed up, and exam scenarios often expect you to scale up to Standard or higher first.

In the portal, open the app, choose Backups, then configure custom backups. Pick the storage account and container, set the frequency and retention, decide whether to keep at least one backup forever, and optionally include the database.

Worked example: you set a daily schedule with 30-day retention and include the app's SQL database. On day 1 the first backup is written to the container. Each day another is added. On day 31 the day-1 copy expires and is removed. On day 40, someone deploys broken code. You open Backups, pick the day-39 copy, and restore it to a staging slot to check it before swapping it live.

A common mistake is assuming the database is captured automatically. It is not, unless you include it. A second mistake is a storage firewall that blocks App Service from writing. The consequence is that backups silently fail or restores bring back code but not data, so test a restore before you need one.

questions.prompt: A city library runs its catalogue web app on a Standard-tier App Service plan. An administrator configures a custom backup with a schedule of every 1 day and a retention period of 10 days. Trace what happens. Step 1: On day 1, the first backup copy is written to the chosen storage container. Step 2: One more copy is added each day, so by the end of day 10 the container holds ten copies, from day 1 through day 10. Step 3: On day 11, a new copy is written and ______. Step 4: On day 15 a faulty release goes out, and the administrator can choose any copy from day 6 through day 14 to restore to a deployment slot for checking. Which completion belongs in Step 3?
choices: nothing is removed, because retention only starts counting after the most recent backup
the day-11 copy overwrites the day-10 copy, so the count stays at ten
the day-1 copy has passed its 10-day retention and is removed, leaving copies from day 2 through day 11
all ten older copies are deleted so the schedule starts a fresh 10-day cycle
questions.why: Retention deletes each copy once it is older than the retention period, so on day 11 only the oldest (day-1) copy expires while the rest remain.

questions.prompt: A small travel agency has not configured anything and relies only on the App Service automatic backups for its booking app, which stores reservations in a linked database. A manager asks what those automatic backups would let them recover. What is the accurate answer?
choices: Everything, including the reservation database, because Azure captures linked databases on its hourly schedule
Only the database, because app files are expected to come from source control
The app's files and its configuration, but not the reservation database
Nothing until a storage account and container are supplied
questions.why: Automatic backups are taken and stored by Azure with no setup and cover app content and configuration, but they never include databases.

questions.prompt: A charity's donation web app runs on an App Service plan in the Shared tier. The administrator wants daily custom backups kept for 21 days. What must happen before the custom backup can be configured?
choices: Turn on the option to keep at least one backup forever
Shorten the retention period to 7 days, the most the Shared tier allows
Scale the App Service plan up to a paid dedicated tier such as Standard or higher
Create a second deployment slot to hold the backups
questions.why: Free and Shared tiers cannot be backed up at all, so the plan must first move to a paid dedicated tier like Standard.

questions.prompt: An engineering firm configured custom backups for its project-tracking app every 1 day, pointing at a storage account container. Two weeks later, while testing a restore, an administrator finds the container has no backup copies at all. The storage account had recently been locked down with a firewall. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The retention period deleted every copy as soon as it was written
The storage firewall is blocking App Service from writing to the container, so the backups are failing silently
Custom backups are stored by Azure, so the container is expected to stay empty
The linked database option was not ticked, which stops the files being written
questions.why: A storage firewall that blocks App Service prevents backups being written, and they can fail without obvious warning, which is why testing a restore early matters.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would set up backups for our production web app and how we would recover from a bad deploy. Name one limit or tradeoff of the approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: App Service gives us two backup options. Automatic backups happen on their own roughly every hour, but they skip databases and we don't control retention. For production I'd set up custom backups. Under the app's Backups page, we point it at a storage account and container we own. We set a schedule, say daily, and a retention period, say 30 days, after which old copies are deleted. We also tick the option to include the linked database, because it isn't captured by default. Our plan has to be on a paid dedicated tier. Free and Shared can't do this, so we may need to scale up. If a deploy breaks things, we restore a recent backup, ideally to a staging slot first to verify it. One tradeoff: a daily schedule means we could lose up to a day of changes, and extra copies cost storage. We should also test a restore regularly.
rubricPoints: Defines a backup as a point-in-time copy of app files, configuration, and optionally a database.
Distinguishes automatic backups from custom backups that need your own storage account and container.
Mentions setting a schedule and a retention period, and that the database must be explicitly included.
Notes that Free and Shared tiers cannot be backed up, so a paid dedicated tier is required.
Describes restoring to the same app, another app, or a slot.
Names a tradeoff, such as data lost between backups, storage cost, or the need to test restores.

suggested.rationale: Choosing backup frequency, retention, and a restore target is a recovery-planning decision that a disaster-recovery planner would let the learner practise directly.

lessons.plain: An App Service is a managed web hosting service: you give it your web app and it runs it, without you looking after servers. By default it sits on the public internet, reachable by anyone and only able to reach public addresses. Networking settings change that in two separate directions. Inbound settings control who can reach your app. Outbound settings control what private things your app can reach, such as a database inside your own private network. Think of a shop: one rule decides who may walk in the front door, and a different arrangement gives staff a back corridor to the warehouse.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you connect a web app to your private network so the app can reach a database there, do you think strangers on the internet can still open the app's public web address? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
App Service networking splits into inbound features, which control traffic arriving at the app, and outbound features, which control calls the app makes. Each feature works in one direction only.

Inbound. Access restrictions are an ordered list of allow or deny rules matched against the caller's IP range, a service tag (a named group of Azure addresses), or a subnet reached through a service endpoint. Rules run from lowest priority number up, and once you add any allow rule, everything not matched is denied. The SCM site (the Kudu management and deployment address) has its own separate rule list. A private endpoint gives the app a private IP address inside your virtual network (an isolated private network in Azure), so internal clients reach it privately; you can then turn off public network access.

Outbound. Virtual network integration routes the app's outgoing calls into a dedicated subnet (a slice of a virtual network) that must be delegated, meaning reserved, for App Service. It is set per App Service plan, needs Basic tier or higher, and lets the app reach private IPs. Hybrid Connections reach one specific host and port, often on-premises, through a relay, with no network change.

Worked example: an app must call a SQL VM at 10.1.2.4 and be reachable only from the office range 203.0.113.0/24. Step one, create an empty subnet and delegate it to App Service. Step two, enable virtual network integration on the app using that subnet; outbound calls to 10.1.2.4 now travel privately. Step three, add an access restriction allowing 203.0.113.0/24 at priority 100; all other callers get HTTP 403. Step four, decide whether the SCM site should copy these rules or keep its own.

Common mistake: assuming virtual network integration makes the app private. It is outbound only, so the public address stays open until you add access restrictions or a private endpoint. In a running system that leaves an internal app exposed to the internet.

questions.prompt: A clinic's booking app runs on App Service. It must be reachable only by staff inside the clinic's virtual network, with nothing reachable from the internet. It must also call a database VM at 10.40.6.9 in that network. The admin works through it. Step one: create a private endpoint for the app in a subnet called pe-subnet, so the app gets the private address 10.40.2.15 and staff reach it there. Step two: (missing). Step three: create a separate empty subnet and delegate it to App Service. Step four: turn on virtual network integration with that delegated subnet, so outbound calls to 10.40.6.9 travel privately. Which action belongs in step two?
choices: Turn on virtual network integration a second time, this time on pe-subnet, so the app's inbound side also becomes private
Turn off public network access for the app, now that internal clients can reach it through the private endpoint
Add an allow rule for 10.40.0.0/16 to the SCM site's access restrictions only, and leave the main site's rule list empty
Add a Hybrid Connection to 10.40.2.15 so that internet callers are sent through the relay instead
questions.why: A private endpoint adds a private way in but leaves the public address open, so public network access must be turned off for the app to be unreachable from the internet.

questions.prompt: A logistics company turns on virtual network integration for its internal reporting app on App Service. The app can now reach a private file server. An engineer then opens the app's normal web address from home over the internet, and the app loads. Why?
choices: The App Service plan is below Basic tier, so the integration did not actually take effect
The SCM site rule list overrides the main site, and the SCM site allows all callers by default
Virtual network integration only handles the app's outgoing calls, so the public inbound address stays open
The delegated subnet was too small, so the integration quietly fell back to public mode
questions.why: Virtual network integration is outbound only, so inbound access has to be locked down separately with access restrictions or a private endpoint.

questions.prompt: An App Service app has these access restrictions. Priority 150: allow 192.0.2.0/24. Priority 250: deny 192.0.2.77/32. No other rules exist. A request arrives from 192.0.2.77. What happens?
choices: It is blocked, because adding any allow rule denies every caller not matched by it
It is allowed, because the priority 150 allow rule is checked first and matches
It is blocked with HTTP 403, because a deny rule always wins over an allow rule
It is blocked, because a single-address rule always beats a range rule
questions.why: Rules are checked from the lowest priority number up, so the priority 150 allow rule matches 192.0.2.77 before the priority 250 deny rule is ever reached.

questions.prompt: A retailer's App Service app must call one inventory server in its own building on port 1433. The on-premises network team will not make any network changes. Which App Service feature fits best?
choices: A private endpoint, which gives the app a private inbound address in a virtual network
Hybrid Connections, which reach one specific host and port through a relay
Virtual network integration with a subnet delegated to App Service
Access restrictions, using an allow rule for the store's public IP range
questions.why: Hybrid Connections reach a single host and port, often on-premises, through a relay without any network change, while private endpoints and access restrictions only affect inbound traffic.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between App Service inbound and outbound networking features, which feature you would use to keep an app off the public internet versus to let it reach a private database, and one limit or tradeoff of your choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: App Service networking has two directions, and each feature only covers one. Inbound features decide who can reach the app: access restrictions are priority-ordered allow or deny rules by IP range, service tag or subnet, with an implicit deny once any allow rule exists, while a private endpoint gives the app a private IP in our virtual network so we can switch off public access. Outbound features decide what the app can reach: virtual network integration sends its outgoing calls through a delegated subnet so it can talk to a private database, and Hybrid Connections reach a single host and port on-premises. To hide the app I'd use a private endpoint; to reach the database I'd use virtual network integration. The tradeoff is that integration needs Basic tier or higher and its own dedicated subnet, and it does nothing for inbound, so on its own the app stays publicly reachable.
rubricPoints: Separates inbound features from outbound features and says each works in one direction.
Describes access restrictions as priority-ordered rules with an implicit deny once an allow rule exists.
Names a private endpoint as the way to give the app a private inbound address.
Names virtual network integration with a delegated subnet as the way to reach private resources outbound.
Warns that virtual network integration alone does not make the app private.
States a limit, such as the tier requirement, the dedicated subnet, or separate SCM site rules.

suggested.rationale: Tracing which path a request takes, inbound through access rules or a private endpoint versus outbound through an integrated subnet, is exactly what a virtual network path tracer would let the learner practise.

lessons.plain: A deployment slot is a second, fully working copy of your web app that lives alongside the live one, with its own web address. You put a new version into the spare slot, check it, and then swap it with the live slot so visitors get the new version almost instantly. If something goes wrong, you swap back. Think of a theatre with two stages on a turntable: the crew sets up the next scene on the hidden stage, and when it is ready the turntable rotates, so the audience never watches the scenery being built.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you could keep a hidden, fully running copy of your website and trade places with the live copy in one step, what would that let you do when a new release turns out to be broken?
lessons.teach:
A deployment slot is a separate live app inside one Azure App Service app (App Service is Azure's managed web hosting). Every app has a production slot; you add others such as staging. Each slot has its own hostname, like myapp-staging.azurewebsites.net, its own deployed code and its own configuration, but all slots share the compute of the same App Service plan (the set of servers you pay for). Slots need the Standard tier or higher; Standard allows 5 slots and Premium allows 20.

A swap exchanges the contents of two slots. Before switching traffic, Azure applies the target slot's settings to the source and warms it up with requests, so users do not hit a cold app. Because the target already runs warm code, the switch causes no downtime, and swapping again rolls back.

Settings move with the code during a swap unless you tick Deployment slot setting, which makes that setting sticky, meaning it stays with the slot.

Worked example: production runs version 1 against the live database. You create a staging slot (portal: the app, Deployment slots, Add slot), deploy version 2, and give staging a connection string to a test database marked as a slot setting. You test the staging hostname. You choose Swap with source staging and target production. Azure gives staging the production connection string, warms it up, then routes traffic: production now runs version 2 on the live database, while staging holds version 1 on the test database, ready for a swap back.

You can also send a percentage of production traffic to a slot for testing, enable auto swap so a deployment to staging swaps itself, or use swap with preview to pause after settings are applied and check before finishing.

Common mistake: forgetting to mark environment-specific connection strings as slot settings. They then travel during the swap, so production could end up pointing at a test database, a real outage or data-loss risk.

questions.prompt: Harbor Tickets runs its booking website on an Azure App Service app (managed web hosting) in the Premium tier. Production runs build 4.2 and uses a live payment key stored in a setting called PAYMENT_KEY. The administrator works through a release like this. Step 1: add a slot named qa. Step 2: deploy build 4.3 to qa, set PAYMENT_KEY on qa to a sandbox (test) key, and tick Deployment slot setting on it. Step 3: test the app on the qa slot's own hostname. Step 4: choose Swap with source qa and target production. Step 5: MISSING. Step 6: Azure sends warm-up requests to the qa slot's app, then switches traffic, so production now runs build 4.3 with the live key and qa holds build 4.2 with the sandbox key. Which choice correctly describes Step 5?
choices: Azure clears every setting on the qa slot, and the administrator must re-enter them after the swap finishes.
Azure copies the sandbox PAYMENT_KEY from qa into production, so after the swap both slots share the sandbox key.
Azure applies the production slot's settings, including the sticky live PAYMENT_KEY, to the app running in qa before any traffic moves.
Azure stops the production app, copies the build 4.3 files onto it, and restarts it, causing a short outage.
questions.why: Before switching traffic, a swap applies the target slot's settings to the source, so the sticky live key stays with production while build 4.3 is warmed up with it.

questions.prompt: Northwind Clinics hosts its patient portal on one App Service app. The team wants a production slot plus seven more slots, eight in total, for different test environments. Which statement is correct?
choices: Any tier works, because each slot runs on its own separate set of servers.
Slots cannot be used for this, because an app can have only a production slot and one staging slot.
They need the Premium tier, because Standard allows only 5 slots and Premium allows 20, and all slots share the same App Service plan's compute.
The Standard tier is enough, because Standard has no limit on the number of slots.
questions.why: Standard allows 5 slots and Premium allows 20, so eight slots need Premium, and every slot shares the compute of the same App Service plan (the servers you pay for).

questions.prompt: Fabrikam Travel has deployed a new search feature to its staging slot. Before releasing it to everyone, the team wants about 10 percent of real production visitors to use the staging version while the rest stay on the current version. Which slot feature fits?
choices: Enable auto swap on the staging slot.
Mark the search setting as a Deployment slot setting.
Use swap with preview and leave it paused.
Send a percentage of production traffic to the staging slot.
questions.why: Routing a percentage of production traffic to a slot lets a share of real users test it, whereas auto swap, sticky settings and swap with preview do not split traffic.

questions.prompt: Tailspin Retail swapped its staging slot into production. Minutes later, real customer orders started landing in the test database that staging used. The release itself worked well during testing. What most likely went wrong, and what is the quickest way to undo the change?
choices: The plan was on the Basic tier. Upgrade to Standard and swap again.
Staging had its own hostname. Delete the staging slot to send the orders back.
The swap skipped warm-up. Restart the production slot to warm it up.
The test connection string was not marked as a Deployment slot setting, so it moved with the code. Swap again to roll back.
questions.why: A connection string without the Deployment slot setting tick travels with the code during a swap, which points production at the test database, and swapping again rolls the change back.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how App Service deployment slots let you release a new version safely, and name one limit or tradeoff they should know about.
lessons.modelAnswer: A deployment slot is an extra live copy of our App Service app with its own address, for example a staging slot next to production. We deploy the new version to staging, test it at its own URL, then swap staging with production. Azure first applies production's settings to the staging code and warms it up, then switches traffic, so users see no downtime, and if the release is bad we just swap back. Settings travel with the code unless we mark them as deployment slot settings, so environment-specific items like database connection strings must be sticky or production could end up on the test database. Tradeoffs: slots require Standard tier or higher with a capped number per tier, and every slot shares the same App Service plan's servers, so a busy staging slot can steal capacity from production.
rubricPoints: A slot is a separate live app with its own hostname inside the same App Service app.
A swap exchanges slots after warming up the target, giving near-zero downtime and easy rollback by swapping back.
Settings move with the code unless marked as deployment slot settings, which stay with the slot.
Connection strings and other environment-specific values should be sticky to avoid production using test resources.
Slots need Standard tier or higher, have a per-tier limit, and share the plan's compute.

suggested.rationale: A deployment strategies engine would let the learner stage, swap, route a traffic percentage and roll back, which is exactly the hands-on skill slots require.

lessons.plain: A virtual network is your own private, walled-off network inside the cloud, where your virtual machines and other resources get addresses and can talk to each other. A subnet is a smaller section carved out of that network. Think of a virtual network as an office building with a block of room numbers, and subnets as floors: each floor gets its own range of room numbers, and no two floors share one. You choose the address ranges up front, so planning sizes and avoiding clashes with other networks matters before anything is built.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you create a subnet that holds 256 addresses, do you think all 256 can be handed to virtual machines? Guess how many are left, and why the cloud might keep some for itself.
lessons.teach:
In Azure, a virtual network (VNet) is an isolated private network that lives in one region (one geographic group of datacenters). You give it an address space, written in CIDR notation (an address plus a slash number saying how many leading bits are fixed). For example, 10.1.0.0/16 fixes 16 bits, leaving 65,536 addresses. You normally use private ranges such as 10.x, 172.16-31.x or 192.168.x, which are not routed on the public internet.

A subnet is a slice of that address space. Subnets inside one VNet must not overlap, and by default resources in different subnets of the same VNet can reach each other. Subnets exist so you can group resources and later attach controls, such as security rules or custom routes, to each group. Some Azure services insist on a dedicated subnet with an exact name, such as GatewaySubnet for a VPN gateway.

Azure reserves five addresses in every subnet. Worked example: subnet 10.1.1.0/24 has 256 addresses. Step one, 10.1.1.0 is the network address. Step two, 10.1.1.1 is the default gateway. Step three, 10.1.1.2 and 10.1.1.3 map to Azure DNS. Step four, 10.1.1.255 is the broadcast address. That leaves 256 minus 5, so 251 usable addresses. The smallest allowed subnet is /29: 8 addresses minus 5 leaves 3.

A common mistake is picking an address space that overlaps another VNet or your on-premises network, for example using 10.0.0.0/16 everywhere. Overlapping ranges cannot be connected later, because a packet to 10.0.1.4 would have two possible destinations. In a running system this means a costly rebuild: changing a subnet's range is blocked while resources still sit in it, so you end up moving or redeploying workloads. Plan non-overlapping ranges, and leave spare room for growth, before you deploy.

questions.prompt: A logistics company is planning a subnet for 50 virtual machines (VMs) inside its VNet 172.20.0.0/16. A VNet (virtual network) is an isolated private network in one Azure region. The team is testing whether the subnet 172.20.8.0/26 is big enough. Step 1: /26 fixes 26 of the 32 address bits. That leaves 6 free bits, so the subnet holds 64 addresses. Step 2: (missing). Step 3: Compare the usable count with the 50 VMs needed and decide whether the subnet fits. Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: Subtract the 5 addresses Azure reserves in every subnet: 64 - 5 = 59 usable addresses.
Subtract 5 reserved addresses for every 16 addresses: 64 - 20 = 44 usable addresses.
Subtract nothing, because a /26 is larger than the /29 minimum: 64 usable addresses.
Subtract only the network and broadcast addresses: 64 - 2 = 62 usable addresses.
questions.why: Azure reserves exactly five addresses in every subnet, whatever its size (the network address, the default gateway, two for Azure DNS, and the broadcast address), so a /26 gives 64 - 5 = 59 usable addresses, enough for 50 VMs.

questions.prompt: A hospital group's on-premises network uses 10.0.0.0/16. It is creating an Azure VNet (virtual network) that it plans to connect to the on-premises network later. Which address space for the new VNet avoids the problem of overlapping ranges?
questions.why: 10.50.0.0/16 covers 10.50.0.0 to 10.50.255.255, which shares no addresses with 10.0.0.0/16. Each of the other choices includes addresses that are also in 10.0.x.x, and overlapping ranges cannot be connected later.

questions.prompt: A design studio has a VNet (virtual network) with address space 10.4.0.0/16. It already has a subnet, meaning a slice of that address space, at 10.4.0.0/24, which covers 10.4.0.0 to 10.4.0.255. Which range can it add as a second subnet in the same VNet?
questions.why: Subnets in one VNet must not overlap. 10.4.1.0/24 (10.4.1.0 to 10.4.1.255) is the only choice that stays outside 10.4.0.0 to 10.4.0.255. Each of the others includes some or all of the existing subnet's addresses.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit wants to add a VPN gateway to its existing Azure VNet (virtual network). A VPN gateway is a service that creates an encrypted link between the VNet and another network. What does the subnet for this gateway require?
choices: It can share any existing subnet that already holds the nonprofit's VMs.
It needs its own dedicated subnet named exactly GatewaySubnet.
Any subnet name works, as long as the subnet is exactly /29.
It must be built in a separate VNet in a different region.
questions.why: Some Azure services insist on a dedicated subnet with an exact name, and a VPN gateway must sit in its own subnet called GatewaySubnet.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a virtual network and a subnet are in Azure, how you would size a subnet for 20 virtual machines, and what goes wrong if you choose address ranges carelessly.
lessons.modelAnswer: A VNet is a private, isolated network in one Azure region, defined by an address space in CIDR notation such as 10.20.0.0/16. Subnets are non-overlapping slices of that space that group resources so we can apply controls to each group; by default subnets in the same VNet can talk to each other. Azure keeps five addresses in every subnet: network address, gateway, two for DNS, and broadcast. For 20 VMs a /27 gives 32 minus 5, so 27 usable, but I would pick a /26 or /24 to leave room to grow, because resizing a subnet that already holds resources is blocked. The big tradeoff is planning: if our ranges overlap another VNet or on-premises, we can never connect them cleanly and would have to rebuild, so we should agree on a non-overlapping address plan first.
rubricPoints: A VNet is an isolated private network scoped to one region with a CIDR address space.
Subnets are non-overlapping slices of the VNet address space used to group resources.
Azure reserves five addresses per subnet, so usable count is total minus five.
Sizing should leave room for growth because resizing occupied subnets is hard.
Overlapping address ranges with other networks prevent later connection and force rework.

suggested.rationale: Placing addresses into subnets and seeing which ranges collide or route is best learned by tracing paths through a simulated virtual network.

lessons.plain: Virtual network peering joins two separate private networks in Azure so machines in each can talk to each other using their private addresses, as if they were one network. A virtual network (VNet) is your own isolated slice of Azure's network. Normally two VNets cannot see each other at all. Peering is like building a private corridor between two office buildings: people walk straight across without going outside. The traffic stays on Microsoft's own backbone network instead of the public internet. The corridor only links the two buildings it touches, so a third building needs its own corridor.
lessons.guessPrompt: Network A is peered with network B, and network B is peered with network C. Do you think a server in A can reach a server in C through B? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Virtual network peering is a direct, private link between two virtual networks (VNets, your isolated Azure private networks). Once peered, resources reach each other by private IP address, with low latency, over Microsoft's backbone. Regional peering links VNets in the same Azure region. Global peering links VNets in different regions.

It works because Azure adds a route for the other VNet's address space (its range of private IP addresses, such as 10.2.0.0/16) to each side's routing. For that to work, the two address spaces must not overlap. If both used 10.1.0.0/16, an address would be ambiguous, and Azure refuses the peering.

Peering is made of two links, one on each VNet. Each link has settings. Allow traffic to remote network permits the connection. Allow forwarded traffic accepts packets that started outside the peer VNet and were passed along by a device in it. Gateway transit lets one VNet share its VPN gateway (the device that connects Azure to on-premises networks) with the peer, which then sets use remote gateways. When both links exist, the status reads Connected. With only one side, it shows Initiated and no traffic flows.

Worked example: VNet A is 10.1.0.0/16, B is 10.2.0.0/16, and C is 10.3.0.0/16. A is peered with B, and B with C. A VM at 10.1.0.4 sends to 10.3.0.4. A's routes know 10.2.0.0/16 but not 10.3.0.0/16, so the packet does not reach C. Peering is non-transitive. To fix it, peer A with C directly, or route through a network virtual appliance in B (a VM that forwards traffic) using user-defined routes and allow forwarded traffic.

Common mistake: assuming a peering also opens the firewall. Network security groups still filter the traffic. A rule that denies the peer's range blocks it even when the peering shows Connected. Also, data crossing a peering is billed in both directions, and global peering costs more.

questions.prompt:
Fabrikam Retail has three virtual networks (VNets, isolated Azure private networks). Hub is 172.20.0.0/16, Spoke-East is 172.16.0.0/16, and Spoke-West is 172.17.0.0/16. Spoke-East is peered with Hub, and Spoke-West is peered with Hub. Both peerings show Connected. Spoke-East and Spoke-West are not peered with each other. A VM at 172.16.2.8 in Spoke-East sends a packet to a VM at 172.17.3.9 in Spoke-West. No network virtual appliance or user-defined routes are in place.

Step 1: Peering adds a route for the peer's address space to each side, so Spoke-East's routing knows 172.20.0.0/16 (Hub).
Step 2: [missing]
Step 3: To make this work, Fabrikam can peer Spoke-East with Spoke-West directly, or route through a forwarding VM in Hub using user-defined routes and allow forwarded traffic.

Which statement correctly fills Step 2?
choices: The packet reaches Spoke-West through Hub, because both spokes share a Connected peering with Hub.
The packet is dropped because 172.16.0.0/16 and 172.17.0.0/16 overlap, so Azure blocks it.
Spoke-East has no route for 172.17.0.0/16, because peering is non-transitive, so the packet does not reach Spoke-West.
The packet reaches Spoke-West only if the peerings are changed from regional to global peering.
questions.why: Each peering only adds the direct peer's address range, so Spoke-East learns Hub's range but not Spoke-West's, and the packet cannot be delivered without a direct peering or forwarding setup.

questions.prompt: An administrator at Northwind Labs creates a peering link on VNet Dev (10.40.0.0/16) pointing to VNet Test (10.41.0.0/16), but nobody creates the matching link on VNet Test. The peering status on Dev shows Initiated. What happens when a VM in Dev tries to reach a VM in Test by private IP address?
choices: Traffic flows only if allow forwarded traffic is enabled on the Dev link.
No traffic flows, because a peering needs a link on both VNets before it becomes Connected.
Traffic flows one way only, from Dev to Test, until the second link is added.
Traffic flows normally, because Initiated means the peering is active and waiting for billing.
questions.why: Peering is made of two links, one per VNet; with only one side created the status is Initiated and no traffic flows in either direction.

questions.prompt: Contoso Health wants to peer its existing VNet Clinic, which uses the address space 10.60.0.0/16. Which of these candidate VNets would Azure refuse to peer with Clinic?
choices: VNet Records using 192.168.0.0/16, located in the same region as Clinic.
VNet Archive using 10.70.0.0/16, located in a different Azure region.
VNet Billing using 10.61.0.0/16, located in the same region as Clinic.
VNet Imaging using 10.60.0.0/16, located in the same region as Clinic.
questions.why: Imaging's address space is identical to Clinic's, so addresses would be ambiguous and Azure refuses peerings whose address spaces overlap; region differences do not cause a refusal.

questions.prompt: At Tailspin Logistics, VNet Orders (10.80.0.0/16) and VNet Warehouse (10.90.0.0/16) are peered, and both links show Connected. A VM in Orders still cannot reach a database VM in Warehouse at 10.90.5.12. What is the most likely cause, based on how peering works?
choices: A network security group on the Warehouse side has a rule denying traffic from 10.80.0.0/16.
Peered VNets can only reach each other through public IP addresses, not private ones.
Connected means only one link exists, so the second link still has to be created.
The peering needs gateway transit enabled before any private traffic can cross it.
questions.why: Peering creates the route but does not open the firewall, so a network security group rule denying the peer's address range still blocks traffic even when the peering shows Connected.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what VNet peering gives you and what it does not, including one limit that would surprise someone designing a three-network layout.
lessons.modelAnswer: Peering connects two VNets so their resources talk over private IPs on Microsoft's backbone, with no public internet and no VPN gateway needed. It works within a region or across regions (global peering). Each VNet needs a link to the other, and the status must show Connected on both sides. The address spaces cannot overlap, because Azure has to know which side owns each address. The big surprise is that peering is not transitive. If A peers with B and B peers with C, A still cannot reach C. You either peer A and C directly or put a forwarding appliance in B with user-defined routes and allow forwarded traffic. Peering also does not bypass security: NSGs still filter the traffic. One tradeoff is cost, since data across a peering is charged in both directions, and more for global peering.
rubricPoints: Peering gives private-IP connectivity between two VNets over the Microsoft backbone, in one region or across regions.
Address spaces of the peered VNets must not overlap.
A link is needed on each side, and traffic flows only when the status is Connected.
Peering is non-transitive, so a third VNet needs its own peering or a forwarding hub with routes.
NSGs still apply, and peered traffic carries a data-transfer charge.

suggested.rationale: Tracing a packet across peered and non-peered VNets in a path tracer makes non-transitivity and the effect of NSGs concrete in a way reading cannot.

lessons.plain: A public IP address is an internet-reachable address that you rent from Azure and attach to something, such as a virtual machine's network card or a load balancer, so the outside world can find it. Without one, a resource inside a virtual network (your private, isolated slice of Azure's network) can talk to its neighbours but cannot be reached directly from the internet. Think of it like a street address for a building in a gated estate: the address lets visitors find the gate, but whether they get through depends on separate security rules.
lessons.guessPrompt: You stop a virtual machine to save money over the weekend, and when you start it on Monday your website's domain name no longer reaches it. What might have changed about the machine's internet address, and how could you prevent it?
lessons.teach:
A public IP address in Azure is a separate resource with its own settings that you associate with another resource: a virtual machine's network interface (NIC, the virtual network card), a public load balancer, a VPN or application gateway, a NAT gateway (a service that gives private machines a shared outbound address), or Azure Bastion.

Three settings matter most. The SKU is the product tier. Standard is the current tier; the older Basic tier is being retired, so new work uses Standard. Standard addresses are secure by default, meaning inbound traffic is blocked until a network security group (NSG, a set of allow and deny rules) permits it, and they can be zone-redundant, meaning they survive the loss of one availability zone (a physically separate datacenter group in a region). The allocation method decides whether the address is static (fixed until you delete the resource) or dynamic (assigned at start and released when the resource is deallocated). Standard addresses are always static. The IP version is IPv4 or IPv6. You can also add a DNS name label, which gives a friendly name ending in the region's cloudapp domain. A public IP prefix reserves a contiguous block of addresses so you can hand out predictable ones.

Worked example: you create a Standard, static IPv4 address and associate it with a VM's NIC. Someone on the internet tries SSH on port 22. Step one, the packet reaches the public IP. Step two, Azure translates it to the VM's private address. Step three, the NSG on the NIC or subnet is checked; with no allow rule for port 22, the packet is dropped. Add an allow rule and it gets through.

Common mistake: using a dynamic Basic address and pointing a DNS record at it. When the VM is deallocated, the address is released and a new one appears on restart, so the record breaks. Another mistake is assuming attaching a Standard IP opens the machine; it does not. In a running system, a fixed static address is what firewalls, partner allow-lists and DNS records depend on, and you must dissociate an address before you can delete it.

questions.prompt: Harbourline Shipping runs a tracking web server on a VM. The admin creates a Standard, static IPv4 public IP address and associates it with the VM's network interface. The network security group (NSG, a set of allow and deny rules) on the VM's subnet has one inbound allow rule, for HTTPS on port 443. Nothing else is allowed. A support engineer at home tries to connect with Remote Desktop on port 3389. Step 1: the connection attempt arrives at the public IP address. Step 2: Azure translates the destination to the VM's private address. Step 3: ______. Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: The packet gets through, because traffic translated to a private address is no longer checked by the NSG.
The packet gets through, because attaching a Standard public IP opens the VM to inbound traffic.
The public IP itself drops the packet before translation, because Standard addresses only accept HTTPS.
The NSG is checked, no rule allows port 3389, and the packet is dropped.
questions.why: Standard public IPs are secure by default, so after translation the NSG decides, and with only port 443 allowed, the Remote Desktop attempt on 3389 is dropped.

questions.prompt: An admin is creating a new Standard SKU public IP address and looks for the allocation method setting. Which allocation method will the Standard address use?
choices: Either one, chosen by the admin, with dynamic as the default.
Static only if a DNS name label is added, otherwise dynamic.
Static: Standard addresses are always static.
Dynamic: Standard addresses get a new address each time the resource starts.
questions.why: Standard public IP addresses are always static, so the address stays fixed until the public IP resource is deleted.

questions.prompt: Corvel Analytics sends data to a partner whose firewall only accepts traffic from addresses on an allow-list. Corvel's VM is deallocated every weekend to save money. The address the partner sees must never change, and new work should use the current product tier. Which public IP configuration fits best?
choices: An IPv6 address, because IPv6 addresses are never released.
Standard SKU, which is always static and keeps the same address through deallocation.
Basic SKU with dynamic allocation, re-sent to the partner after each restart.
Basic SKU with dynamic allocation, plus a DNS name label for the partner to use.
questions.why: A Standard address is static, so it survives the weekend deallocation and the partner's allow-list keeps working, while Basic is the older tier that is being retired.

questions.prompt: At Pinewell Clinics, an admin tries to delete a public IP address that is still associated with the NAT gateway (a service that gives private machines a shared outbound address) for a subnet. The deletion does not go through. What is the reason?
choices: Public IP addresses used by a NAT gateway are permanent and can never be deleted.
Only dynamic addresses can be deleted, so the admin must first switch it to dynamic.
The address must be dissociated from the NAT gateway before it can be deleted.
An NSG allow rule must be added before the address can be deleted.
questions.why: A public IP is a separate resource, and you must dissociate it from the resource it is attached to before you can delete it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would set up a public IP for a web server that partners will add to their firewall allow-lists, including why you chose each setting and one limit or tradeoff of exposing a VM this way.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd create a Standard SKU public IPv4 address, because Standard is the current tier and Basic is being retired. Standard is always static, which is exactly what we need: partners will put this address in their allow-lists, and a dynamic address could change after the VM is deallocated and break their rules and our DNS record. I'd make it zone-redundant so losing one zone doesn't take the address away, and add a DNS name label for a friendly name. Attaching it to the NIC alone won't let anyone in, since Standard is secure by default, so I'd add an NSG rule allowing only HTTPS. The tradeoff is that a public IP on a single VM exposes it directly and ties traffic to one machine; for scale or reduced exposure we might put the address on a load balancer instead, and static addresses keep costing money while reserved.
rubricPoints: Chooses the Standard SKU and notes Basic is being retired.
Explains static versus dynamic and why static suits allow-lists and DNS.
States that Standard public IPs block inbound traffic until an NSG allows it.
Mentions resilience such as zone redundancy or a DNS name label.
Names a tradeoff such as direct exposure, cost, or a load balancer being better for scale.

suggested.rationale: Tracing a packet from the internet through a public IP to a NIC and its NSG makes the learner see what the address does and does not allow, which the planned path tracer is built for.

lessons.plain: A user-defined route is a custom signpost you add to an Azure virtual network to change where traffic goes next. Azure normally routes traffic automatically. Machines in the same network reach each other directly, and traffic bound for the internet goes straight out. Sometimes you want traffic to take a detour instead, for example through a firewall that inspects it first. Think of a satnav that picks the fastest road. A user-defined route is like you telling it: always drive past the checkpoint before leaving town. You collect these signposts in a route table and attach it to a subnet, which is a slice of the network.
lessons.guessPrompt: Azure already sends a virtual machine's internet-bound traffic straight out. If your company insists that all of it pass through a firewall machine first, what would you need to change, and where would you change it?
lessons.teach:
A user-defined route (UDR) is a custom routing rule you create in Azure to override the default path traffic takes. Each route has an address prefix, which is the destination range in CIDR notation such as 0.0.0.0/0 (meaning everything). It also has a next hop type, which says where to send matching traffic. The main types are Virtual appliance (a VM you name by its private IP, usually a firewall, called a network virtual appliance or NVA), Virtual network gateway (a VPN gateway), Internet, Virtual network, and None, which drops the traffic. Routes live in a route table, which is a resource you associate with one or more subnets. A subnet can have only one route table, and the table only affects traffic leaving that subnet.

Azure already creates system routes, which are the built-in defaults. To pick a route for a packet, Azure first chooses the longest prefix match, meaning the most specific range that contains the destination. If two routes have the same prefix, a user route beats a BGP route learned from a gateway, and a BGP route beats a system route.

Here is a worked example. Subnet Web is 10.0.1.0/24 inside VNet 10.0.0.0/16, and a firewall VM sits at 10.0.100.4. You create a route table with 0.0.0.0/0, next hop Virtual appliance 10.0.100.4, and associate it with Web. A VM at 10.0.1.5 sends to 8.8.8.8. That address matches only the /0 routes. The system /0 says Internet and your user /0 says appliance, so your route wins and the packet goes to the firewall. The same VM sends to 10.0.2.10. The system route for 10.0.0.0/16 is more specific than /0, so that traffic stays direct inside the VNet.

A common mistake is forgetting to enable IP forwarding on the firewall VM's network interface. Without it, Azure discards packets that are not addressed to the VM itself. Another is routing only one direction, which causes asymmetric paths that the firewall drops. In production, either mistake silently blackholes traffic, so the subnet appears to lose connectivity.

questions.prompt:
Contoso Clinics has a VNet 172.16.0.0/16. Subnet App is 172.16.2.0/24, and a network virtual appliance (a firewall VM) sits at 172.16.50.4. An administrator creates a route table containing one user-defined route, 172.16.3.0/24 with next hop Virtual appliance 172.16.50.4, and associates it with App. A VM at 172.16.2.8 sends a packet to 172.16.3.20.

Step 1: The table is associated with App, and the packet is leaving App, so the user route is considered.
Step 2: Routes whose prefix contains 172.16.3.20 are the system route 172.16.0.0/16 (next hop Virtual network), the user route 172.16.3.0/24 (Virtual appliance), and the system 0.0.0.0/0 (Internet).
Step 3: ???
Step 4: The packet is sent to 172.16.50.4.

Which statement correctly fills Step 3?
choices: The /24 is the longest prefix match (most specific range), so the user route is chosen.
The routes conflict, so Azure falls back to next hop None and the packet is dropped.
The /16 system route covers the most addresses, so it is chosen and the packet goes directly inside the VNet.
The 0.0.0.0/0 route matches every destination, so it always wins and the packet goes to the Internet.
questions.why: Azure first picks the most specific matching prefix, and /24 is more specific than /16 or /0, so the user route to the appliance wins.

questions.prompt: At Fabrikam, subnet Payments has a route table sending 0.0.0.0/0 to a firewall VM at 10.20.9.4 (next hop Virtual appliance). The route is correct and associated, but VMs in Payments suddenly cannot reach anything on the internet. The firewall VM itself is running. Which missing setting most likely explains this?
choices: The route table must also be associated with the firewall's own subnet before any route takes effect.
System routes always override user routes for 0.0.0.0/0, so the user route is ignored.
The next hop type should be Internet, because Virtual appliance cannot be used with 0.0.0.0/0.
IP forwarding is not enabled on the firewall VM's network interface, so Azure discards packets not addressed to the VM itself.
questions.why: Without IP forwarding on the appliance's network interface, Azure drops traffic passing through it, silently blackholing the subnet.
