Step 3, accept a policy keeping 24 hours of points with app-consistent snapshots every 4 hours. Step 4, wait for initial replication to finish and status to show Protected. Step 5, run a test failover into an isolated network to prove it works.

Common mistake: placing the vault in the source region. If that region goes down, your recovery controls go down with it. Also, ASR is not backup; it protects against site loss, not against deleting a file last month.

questions.prompt: A clinic runs a patient-records database on an Azure VM in Australia East and wants it protected in Australia Southeast with Azure Site Recovery. Step 1: create a Recovery Services vault in Australia Southeast so the recovery controls survive if Australia East fails. Step 2: enable replication for the VM, choosing Australia Southeast as the target region, plus a target resource group and target virtual network. Step 3: ASR installs the Mobility service on the VM. Disk writes land first in a cache storage account in Australia East, then move to replica managed disks in Australia Southeast. Step 4: in the replication policy, keep 48 hours of recovery points and ______. Step 5: wait for the status to show Protected, then run a test failover into an isolated network. Which choice best completes Step 4?
choices: take app-consistent snapshots at a regular interval, because they flush in-memory data and are safer for a database
extend retention to 60 days so ASR can restore records deleted last month
move the cache storage account to Australia Southeast so no data waits in the source region
rely on crash-consistent points only, because they already include in-memory database data
questions.why: App-consistent points flush in-memory application data before capture, which makes them the safer recovery point for a database than crash-consistent points taken as if power were pulled.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's manager says: "If our main region fails, we can afford to lose at most the last 5 minutes of shipment updates." Which disaster-recovery target is the manager describing?
choices: Recovery point objective (RPO)
Recovery time objective (RTO)
Replication policy retention
Recovery plan order
questions.why: RPO is how much recent data you can afford to lose. RTO is how long you can afford to be down.

questions.prompt: A design studio protects a file-server VM in East US with Azure Site Recovery, replicating it to West US. Three weeks ago, an employee deleted a project folder by mistake, and now the team wants it back. What is the right conclusion?
choices: Change the replication policy to app-consistent snapshots and the folder will reappear.
ASR protects against losing a whole site, not against old deletions. Recovering the folder needs a backup solution.
Run a failover to West US. The replica still holds the folder from three weeks ago.
Run a test failover into an isolated network to recover the deleted folder.
questions.why: ASR continuously copies changes, including the deletion, and keeps only short-term recovery points. It is not a backup and cannot bring back a file deleted weeks ago.

questions.prompt: An online retailer replicates three VMs with Azure Site Recovery: a database VM, an application VM and a web front-end VM. During a failover, the database must start first, then the application VM, then the web VM. Which ASR feature handles this?
choices: The Mobility service
A cache storage account
A replication policy
A recovery plan
questions.why: A recovery plan groups VMs into an ordered script that controls which machines start first during failover.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, what you have to set up to protect an Azure VM with Site Recovery and why each choice matters. Include one limit or tradeoff of relying on it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Site Recovery keeps a near-live copy of a VM in a second region. I create a Recovery Services vault in the target region so the controls survive if the source region fails. Then I enable replication on the VM and pick the target region, resource group, virtual network and disk type. ASR adds the Mobility service extension to capture disk writes, buffers them in a cache storage account in the source region, and writes them to replica managed disks in the target. A replication policy decides how long recovery points are kept and how often app-consistent snapshots happen; those matter for databases. A recovery plan orders startup across VMs, and test failover proves it works without touching production. The tradeoff: it costs extra storage and compute in the second region, and because changes replicate quickly, an accidental deletion or corruption copies across too, so it does not replace backups.
rubricPoints: Says ASR continuously replicates VMs to a different target region for disaster recovery.
Places the Recovery Services vault in the target region and explains why.
Names the key choices: target region, resource group, virtual network and replication policy.
Mentions the Mobility service and cache storage account role in replication.
Distinguishes app-consistent from crash-consistent recovery points or mentions test failover.
States a limit such as extra cost or that replication is not a substitute for backup.

suggested.rationale: A disaster-recovery planner would let the learner choose regions, vault placement and replication policies against RPO and RTO targets and see the consequences, which is the core of this objective.

lessons.plain: A failover with Azure Site Recovery means switching a workload, such as a virtual machine, from its home Azure region (a group of datacenters in one geographic area) to a copy kept running in a second region, so the service keeps working when the first region has trouble. Site Recovery is Azure's managed disaster-recovery service. It copies a machine's disks to the other region all the time. Think of a spare generator that is already wired in: when the main power fails, you flip the switch, and the lights come back on from the spare. Failover is flipping that switch on purpose.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you want to prove your disaster-recovery copy really works without disturbing the live production system, what do you think the failover test should do differently from a real failover?
lessons.teach:
Failover in Azure Site Recovery is the action that starts a replicated virtual machine in the secondary (target) region from a saved recovery point. Replication is the continuous copying of disk changes to that region. A recovery point is a snapshot of the machine at one moment. You choose one when you fail over. Latest processed starts fastest. Latest first processes data still waiting, so it loses the least. Latest app-consistent was taken while applications had flushed their data to disk, so databases come up clean. Custom lets you pick an older point, which helps if the newest copies contain a problem.

Two measures guide the choice. RPO (recovery point objective) is how much recent data you can afford to lose. RTO (recovery time objective) is how long you can afford to be down.

A test failover starts the copy in an isolated virtual network, a private network you pick that is not connected to production. Live replication carries on untouched. Afterwards you run cleanup, which deletes the test machines. A real failover moves the workload for real.

Worked example: a web VM in East US replicates to West US, and East US has an outage. Step 1: in the Recovery Services vault (the container that holds the replication settings), open the replicated item and choose Failover. Step 2: pick Latest processed to keep downtime short. If the source can still be reached, tick the option to shut it down first. Step 3: Site Recovery creates the VM in West US, in the target network you configured earlier. Step 4: you check that the site works, then Commit, which locks in that recovery point. Step 5: you Re-protect, which reverses replication so West US now copies back to East US, ready for a later failback (moving home again). A recovery plan groups several VMs so they fail over in a set order.

Common mistake: running a test failover into the production network. This can cause IP address conflicts and send real users to test machines. A second mistake is skipping re-protect after a real failover, which leaves the running workload with no disaster-recovery copy at all.

questions.prompt: A logistics company replicates its inventory server, a virtual machine (VM), from UK South to UK West using Azure Site Recovery, a service that keeps a copy of a machine ready in another region. At 14:20 a faulty script wrote bad data across the server's disks. The team only noticed at 14:50, then UK South also became unreachable, so they must fail over. Failover means starting the replicated VM in the target region from a saved recovery point, which is a snapshot of the machine at one moment. Their reasoning, step by step: Step 1: Latest and Latest processed both reflect the newest disk changes, all of which come after 14:20, so either would bring the bad data along. Step 2: The most recent app-consistent point, taken while applications had flushed their data to disk, is from 14:35, also after the bad write. Step 3: (missing). Step 4: After checking that the inventory data looks correct, they Commit, which locks in the chosen recovery point. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Choose Custom and select a recovery point from before 14:20, accepting some lost data
Run a test failover into the production network first to see which point looks right
Choose Latest, because it processes waiting data first and so loses the least
Choose Latest app-consistent, because a clean application state outweighs the bad data
questions.why: Every newer point contains the bad write, so a Custom older point from before 14:20 is the only one that avoids it, at the cost of losing the changes made after it.

questions.prompt: A retail firm writes its disaster-recovery targets for an ordering app: "We can be offline for up to 3 hours, but we must lose no more than 10 minutes of orders." Which measure does the 10-minute figure describe?
choices: RTO, the recovery time objective, which is how long the app can be down
RPO, the recovery point objective, which is how much recent data can be lost
The commit window, which is how long you have to lock in a recovery point
Replication, the continuous copying of disk changes to the target region
questions.why: RPO measures how much recent data you can afford to lose, while the 3-hour figure for downtime is the RTO.

questions.prompt: A hospital's payroll VM replicates from Central US to North Central US. Auditors want proof each quarter that it can start in the second region, but payroll staff must not be affected and replication must keep running. What should the administrator do?
choices: Run a real failover, check the VM, then Re-protect to send replication back
Pause replication, start a copy by hand in the target region, then resume it
Run a test failover into the production virtual network so staff can try it
Run a test failover into an isolated virtual network, check it, then run cleanup
questions.why: A test failover into an isolated network (one not connected to production) leaves live replication untouched, and cleanup then deletes the test machines.

questions.prompt: After an outage, a media company performed a real failover of its streaming VMs from Japan East to Japan West, confirmed the service worked, and clicked Commit. Nothing else was done. Two weeks later, what is the main risk?
choices: The running VMs in Japan West have no disaster-recovery copy, because Re-protect was skipped
Commit expires after two weeks, so the VMs return to an older recovery point
The test machines from the failover are still running and cause IP address conflicts
The VMs will fall back to Japan East on their own and drop active viewers
questions.why: Re-protect reverses replication so the new region copies back to the original one; without it the running workload has no disaster-recovery copy at all.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would carry out a failover of an Azure VM to its secondary region with Site Recovery, including how you would test it first and what you do afterwards. Name one tradeoff when choosing a recovery point.
lessons.modelAnswer:
Site Recovery keeps copying our VM's disks to the secondary region. Before any real emergency, I'd run a test failover into an isolated virtual network. That proves the copy boots and the app works without touching production or stopping replication, and then I'd run cleanup to delete the test VMs.

In a real outage, I'd open the Recovery Services vault, select the replicated item or a recovery plan, and choose Failover. Then I'd pick a recovery point and shut down the source if it's still reachable. Once the VMs start in the target region, I'd verify the app and commit. Next I'd re-protect so replication runs back toward the original region, which lets us fail back later.

The tradeoff: Latest loses the least data but takes longer, because pending data must be processed first. Latest processed starts faster but may lose a little more. App-consistent is safest for databases but may be older.
rubricPoints: Defines failover as starting the replicated VM in the secondary region from a recovery point.
Distinguishes a test failover in an isolated network, followed by cleanup, from a real failover.
Describes the sequence after a real failover: verify, commit, then re-protect to reverse replication.
Names a recovery point tradeoff between data loss (RPO) and downtime (RTO).
Mentions recovery plans for ordering multiple VMs, or warns against testing in the production network.

suggested.rationale: A disaster-recovery planner would let the learner practise choosing recovery points, testing failover in isolation, then committing and re-protecting, all in a safe simulated setting.

lessons.plain: Backups run quietly every night, so you need two kinds of feedback to trust them. Alerts are the smoke alarm: they tell you right away when something goes wrong, such as a backup job failing or someone deleting backup data. Reports are the monthly statement: they show trends over weeks, such as which machines are protected, how many jobs succeeded, and how much backup storage you use. In Azure, alerts come through Azure Monitor, the platform's monitoring service. Reports come from backup history collected in a central log store. Configuring both means you hear about trouble today and can still spot slow problems over time.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your manager wants a chart showing backup success rates across ten vaults for the last three months. Where do you think the data for that chart has to live, and what would you have to set up before the chart can show anything?
lessons.teach:
Azure Backup stores protected data in a vault, a managed container for backup copies. A Recovery Services vault is the older type and a Backup vault is the newer type. Each vault records jobs, which are individual backup or restore runs, and the outcome of each one.

Alerts are notifications triggered by a condition. Azure Backup now raises built-in Azure Monitor alerts for important events. Job failure alerts fire when a backup or restore fails. Security alerts fire for risky actions such as stopping protection and deleting backup data. To get an email, text or webhook, route these alerts to an action group, which is a reusable list of who or what to notify. You can do that with an alert processing rule, which attaches actions to alerts or mutes them. You can also build metric alert rules on backup health metrics. The older classic backup alerts are being retired, so prefer the Azure Monitor ones.

Reports are dashboards built on historical data. Backup Reports in Backup center use Azure Monitor workbooks, which are interactive report pages, and they read from a Log Analytics workspace, a central store of log records you can query. Each vault sends its records only after you add a diagnostic setting, which is a per-resource export rule. The resource-specific table mode is the recommended choice for these settings.

Worked example. You have three vaults in two regions. Step 1: on each vault, add a diagnostic setting that sends the backup categories to one shared workspace. Step 2: wait, because data can take hours to arrive, often up to a day. Step 3: open Backup Reports and select that workspace. Step 4: read the tabs, which cover a summary, backup items, usage in storage, jobs, policies and optimisation hints such as items with no recent backups. Separately, a job fails at 02:00, the built-in alert fires and the action group emails the on-call engineer.

The common mistake is opening Backup Reports and seeing them empty because no diagnostic settings exist. Reports cannot show history that was never collected. The cost of that gap is an audit with no evidence and failures nobody noticed.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm, Ledgerline, protects 14 file shares in one Backup vault. The owner wants a text message whenever anyone deletes backup data. Here is the setup so far. Step 1: confirm that Azure Backup's built-in Azure Monitor security alerts are in use, because deleting backup data is a risky action that raises a security alert. Step 2: create an action group named LedgerlineOwnerSMS that sends a text to the owner's phone number. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: test it by deleting data from a disposable test item and checking that the owner's phone gets the text. Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Turn on classic backup alerts and add the owner's phone number to the vault's notification settings
Add a diagnostic setting on the vault so the deletion record reaches a Log Analytics workspace, and the text is sent from there
Open Backup Reports and pin the security alerts tab to the owner's dashboard
Create an alert processing rule that attaches the LedgerlineOwnerSMS action group to the vault's alerts
questions.why: An alert processing rule is what attaches an action group to the built-in alerts, so a fired security alert actually results in the text message.

questions.prompt: Harbor Logistics has five Recovery Services vaults. A new administrator opens Backup Reports, selects the company's Log Analytics workspace and sees no data at all, even though backup jobs have been running for months. No one ever changed any vault settings after the vaults were created. What is the most likely cause?
choices: None of the vaults has a diagnostic setting, so no backup records were ever sent to the workspace
The built-in job failure alerts are not routed to an action group
Backup Reports only show data for vaults in the same region as the workspace
Backup Reports only work with Backup vaults, not Recovery Services vaults
questions.why: Reports read history from a Log Analytics workspace, and a vault only sends its records there after you add a diagnostic setting, so history that was never collected cannot appear.

questions.prompt: At a hospital IT team, someone stops protection on a database server's backups late on a Friday. Which kind of built-in Azure Backup alert is meant for this event?
choices: A metric alert, which Azure Backup raises automatically for every vault
A security alert, because stopping protection is treated as a risky action
No alert, because stopping protection is an ordinary configuration change
A job failure alert, because the next scheduled backup will not run
questions.why: Built-in security alerts fire for risky actions such as stopping protection and deleting backup data, while job failure alerts are for backup or restore runs that fail.

questions.prompt: An engineer at Northwind Bakeries added diagnostic settings to two Backup vaults 20 minutes ago, all sending to the same Log Analytics workspace. Backup Reports still shows nothing for these vaults. What should the engineer do next?
choices: Switch the diagnostic settings away from resource-specific table mode, which delays reports
Wait, because data can take hours to arrive in the workspace, often up to a day
Delete and recreate the diagnostic settings, because they should show data within minutes
Create an alert processing rule, because reports stay empty until an action group is attached
questions.why: After a diagnostic setting is added, backup data can take hours, often up to a day, to reach the workspace, so empty reports after 20 minutes are expected.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between backup alerts and backup reports in Azure, what each one needs to be configured, and one limit of relying on reports alone.
lessons.modelAnswer: Alerts and reports answer different questions. Alerts say "something just went wrong." Azure Backup raises built-in Azure Monitor alerts for failed backup or restore jobs and for risky actions like deleting backup data. To actually be notified, you route those alerts to an action group, for example an email or webhook, usually through an alert processing rule. Reports answer "how have we been doing over time?" They show protected items, job success trends, storage usage and policy hints in Backup Reports, which are workbooks reading a Log Analytics workspace. For reports to work, every vault needs a diagnostic setting sending its backup data to that workspace, ideally in resource-specific mode. The limit is that reports lag by hours and only include data collected after the setting existed. That makes them useless for reacting to tonight's failure, which is why you need alerts too.
rubricPoints: Alerts give near-real-time notice of failures or risky actions, while reports show trends over time.
Notifications reach people through action groups, often attached with alert processing rules.
Backup Reports read from a Log Analytics workspace using Azure Monitor workbooks.
Each vault needs a diagnostic setting sending backup data to the workspace before reports show anything.
Report data is delayed and has no history from before collection began, so it cannot replace alerts.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing the right alert or report mechanism for a scenario, and no listed mission or planned engine has the learner configure backup monitoring, so reasoning through scenarios adds the most.

scenarios.title: Larkspur Logistics: Safe Access, Required Tags, and a Spending Warning
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined Larkspur Logistics, a fictional parcel-tracking company, as a junior Azure administrator. Larkspur keeps its user accounts in Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft's cloud identity directory: the central list of people and groups who can sign in, and what they belong to. Larkspur's Azure resources live in one subscription called Larkspur-Prod. A subscription is the billing and management container that every resource is charged to. Inside it is a resource group called rg-tracking. A resource group is a folder-like container that holds related resources, such as the tracking database and web app, so they can be managed together.

Your manager, Dana, gives you four requests on your first morning.

First, Priya, a contractor from a partner firm, needs to look at the settings of everything in rg-tracking so she can write a report. She must not change anything, and she must not see any other part of the subscription. Priya already has a work account at her own company and should not get a full Larkspur employee account.

Second, last week someone nearly deleted rg-tracking by mistake. Dana wants deletion of that resource group and its resources blocked, but the team must still be able to change settings and deploy updates there every day.

Third, the finance team says many resources have no CostCenter tag. A tag is a label made of a name and a value, for example CostCenter = 4410, attached to a resource so costs can be sorted and reported. Finance wants every new resource anywhere in Larkspur-Prod to be blocked from creation unless it carries a CostCenter tag.

Fourth, finance has a monthly limit of 2,000 US dollars for Larkspur-Prod. They want an email warning when actual spending for the month reaches 80 percent of that amount.

1. Explain how you would give Priya the access she needs. Name the type of Entra ID account you would use, the built-in Azure role, and the scope you would assign it at, and say why you would not use a broader role or scope.
2. Name the control you would use to stop deletion in rg-tracking while still allowing daily changes. State the exact type you would choose and why the other type would cause problems.
3. Name the Azure feature you would use to block new untagged resources, the effect it should use, and where you would assign it. Say what happens to existing resources that already lack the tag.
4. Describe what you would set up to warn finance at 80 percent of the 2,000 dollar monthly limit, and state one important thing this setup does not do.
modelAnswer: Invite Priya as a guest (external) user in Microsoft Entra ID. A guest user is an account in Larkspur's directory that points to an identity she already has elsewhere, so she signs in with her own company credentials and no full employee account is created. Then assign her the built-in Reader role. A role is a named set of permissions, and Reader lets someone view resources and their settings but not create, change, or delete anything. Assign it at the scope of the rg-tracking resource group. Scope is the level where a role assignment applies, and the assignment flows down to everything beneath that level. Contributor would be wrong because it lets her change and delete resources. Assigning at the subscription scope would be wrong because she would then see every resource group in Larkspur-Prod. This follows least privilege: give only the access needed, at the narrowest level that works.

Use a resource lock, which is a setting that overrides normal permissions to block certain actions. Apply a Delete lock, shown as CanNotDelete in some tools, on the rg-tracking resource group. The lock is inherited by every resource inside the group, so nobody can delete the group or its resources, even a user with the Owner role, until someone with the right permission removes the lock first. People can still read and change settings, so daily updates keep working. A ReadOnly lock would be the wrong choice because it blocks changes as well as deletion. Deployments and setting updates in rg-tracking would fail, and the team's normal work would stop.

Use Azure Policy, a service that checks resources against rules and can block or flag ones that break them. Assign a policy definition that requires a tag, here the built-in rule for requiring a tag on resources, with the tag name set to CostCenter. Use the Deny effect, so any attempt to create a resource without the tag is rejected. Assign the policy at the Larkspur-Prod subscription scope so it covers every resource group in that subscription. Existing resources that already lack the tag are not deleted or changed by a Deny policy. They are reported as non-compliant in the policy compliance view, so the team can find them and add the tag. A common mistake is assuming resources automatically copy tags from their resource group. They do not, unless a separate policy is set up to add the tag from the group.

Create a budget in Cost Management, Azure's tool for tracking and reporting spending, at the Larkspur-Prod subscription scope. Set the amount to 2,000 dollars, reset monthly. Add an alert condition based on actual cost at 80 percent, which works out to 1,600 dollars, and enter the finance team's email addresses as alert recipients. Optionally, link an action group, which is a reusable list of notification targets. The key limitation is that a budget only sends warnings. It does not stop resources or block spending, so costs can keep rising past 2,000 dollars unless someone acts on the alert.

scenarios.title: Larkspur Logistics: sharing, protecting, and ageing delivery records
scenarios.scenario:
Larkspur Logistics is a fictional regional courier company. It keeps scanned delivery receipts in Azure Blob Storage, Microsoft's service for storing unstructured files (called blobs) inside a storage account, which is the top-level Azure resource that holds your data and its settings. Inside the account, blobs are grouped into containers, which work like folders. You have just joined the cloud team, and your lead hands you four requests.

First, an outside auditing firm needs read-only access to the container named receipts for the next 14 days. Last year the team gave a partner a shared access signature, or SAS, which is a signed web address (URL) that grants specific permissions on storage for a limited time without sharing a password. That SAS was signed with the storage account's access key, one of two master passwords that give full control of the account. When the partnership ended early, the only way to cancel that link was to rotate (replace) the account key, and that broke every application using the old key. Your lead wants a way to cancel the auditor's access early without touching the account keys.

Second, Larkspur's compliance officer says the receipts must stay readable if one datacenter building in the region fails. They must also survive the loss of the whole Azure region, which is a geographic area containing several datacenters. During a regional outage, staff must still be able to read the receipts from the backup copy without waiting for anyone to switch the account over.

Third, receipts are read often in their first month, rarely for the next two months, and almost never after that. By law they must be kept for 7 years and then removed. Today all receipts sit in the Hot access tier, which is the storage price level with the highest storage cost and the lowest cost to read data. Your lead wants storage costs reduced automatically, with no manual work.

Fourth, last week a script overwrote 200 receipts with blank files. Another engineer once deleted an entire test container by mistake. Your lead wants both kinds of accident to be recoverable from now on.

Write your answers:
1. Explain how to give the auditors 14 days of read-only access in a way that can be cancelled early without rotating the account keys, and say why this works.
2. Name the redundancy option that meets the compliance officer's requirement, and explain why the closest alternatives fall short.
3. Describe the feature and the rules you would set up to cut storage costs and enforce the 7-year retention. Include one risk the team must understand about the coldest tier.
4. Name the features that make overwritten blobs and a deleted container recoverable, and say what each one protects.
modelAnswer:
Create a stored access policy on the receipts container. A stored access policy is a named set of rules saved on the container itself. Give it read and list permissions and an expiry time 14 days from now. Then issue a service SAS that refers to that policy by name, rather than writing the permissions and expiry inside the URL. A service SAS is a SAS limited to one storage service and signed with an account key.

This works because the storage service checks the policy every time someone uses the SAS. To cancel access early, you delete the policy or change its expiry to a time in the past. The auditor's link stops working straight away, and the account keys never change, so no other application breaks.

The common mistake is issuing an ad-hoc SAS, which is a SAS with permissions and expiry built into the URL itself. The only way to cancel an ad-hoc SAS is to rotate the key that signed it, and that is exactly what broke applications last time. A container can hold at most five stored access policies.

Choose read-access geo-zone-redundant storage (RA-GZRS). In the primary region it keeps three copies spread across availability zones, which are physically separate datacenter locations within one region. So the loss of one building does not take the data offline. It also copies the data, with a short delay, to a paired secondary region, so the data survives the loss of the whole region. The read-access part gives staff a separate read-only address for the secondary copy, which they can use during an outage without waiting for a failover. A failover is the process of switching the account so the secondary region becomes the main one.

Here is why the closest alternatives fall short. Zone-redundant storage (ZRS) protects against a zone failure but keeps no copy outside the region. Geo-redundant storage (GRS) keeps its three primary copies in a single datacenter, so it does not spread them across zones. Plain GZRS has the right copies but does not let you read the secondary until a failover happens. RA-GRS allows secondary reads but still lacks zone spreading in the primary region.

Use blob lifecycle management. This is a policy on the storage account containing rules that automatically move blobs to a cheaper tier, or delete them, based on age.

Set up a rule scoped to the receipts container, using days since each blob was last modified. Move blobs to the Cool tier after 30 days. Cool is cheaper to store but costs more to read. Move them to the Archive tier after 90 days. Archive is the cheapest tier to store but is offline. Delete blobs after about 2,555 days, which is 7 years. The policy runs on its own, roughly once a day, with no manual work.

The risk is that archived blobs cannot be read directly. They must first be rehydrated, meaning moved back to an online tier like Hot or Cool, and that can take hours. Auditors cannot get an archived receipt instantly.

The cooler tiers also have minimum storage periods. Deleting or moving a blob out early still incurs a charge: 30 days for Cool, 90 for Cold, and 180 for Archive.

Turn on blob versioning. Versioning automatically keeps the previous version of a blob every time it is overwritten or deleted. With it, the 200 blanked receipts could be restored by promoting their earlier versions back to current.

Also turn on blob soft delete. Soft delete keeps deleted blobs and deleted versions for a retention period you choose, from 1 to 365 days, so they can be undeleted during that window.

Finally, turn on container soft delete. This keeps an entire deleted container, and everything in it, restorable for its own retention period. It is a separate setting, so blob-level protection alone would not have saved the deleted test container.

A common mistake is assuming blob soft delete covers container deletion. It does not; container soft delete is a separate setting.

scenarios.title: Brightwell Supply: launching a safer, faster ordering site
scenarios.scenario:
Brightwell Supply is a fictional company that sells baking ingredients to small cafes. You have just joined as a junior cloud administrator. The customer ordering website runs on Azure App Service, which is a managed web hosting service: you upload your web app and Azure runs the servers for you. The site sits on an App Service plan, which is the set of compute resources (the size and number of virtual servers, called instances) that your web apps share. The plan is on the Standard tier, a pricing level that includes deployment slots and autoscale.

A nightly stock-counting job runs on a single Azure virtual machine (VM), which is a rented computer in Azure that you manage yourself. The VM is described in a Bicep file. Bicep is a short, readable language for describing Azure resources; Azure converts it into an Azure Resource Manager (ARM) template, the JSON format the Azure deployment service reads. The Bicep file contains a parameter (a value you can supply when you deploy, instead of editing the file) written as: param vmSize string = 'Standard_B2s'. A resource group is a named folder that holds related Azure resources; this VM lives in a resource group called rg-brightwell-batch.

Your manager lists four problems.

1. Last month a new website release had a bug, and the site was broken for 20 minutes while the old version was re-uploaded. Describe how to release new versions so customers see no downtime and a bad release can be undone in seconds.

2. Every Monday morning, cafes place their weekly orders and the site slows down. For the rest of the week it is quiet. Explain whether you should scale up or scale out the App Service plan, and describe the setting that handles the Monday spike without paying for extra capacity all week.

3. The stock-counting job now runs too slowly. You decide to change the VM size to Standard_D2s_v5. Using the Bicep file described above, explain how to make this change and deploy it to rg-brightwell-batch, and state one effect on the running VM.

4. The manager worries that if one Azure datacenter in the region fails, the nightly job stops. You plan to run a second copy of the VM. Explain how to place the two VMs so that a single datacenter failure does not stop both.
modelAnswer: Use deployment slots. A deployment slot is a separate live copy of the web app, with its own address, that runs on the same App Service plan. Create a slot named staging, deploy the new release to it, and test it at the staging address while customers keep using the production slot. When the release looks good, perform a swap: Azure warms up the staging copy and then exchanges the two slots, so the new version becomes production with no downtime. If a bug appears, swap again and the previous version is back in production within seconds, because the old version is still sitting in the other slot. The Standard tier already supports slots, so no tier change is needed. Common mistake: deploying straight to production, which is exactly what caused the 20-minute outage.

Scale out, not up. Scaling up means moving to a bigger, more powerful instance size (a higher pricing tier); scaling out means adding more instances of the same size so the load is shared. A short, predictable spike from many users is best handled by scaling out. Configure autoscale on the App Service plan. Autoscale is a setting that adds or removes instances automatically according to rules. For example, add one instance when average CPU is above 70 percent for 10 minutes, and remove one when it is below 30 percent, with a minimum of 1 and a maximum of, say, 4 instances. A schedule-based rule that raises the instance count on Monday mornings is also acceptable. Either way, extra instances exist only while they are needed. Common mistake: permanently scaling up to a large tier, which costs more all week and still limits you to one server.

Because the size is a parameter, you do not need to edit the resource definition. Either change the default to param vmSize string = 'Standard_D2s_v5', or leave the file alone and supply the new value when you deploy. Deploy to the resource group, for example with the Azure CLI: az deployment group create --resource-group rg-brightwell-batch --template-file main.bicep --parameters vmSize=Standard_D2s_v5. Azure compares the file with what already exists and updates only the VM size. Effect on the running system: changing a VM's size restarts the VM, so schedule the change outside the nightly job window. It is also worth confirming that the new size is available in the region first.

Deploy the two VMs into different availability zones. An availability zone is a physically separate datacenter, or group of datacenters, within one Azure region, with its own power, cooling, and networking. Put VM 1 in zone 1 and VM 2 in zone 2, for example by setting the zones property in the Bicep file or choosing the zone on the portal's VM creation page. If one datacenter fails, the VM in the other zone keeps running. The zone must be chosen when the VM is created, so the existing VM cannot simply be switched to a zone by changing a setting. An availability set, which spreads VMs across separate racks inside a single datacenter, protects against rack-level hardware failure but not against losing a whole datacenter, so zones are the correct choice for this requirement.

scenarios.title: Connecting and Securing the Web Tier at Harborline Logistics
scenarios.scenario:
Harborline Logistics, a fictional shipping company, is moving its order-tracking app into Azure. You are the new junior administrator. Here are a few terms first.

A virtual network (VNet) is a private network you create in Azure. Its machines talk to each other using private IP addresses. A subnet is a smaller address range carved out of a VNet. A virtual machine (VM) is a server that runs in Azure. A network security group (NSG) is a list of allow and deny rules for network traffic. You can attach an NSG to a subnet, to a VM's network interface (NIC, the VM's network card), or to both. Each NSG rule has a priority number. Lower numbers are checked first, and the first rule that matches decides the outcome. Every NSG also contains built-in default rules at very high numbers. For inbound traffic these allow traffic from inside the virtual network, allow traffic from the Azure load balancer, and then deny everything else at priority 65500.

The current setup looks like this. VNet vnet-app (10.1.0.0/16) has a subnet named web (10.1.1.0/24) holding two VMs, web1 and web2. A separate VNet, vnet-data (10.2.0.0/16), holds a database VM at 10.2.1.4. The two VNets are not connected. A third VNet, vnet-reports, is being connected only to vnet-data.

The web subnet has an NSG named nsg-websubnet with two custom inbound rules. Priority 100 allows TCP port 443 (HTTPS, encrypted web traffic) from any source. Priority 200 denies TCP port 3389 (RDP, Remote Desktop) from any source. For testing, web1 also has a public IP address, which is an address reachable from the internet. Its NIC has its own NSG, nsg-web1, with one custom inbound rule: priority 150 allows TCP 3389 from the Internet. When traffic comes in, Azure checks the subnet's NSG first and then the NIC's NSG. The traffic gets through only if both allow it.

Your manager wants four things.

1. The web VMs must reach the database VM using private IPs, without the traffic crossing the public internet. Name the control that does this. Also say whether vnet-reports will be able to reach vnet-app once it is connected only to vnet-data.

2. Before anything changes, a colleague asks two questions. Can someone on the internet open an RDP session to web1's public IP? Can someone on the internet reach web1 on HTTPS (port 443)? Explain the result for each, rule by rule.

3. Security wants admins to stop using public RDP. Admins should reach the VMs with no public IPs on them at all. Azure Bastion is a managed service that lets admins open RDP or SSH (a remote command-line login) sessions to VMs through a web browser over port 443. It requires its own dedicated subnet, which must have the exact name AzureBastionSubnet. Describe what to set up and what to remove.

4. The app should be reachable by staff only from inside the company network, spread across web1 and web2. A load balancer is a service that shares incoming traffic among a group of VMs called the backend pool. A public load balancer has an internet-facing address. An internal load balancer has only a private address. A health probe is a regular check the load balancer sends to each VM; if a VM fails the check, it is marked unhealthy. Someone builds an internal load balancer with frontend IP 10.1.1.10, backend pool web1 and web2, and an HTTP probe on port 80 at the page /health. Afterwards, users only ever get responses from web1. Web2's /health page currently returns an error. Explain why this happens, and name one common setup mistake that would make both VMs look unhealthy.
subParts: Connect the app and data VNets
Evaluate NSG rules for RDP and HTTPS
Replace public RDP with Azure Bastion
modelAnswer: Use virtual network peering between vnet-app and vnet-data. Peering is a direct link between two VNets. Once it is in place, VMs in each VNet can reach each other by private IP, and the traffic stays on Microsoft's own network instead of the public internet. Peering is set up as a link in each direction, so the connection must exist from both sides before traffic flows. vnet-reports will NOT be able to reach vnet-app. Peering is non-transitive, which means a peering only connects the two VNets named in it. A third VNet peered to just one of them gets no route through to the other. To let vnet-reports reach vnet-app, you would need a separate peering between those two VNets (or other routing, which is beyond this scenario). The common mistake is assuming that A to B plus B to C gives A to C.

RDP is blocked. Inbound traffic is checked against the subnet NSG first. In nsg-websubnet, priority 100 (port 443) does not match RDP. Priority 200 (deny TCP 3389 from any) does match, so the traffic is dropped right there. The allow rule at priority 150 in nsg-web1 never gets a chance, because traffic must be allowed by both NSGs. HTTPS is also blocked, which surprises many beginners. In the subnet NSG, priority 100 allows 443, so the traffic moves on to the NIC NSG. nsg-web1 has no custom rule that allows 443. The default rules allow only traffic from inside the virtual network and from the Azure load balancer, so internet traffic falls through to the default deny-all rule at 65500. Result: neither works. To allow HTTPS from the internet, nsg-web1 would also need an allow rule for 443. The general lesson is that an allow in one NSG is never enough when a second NSG sits in the path.

Create a subnet in vnet-app named exactly AzureBastionSubnet. Bastion will not deploy into a subnet with any other name, and nothing else should be placed in that subnet. Deploy Azure Bastion into that subnet. Bastion uses its own public IP, so admins connect to Bastion through the browser over HTTPS on port 443. Bastion then opens the RDP or SSH session to the VM over the VM's private IP. Next, remove the public IP from web1 and delete the priority 150 rule that allows RDP from the Internet in nsg-web1. After this, port 3389 is never exposed to the internet, which shrinks the attack surface. Admins still get remote access through Bastion. The common mistake is setting up Bastion but leaving the VM's public IP and the open RDP rule in place, which keeps the old exposure alive.

An internal load balancer is the right choice here. Its frontend, 10.1.1.10, is a private address, so only clients that can reach the virtual network privately can use it, and nothing is exposed to the internet. Users only see web1 because the health probe sends HTTP requests to /health on port 80 on each VM. Web2's page returns an error, so the probe marks web2 unhealthy, and the load balancer stops sending new connections to it. Every new request goes to web1, the only healthy VM. This is the probe working as designed, not a fault in the load balancer. The fix is to repair web2's /health page or app, or to correct the probe if it points at the wrong port or path. Once web2 passes again, it rejoins the rotation. One common mistake that makes both VMs look unhealthy is an NSG rule that blocks the probe traffic, for example a custom deny-all inbound rule placed at a lower priority number than the default rule that allows the Azure load balancer. The probes then fail on every VM, both are marked unhealthy, and the app stops responding through the load balancer even though the VMs themselves are running.

scenarios.title: Keeping Harborline Logistics' Order Server Watched and Recoverable
scenarios.scenario:
Harborline Logistics is a small fictional shipping company. Its order website runs on one Azure virtual machine (a VM, which is a computer that Azure runs for you in its data centre) named vm-orders, in the East US region. A region is a geographic area where Azure has data centres. The website reads from a database VM named vm-db, which sits in a different subnet (a subnet is a smaller address range inside a virtual network, which is a private network you build in Azure). You have just joined the operations team, and your lead gives you four tasks.

First, vm-orders has slowed down several times when its processor was overloaded. Azure Monitor (Azure's built-in service for collecting and acting on data about your resources) already records a metric called Percentage CPU. A metric is a number sampled at regular intervals, such as CPU use every minute. Your lead wants the on-call engineer to get an email and a text message whenever average CPU stays above 85 percent for 10 minutes. The team also patches the server every Saturday from 01:00 to 03:00, and nobody should be paged during that window, when high CPU is expected.

Second, after a firewall change this morning, vm-orders can no longer reach vm-db on TCP port 1433, the port the database listens on. Your lead wants to know which network rule is blocking the traffic. After the fix, the team also wants ongoing, automatic checks of that connection, with a record of how reachable it was and how long replies took over time.

Third, there is no backup yet. Your lead wants vm-db backed up once every night at 23:00, with each nightly copy kept for 30 days. Last week a developer also deleted a single configuration file on vm-db. Your lead wants to know how that one file could be brought back without replacing the whole VM.

Fourth, management is worried about a full outage of the East US region. They want vm-orders to be able to come back up in West US 2 with very little data lost. They also want proof that this works before a real disaster happens, without disturbing the live website.

1. Name the three Azure Monitor pieces you would configure for the CPU notifications and the Saturday quiet period, and say what each one does.
2. Name the tool you would use to find the blocking rule, and the tool you would use for ongoing checks of the vm-orders to vm-db connection.
3. Name the storage container for the backups and the setting that controls the nightly schedule and the 30-day keep period. Then explain how to recover the single deleted file.
4. Name the service that keeps a copy of vm-orders running in West US 2, and explain how to prove that the recovery works without touching production, and what to do in a real outage.
subParts: Diagnosing and continuously monitoring the database connection
Nightly VM backup and single-file restore
Cross-region disaster recovery and safe testing
modelAnswer: Create a metric alert rule on vm-orders. An alert rule is a condition that Azure Monitor checks on a schedule. Here the signal is Percentage CPU, the aggregation is Average, the threshold is greater than 85, and the time window (lookback period) is 10 minutes. When the condition is met, the rule fires an alert. Attach an action group to the rule. An action group is a reusable list of who to notify and how. In this case it holds the on-call engineer's email address and SMS phone number. Finally, create an alert processing rule. This is a rule that changes what happens to alerts after they fire. Give it a recurring schedule of every Saturday from 01:00 to 03:00, scope it to vm-orders (or its resource group), and set it to suppress notifications. Alerts are still recorded during that window, but the action group is not called, so no one is paged. A common mistake is to disable the alert rule for the weekend and forget to turn it back on. The server is then unwatched until someone notices.

Use Azure Network Watcher, which is Azure's set of network diagnostic tools for a region. Its IP flow verify feature tests whether a packet with a given source, destination, port and protocol (here vm-orders to vm-db, TCP 1433) would be allowed or denied. It also names the exact network security group rule that made the decision. A network security group is a list of allow and deny rules that filters traffic to subnets or network interfaces. Connection troubleshoot is also acceptable, because it tests the path between the two VMs and reports where traffic is blocked. For ongoing checks, use Connection Monitor, a Network Watcher feature. It runs repeated tests from a source to a destination on a chosen port and records whether each test succeeded (reachability) and the round-trip time (latency) over time. You can view trends and alert on failures. A common mistake is to rely on a one-time test only. A later rule change could break the connection again and nobody would know until users complained.

Create a Recovery Services vault. A vault is a storage container in Azure that holds backup copies and the settings for them, and the Recovery Services vault is the type used for Azure VM backups. It should be in the same region as vm-db. Then create a backup policy for Azure VMs. A backup policy is the set of rules that decides when backups run and how long copies are kept (retention). Set it to a daily schedule at 23:00 with daily retention of 30 days, and enable backup for vm-db using that policy. To get back the single deleted file, use file recovery (item-level restore) from a chosen recovery point. A recovery point is one saved backup copy from a specific time. Choose a recovery point from before the deletion. Azure then provides a script that temporarily mounts that backup's disks as drives on a machine. You copy the file back, then unmount the drives. A common mistake is to restore or replace the entire VM just to get one file. This causes needless downtime and overwrites any changes made since that backup.

Use Azure Site Recovery, a disaster-recovery service that continuously copies (replicates) a VM's disks from one region to another. Enable replication for vm-orders with East US as the source and West US 2 as the target. This is managed through a Recovery Services vault in the target region. Site Recovery keeps creating recovery points, so very little recent data would be lost if East US failed. To prove the setup works safely, run a test failover. This starts a copy of vm-orders in West US 2 from a recovery point, attached to an isolated, non-production virtual network. Production keeps running and is not affected. After checking that the copy works, run a cleanup of the test failover to delete the test VM. In a real East US outage, run a failover to West US 2. This makes the replica the live server. Then commit the failover, and later re-protect it (reverse replication) so you can fail back once East US recovers. A common mistake is to run the test failover into the production virtual network. This can cause address conflicts or let a duplicate server handle real traffic.
